comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Proposal: close out the three post-ruling residuals (August 2026)

The 2026-07-15 ruling settled topology (no consolidation; AAuth kept; approval-revision standalone). Three content-level residuals remain on this tracker. Proposed rulings and execution plan, each grounded in the current drafts at main:

### A. S8 residual — thin administrative metadata to `owner` + `tenant`, and fix the scope circularity

**Evidence.** `{#admin-metadata}` (management.md:324) defines six MAY-members. Two are load-bearing: `owner` is consumed by approval routing (management.md:414) and carries the accountability distinction from `subject`/`approver`; `tenant` is the one boundary the filter-scope text itself names ("a tenant-wide incident responder", `{#filter-scope}`). The other four have no interoperable semantics anywhere in the document set: `risk_class` and `labels` are explicitly deployment-defined opaque taxonomy, `retention` duplicates what the audit-horizon machinery already governs normatively, and `admin_domain` is a second tenant-shaped boundary with no distinct rule behind it.

**The circularity, precisely.** Filter scopes are granted over filter members; administrative metadata "drives" filter scope; and the metadata is mutable by callers whose scope covers the Mission. Whoever can write `tenant` can therefore move a Mission across the very boundaries that authorize visibility — including granting scope to themselves or escaping the scope that authorized the write. The existing audited-event requirement records this; it does not prevent it.

**Proposed ruling.** Thin the object to `owner` and `tenant` (deployments remain free to keep arbitrary private metadata; the spec stops naming members it cannot give semantics). Add one rule: a change to a scope-affecting member is a management operation that MUST be authorized under both the pre-change and the post-change filter scope (or by a grant explicitly spanning both), and MUST NOT be performable under a scope the change itself would create. Nothing interoperable is lost; the mutable surface feeding the circularity shrinks to the two members that earn it.

### B. S5 residual — ratify the runtime pilot, delegate execution to #238

The July recommendation (pilot the ~350 non-wire-MUST recategorization on the runtime profile, riding #238's core-vs-assurance-extension framing) has gotten materially cheaper since: the August restructuring (#462 → #489) gave runtime an abstract decision output, three canonical projections, and a clean conditions/obligations split — the wire-versus-internal seam the recategorization needs now exists as document structure rather than a category exercise. **Proposed ruling:** ratify the pilot option here; execution rides #238 in the coordinated tier; no text changes under this issue.

### C. S6 content-level thins — two yeses, one retirement

- **Mandate → trim to the steps-1–8 JWS: yes.** Keeps the load-bearing artifact, drops the speculative depth.
- **Audit deep end → scoped to the SCITT upgrade path: yes.** Sequences naturally with #282 (one committed-evidence envelope), which the August triage flagged as needing to precede further evidence surfaces.
- **Discovery → thinned to its two floors and folded into the Security Model: formally retire.** Overtaken by a ratified decision: PR #453 made discovery a two-mode profile (ceiling + contextual adjudication) precisely so the floors bind both modes. Thinning it now would contradict that design.
- Metering promotion (`max_budget`/`max_calls`) stays tracked at #251 — no action here.

### Execution plan on approval

1. One small PR ("wave-3 residual cuts"): management.md item A (member removals + circularity rule + example/filter-scope touch-ups), mandate.md trim, audit.md SCITT scoping. Validated per house process (render, lint, manifest checker).
2. Record the S5 ruling here and carry it as an execution note on #238.
3. Close this tracker; the surviving threads live in #238 (S5), #251 (metering), and #302 (the stack rank).

Approve as-is, or override any individual call — A's thin-vs-park, B's pilot-vs-full-pass-vs-decline, and each C item are independently decidable.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Amended proposal (supersedes the previous comment's rulings where they differ)

External review of the proposal surfaced factual errors in its evidence and better execution boundaries. All six amendments verified against main and accepted; corrections first, then the revised ruling set.

**Corrections to the earlier evidence.** `owner`, `admin_domain`, `tenant`, and `label` are wire filter members with standardized matching semantics (`{#filter}`); management.md:414 is the `owner` filter member, not approval routing; and `retention` selects a policy rather than duplicating the audit horizon. So thinning is a **breaking filter-surface reduction adopted on minimality grounds** — the members' vocabularies are deployment-defined but their matching is interoperable — not a free cut. Disclosed as such.

### A (amended): thin to `owner` + `tenant`; immutable by default; fix the enumeration contradiction
- Remove `admin_domain`, `risk_class`, `labels`, `retention` from administrative metadata AND the corresponding `admin_domain`/`label` filter members, disclosed as a filter-surface reduction.
- Circularity fix, corrected: dual pre/post scope is necessary but NOT sufficient — a responder whose scope spans tenants A and B may revoke in both without being authorized to re-home between them. MVP rule: **`owner` and `tenant` are fixed at metadata creation**; changing either requires an explicit reclassification/re-home authority distinct from enumeration and lifecycle grants; where a deployment supports such changes: pre- AND post-change scope, an authorization grant independent of the proposed new values, atomic compare-and-set, and an audit record carrying both old and new values. (The metadata-update protocol remains deferred; this closes the latent gap without standardizing the operation.)
- Fix the contradiction: management.md:365 says summaries MAY include administrative metadata while the summary definition's fixed member list forbids it — remove the MAY sentence; `owner`/`tenant` stay issuer-side and filterable; no new response projection in this pass.

### B (amended): post-#238 normative audit, not a demotion pass and not inside #238
#238 is relocation-only by its own text and cannot carry a semantic conformance change. Revised ruling: (1) #238's coordinated relocation proceeds first with #242/#287/#252; (2) a SEPARATE normative-delta PR follows, with the keep-criterion "retain any requirement affecting interoperability, authorization outcomes, security invariants, or a claimed assurance property" (wire-visibility is not the axis: atomicity, fail-closed processing, authorization intersection, state verification, and replay protection stay normative with no wire field); (3) it ships with a before/after requirement ledger and negative tests. Count refreshed: 293 MUSTs across runtime/authzen/runtime-evidence (300 with capability-binding), not ~350.

### C Mandate (amended): approve pending an exact keep/cut ledger
The trim removes step 9's mandatory SCITT existence proof — the only defense against a compromised issuer key minting and backdating a Mandate — so the ledger is a precondition, not paperwork:
- **Keep**: the plain JWS artifact and claims, verification steps 1-8, state freshness, the failure taxonomy, evidence-not-credential.
- **Cut**: step 9 as a MUST, and the issuer conformance requirement to register high-consequence Mandates; SCITT registration becomes an optional audit upgrade.
- **State the residual explicitly**: a signature-only Mandate cannot prove it existed before issuer-key compromise.
- **Decide before executing**: whether SD-JWT/selective disclosure and vertical derivation survive the trim — "JWS" alone is ambiguous.

### C Audit (amended): defer to post-#282
Already an optional SCITT-only extension at main (Status section; the registration mechanism profiles SCITT directly), so "scope to the SCITT path" is a no-op today. The real end state — audit as the mapping from the common Mission Evidence envelope (#282) into SCITT Signed Statements and Receipts — requires #282 first. Removed from the wave-3 execution; sequencing to be recorded on #282.

### Unchanged rulings
Discovery thin: retired (contradicts the ratified two-mode design, PR #453). Metering promotion: stays at #251. S5 pilot framing: replaced by B above.

### Execution plan (amended): separate PRs, security-sensitive reductions reviewed independently
1. **PR 1 — management.md only**: A in full (member + filter removals, immutability/re-home rule, contradiction fix).
2. **PR 2 — mandate.md only**: the C trim, opened only after the keep/cut ledger and the SD-JWT/derivation decision are recorded here.
3. **#282 comment**: the audit re-mapping sequencing.
4. **#238 comment**: the post-relocation normative-audit plan and keep-criterion.
5. Close this tracker when 1-4 are done; surviving threads: #238 (S5 successor), #251, #282, #302.

## Mandate trim: keep/cut ledger (precondition for PR 2, per the amended ruling)

**Keep (everything with interop or security semantics):**
- The plain JWS artifact, JOSE header, Mandate claims, State at Issuance, Minting, worked example.
- Verification steps 1-8, the failure taxonomy, and the evidence-not-credential rule.
- **Selective Disclosure (SD-JWT)**: kept. RFC 9901 is a ratified dependency by the draft's own dependency statement, the section is self-contained, and holder-side subsetting of `authority_set` is a real privacy capability with interoperable semantics. The S6 thin targeted the registration deep end, not this.
- **Vertical Derivation**: kept. The subsection is informative use-case around one normative, load-bearing rule — a rail MUST NOT derive authority on possession of a Mandate alone and MUST independently authenticate the presenter — which is the mandate-as-credential misuse defense. Cutting it removes a security rule, not depth.
- Cross-domain verification, Mission Evidence section (reframed, below), Security and Privacy Considerations.

**Cut:**
- **Verification step 9** (mandatory SCITT existence-proof Receipt before high-consequence reliance): verification becomes steps 1-8; registration-backed existence checking moves to an optional hardening under the audit profile.
- **The issuer conformance MUST to register high-consequence Mandates**: becomes SHOULD, conditional on the deployment running the audit transparency profile.

**Residual, stated explicitly in Issuer Key Compromise:** a signature-only Mandate cannot prove it existed before an issuer-key compromise; a key-holding attacker can mint a backdated Mandate that verifies exactly as a genuine one. Audit registration, where deployed, remains the bound (independent timestamped existence for genuine Mandates; unregistered-or-attributable trace for forged ones), and the compromise-time guidance (treat unanchored `iat` under a compromised `kid` as unverifiable) stays.

Executing as PR 2 (mandate.md only) per the amended plan.

issues.title: Name swarm execution: class-grain authorization, instance-grain attribution
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The family already contains every mechanism a homogeneous agent swarm needs, but never names the pattern, and the delegation documents can read as if multi-instance execution must route through delegation machinery:

- The core's OPTIONAL `controls.agent_deployment` pins the Mission to an Agent Deployment, whose `client_id` is the OAuth projection of the class.
- The instance substrate (Client Instance Assertion, AI Agent Instance Profile) gives each running instance attested identity beneath the shared `client_id`, and the runtime profile already forbids a sender-constraint key shared across a client's instances, so attribution stays per-instance.
- `max_derivations` (with its atomic check-and-increment) is a natural fan-out ceiling, and consumption bounds attach at Mission grain, so a swarm shares one budget.
- The containment story keeps the kills separable: instance credentials, the Deployment (registry, fail-closed), or the Mission itself.

What is missing is the sentence that ties these together: many attested instances of one pinned Deployment executing one Mission is **multiplication, not delegation**. No `act` hop, no Child Mission, no attenuation chain. Late binding is attestation. The invariant is that the class is an authorization subject, never an attribution subject.

This also sharpens the answer to the group-authorization gap in draft-chen-oauth-agent-authz-use-cases: one grant, late-bound members, atomic lifecycle, per-member attribution, all without a shared identity, for the homogeneous case. The deliberately-undefined remainder narrows to per-member differentiated bindings inside one grant, which the family answers with Child Missions instead.

## Proposal

Naming and boundaries only, no new mechanism:

1. **Architecture**: beside the three objects, name swarm execution (a Mission pinned to an Agent Deployment, executed concurrently by N attested instances) and state the decision ladder: same principal and same authority is the swarm, a different principal acting inline is a delegated token with an `act` hop, a durable sub-agent is a Child Mission, offline narrowing is attenuation.
2. **Child Delegation**: extend the existing when-to-use guidance (inline delegated token vs parked Child Mission) with the zeroth branch: same-principal multiplication needs neither.
3. **Core**: one clarifying sentence on `controls.agent_deployment`: under a class pin, every attested instance of the pinned Deployment may derive, and `max_derivations` is the explicit fan-out ceiling (the atomic check already exists for exactly this concurrency).
4. **Security Model**: a swarm blast-radius consideration: the three kills stay separable (instance, Deployment, Mission), and evidence distinguishes instances, which the per-instance key requirement already forces.

## Non-goals

No group-native grant carrying per-member subject-audience-scope bindings: differentiated members remain Child Missions with lineage, and a shared undifferentiated grant identity remains refused.

issues.title: Name the context asymmetry and sequence-aware evaluation: the undertaking's history as a decision input
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The family states that the resource owns its operation and constraint semantics (the ontology direction, consolidation tracked in #280) but never states the dual with equal force: the Mission owns the why and where the undertaking stands, and that context exists nowhere else in the stack. A resource evaluates each request at perfect local resolution and zero task resolution.

The sharpest consequence is sequence-aware risk. "Delete database" in isolation is indistinguishable from catastrophe. "Delete database, inside an approved migration whose copy steps already completed" is a priced, checkable step. The only place that judgment is possible is the layer where Decision and Execution Evidence join on the Mission's identity. Deployments can already build this, because a PDP can consult its own evidence store, but the pattern is unnamed, has no stated guardrails, and is therefore not interoperable or claimable.

## Proposal

Naming and guardrails, no new wire object:

1. **Architecture**: state the asymmetry as the dual of the ontology contract, in or beside the same section. The resource owns what an action means. The Mission owns why it is happening and where the undertaking stands. A risk decision composes both: semantics without purpose prices every delete the same, and purpose without semantics cannot read the call.
2. **Runtime profile**: add an OPTIONAL Decision Input, the undertaking's recorded history. Policy MAY evaluate predicates over the Mission's prior decision and execution records (for example, a precondition that a named action class completed) as deployment-local context keyed on the Mission's identity. Guardrails: history is a decision input and never a grant, evaluation MUST fail closed when required history is unavailable or the store cannot be consulted, and the input follows the same freshness discipline as Mission state. Cross-PDP history composes through the deployment's evidence store or registered transparency records and is otherwise out of scope.
3. **AuthZEN binding**: say how the decision context carries a history predicate or its result, consistent with the binding's existing context conventions, so two implementations mean the same thing by "the copy steps completed."
4. **Security considerations**: the history input is attacker-adjacent where evidence producers are compromised, which is the existing evidence-integrity story, and it must never launder Shaping Evidence into authorization (the existing prohibition stands).

## Relationship to existing text

The runtime profile's Decision Inputs section is the natural home for item 2. The shaping profile's rule that Shaping Evidence is never a permit input is unchanged and is the model for the guardrail language. This proposal names what a conforming deployment may already do, so the reference security architecture's dependency claims are unaffected.

## Non-goals

No semantic intent inference at enforcement time (advisory only, unchanged), no new evidence object, no requirement that any deployment maintain queryable history.

issues.title: Informative derivation-policy guidance: the artifact, its contract, and a worked rule
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

Derivation policy is the first artifact every deployment must author and the least specified thing in the family. The core fixes the contract (derivation is mechanical, happens once at the approval event, over the policy and capability catalog in force) and the modes (narrowing and template), but no document shows what the policy is as an artifact: no worked rule, no testing discipline, no authoring workflow, no ownership split. Reviewers consistently land on this as the gap between the architecture and a staffable plan, and the analogy the family offers (the same onboarding work scope design was) names the workload without shaping it.

## Proposal

Informative guidance only, no policy language standardized, most naturally an appendix to the core or a section in the shaping profile:

1. **The contract, stated once**: a derivation policy is a function from a validated Mission Intent and registry facts (eligibility bounds, risk tier, deployment pin) to an Authority Set, deterministic, no model in the loop, no discretion at decision time.
2. **One or two worked rules** in a language-neutral shape: match conditions over validated Intent fields, registry facts consulted, entries emitted with their constraints and notice classes, and what the rule never emits.
3. **The testing discipline**: fixture Intents with expected Authority Sets, run per policy change, diff-reviewed, with `policy_version` as the record's pointer to the version that derived each Mission.
4. **Ownership**: the issuer's operator owns the function and ceilings, resource owners own the entries touching their services (consistent with the ontology-contract division in #280).
5. **The economics, honestly**: the authoring surface is bounded by resources and action classes rather than integrations, amortized across Missions, with templates carrying the common cases, and the three health signals a deployment should watch (unmapped-resource rate, template-hit rate, rule-exception rate).

## Non-goals

No normative policy language, no new endpoint or artifact, no conformance class for policies.

issues.title: Operational availability considerations: state distribution, staleness bounds, and outage semantics
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The family makes fail-closed enforcement a tier-0 dependency on Mission state freshness, and deployments will put business-critical unattended work (CI, scheduled jobs, RPA) on that path. The availability story is currently distributed across one-line statements (bounded caching, never fail-open; the permit-as-lease model; the break-glass path) without an operational-considerations treatment relating the pieces. The first questions an architecture review board asks (what happens when the Issuer is down, for how long can it be down, what exactly halts) have answers implied by the design but stated nowhere together.

## Proposal

An operational/availability considerations section, most naturally in the runtime profile with a pointer from Status and the Security Model:

1. **Availability follows the artifact, not the issuer**: Mission state distributes as signed, TTL-bounded artifacts (Status responses, the Mission Status List), cacheable and replica-servable like key material, so control-plane unavailability within the bound degrades nothing on the data plane.
2. **The staleness bound is also the ride-through**: guidance to choose published bounds with the Issuer's recovery objective in view, since a bound shorter than recovery time is a designed halt.
3. **Blast-radius semantics stated once**: an outage past the bound halts PDP-gated classes and only them, issuance-gated paths ride to token expiry, ungated paths are unaffected, and new issuance stops.
4. **Break-glass claim semantics** consolidated with the above: dual control, auto-expiry, same evidence as the bypassed path, enforcement claim suspended for what it touches while active.
5. **Replication guidance** for the Mission record and status surfaces (small state, read-mostly, verifiable artifacts), explicitly not a consensus-protocol mandate.

## Non-goals

No SLO numbers standardized, no new wire surfaces, no high-availability architecture mandated. This names the design space and the semantics so deployments can state their posture in the enforcement-scope statement.

issues.title: Core: state the boundary between free-text Intent constraints and machine-enforceable bounds in derivation
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The core defines the Intent's `constraints` as free-text strings that "inform derivation and consent rendering," and separately defines derivation as mechanical: a deterministic function over the validated Intent and registry facts, with no model in the loop. An external review of the handbook caught the gap between those two sentences: a mechanical function cannot parse "Q3 2026, audit-committee" out of a free-text array, so either the free-text constraints bind at disclosure only, or derivation is quietly interpretive. The phrase "inform derivation" leaves the trust boundary unstated, and the whole safety story leans on it.

## Proposal

One or two clarifying sentences in the Intent member definitions and/or {{authorization-derivation}}, no new members and no new mechanism:

1. Derivation consumes the Intent's structured members only: `resources`, `controls`, and `proposed_authority` entries with their machine-actionable constraints, evaluated against the deployment's derivation-policy rules and registry facts.
2. The Intent's free-text `constraints` are disclosure and bounding context. They are what the Approver reads beside the derived authority and what a human rule author reads when writing the rule. They are never parsed for machine semantics.
3. A bound the PDP must enforce therefore enters as structure at one of two doors: an untrusted `proposed_authority` entry (the shaper may translate the request's words into a structured candidate; the AS only ever narrows it), or the derivation-policy rule itself. The Approver's disclosure review is the check that the structure matches the words.

## Non-goals

No NLP or extraction step in the trusted path, no new Intent members, no constraint grammar. Relates to #309 (the informative derivation-policy guidance should restate the same boundary in its contract statement).

## Where it bites

Without the boundary stated, an implementer can read "inform derivation" as license to parse free text inside the AS, which puts attacker-influenceable natural language on the trusted side of the admission boundary, the exact move the model exists to reject.

## Analysis and recommendation (2026-08-12)

**Analysis**

Line references are `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md` on current main.

- The gap is one sentence wide. `constraints` (L771-774, {{mission-intent}}): "An array of strings. Human-readable bounds on the task ... These inform derivation and consent rendering." That is the only occurrence of "inform derivation" in the draft (L774). `controls` (L806-807) is defined as "an object of machine-actionable bounds", so the free-text/structured split already exists at the member level; only the `constraints` sentence blurs it.
- Derivation is already stated mechanical with exactly two modes (L1066-1072): narrowing mode over the submitted `authorization_details` proposal and template mode, "a deployment-configured mapping, keyed on the Intent's `purpose` or `resources` ... The mapping is a lookup, never synthesis" (L1083-1090). Neither mode names `constraints` as an input, and generative derivation "from the Intent's free text or with model assistance, is not one of this profile's modes" (L1103-1108, local-policy extension carve-out).
- Half the boundary is also already stated: "The Intent's `goal`, `constraints`, and other members describe and bound the task but grant no authority by themselves ... they constrain what the AS MAY derive, never widen it" (L1122-1127). What is missing is the affirmative half: how a free-text string can "constrain" a mechanical function at all. The answer is via humans (Approver at consent, rule author at template authoring), never via machine parsing, and the draft never says so.
- Disclosure and commitment are in place: the Approver consents to the derived Authority Set with `goal`, `constraints`, `expires_at`, and `controls` rendered as context (L1702-1710); client strings including `constraints` MUST render as inert text (L1747-1751); `intent_hash` commits the approved Intent, separate from `authority_hash` (L748-750, L1815-1819; PLAN.md D57, domain separation task/authority/provenance). So free-text `constraints` already bind at disclosure and are tamper-evident; nothing yet forbids the AS parsing them for semantics.
- Post-D67 (PLAN.md L152) the proposal's structured door moved: `mission_intent` is task-only (`proposed_authority` refused under the closed top level, L976-981) and the proposal rides top-level `authorization_details` (L946-951), untrusted, proposal-never-authority (L960-965, L983-987), with Common Constraints (L1360-1368) as the shared machine-enforceable vocabulary and fail-closed narrowing per D56 (never silent-drop-widen). The issue's Proposal item 1 and item 3 still name `proposed_authority` as an Intent member; the substance holds, the carriage is stale.

**Recommendation**

Adopt the issue's boundary with the D67 carriage correction. Free-text `constraints` are Approver-disclosure and rule-author context committed by `intent_hash`; the AS MUST NOT parse them, or any free-text Intent member, for machine semantics or alter the derived Authority Set based on their content. A bound the deployment enforces enters as structure at one of two doors: a `constraints` member (Common Constraint or deployment-defined) in the top-level `authorization_details` proposal, or the Intent's `controls` and the template-mode mapping keyed on `purpose`/`resources` (a lookup on member values, never interpretation of prose). The Approver's review of the rendered Authority Set beside the free-text strings is the check that structure matches words; the generative local-policy carve-out at L1103-1108 stays as is, explicitly outside the profile's modes.

**Solution sketch**

Two edit sites, two or three sentences total, no new members or mechanism:

1. `constraints` member (L771-774): replace "These inform derivation and consent rendering." with rule text shaped as: "They are disclosure and bounding context: the Approver reads them beside the derived Authority Set ({{approval-event}}), and a deployment's rule author reads them when configuring a template-mode mapping ({{authorization-derivation}}). The AS MUST NOT parse them for machine semantics; a machine-enforceable bound enters as structure ({{authorization-derivation}})."
2. {{authorization-derivation}}, after the L1122-1127 paragraph: "Derivation consumes structured inputs only: the `authorization_details` proposal with its `constraints` members ({{common-constraints}}), and the Intent's `resources`, `purpose`, and `controls`. Free-text members (`goal`, `constraints`, `success_criteria`) are never parsed for machine semantics; the Approver's review of the rendered Authority Set beside them ({{approval-event}}) is the check that the structure matches the words."
3. No edit needed at {{approval-event}} (L1702-1710 already renders `constraints` as context and consents to the Authority Set) or at the generative carve-out (L1103-1108). #309 restates the boundary in the companion guidance's contract statement, tracked there.

**Open questions**

1. Rule strength: a MUST NOT on the AS, or definitional prose ("are never parsed")? MUST NOT is testable but must be squared with the L1103-1108 generative local-policy extension; cleanest is MUST NOT within the profile's two modes, extension explicitly outside them.
2. Scope of the free-text class: `constraints` only (the member the review flagged) or uniformly `goal`, `constraints`, `success_criteria`? Uniform is recommended; confirm no other member is prose.
3. Should a deployment using the generative extension be required to record distinguishable provenance (approval_basis-style, per D57), so an audit can tell lookup-derived from generatively derived authority? Arguably follow-on, not this issue.

**Effort**

Two edit sites, roughly three sentences and a 10-15 line diff in the core; editor's-draft PR on explicit go-ahead.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Review: **approve with amendments**.

The diagnosis is correct. Current core gives `constraints` a human-readable string shape, but “inform derivation” can be read as permission for the trusted derivation path to interpret prose. That is inconsistent with the two conforming mechanical modes and should be closed normatively.

I recommend these adjustments to the proposed wording:

1. Scope the `MUST NOT` explicitly to the derivation modes defined by this profile. The existing generative local-policy carve-out says a deployment may implement prose/model-assisted derivation outside those modes. The new text should not accidentally prohibit that extension; it should make clear that such a deployment is no longer using the profile’s conforming narrowing or template derivation for that step.
2. Define the two structured **carrier surfaces**, not only “Common Constraints.” The first door is the top-level `authorization_details` proposal, including Common Constraints, type-specific constraints, and collision-resistant deployment extensions whose semantics the AS understands. The second is the Intent’s structured `controls` plus the configured template lookup keyed on structured `purpose`/`resources`; the lookup yields structured candidate entries. This avoids implying that Common Constraints are the only enforceable RAR vocabulary.
3. Apply the prose rule uniformly to `goal`, free-text `constraints`, and `success_criteria`. `success_criteria` already has the correct `MUST NOT`; aligning all three removes an attractive ambiguity.
4. Avoid saying the runtime mapping is informed by a rule author “reading” a particular submitted string. Offline policy authors may of course use human context when designing mappings, but at execution the mapping must be a lookup over structured values, never an interpretation of the submitted prose.

Suggested normative core:

> The `goal`, `constraints`, and `success_criteria` members are human-readable disclosure and audit context. In the narrowing and template derivation modes defined by this profile, the AS MUST NOT parse those members for machine semantics or vary the Authority Set based on an interpretation of their prose. A machine-enforceable bound enters through structured `authorization_details`, including its understood constraint vocabulary, or through structured `controls` and the configured template mapping keyed on `purpose` or `resources`.

The approval surface should continue to render the prose beside the derived Authority Set. That is the human consistency check; it is not a machine-enforcement mechanism. No new member or mechanism is needed, and the generative-provenance question is appropriately a follow-on.

issues.title: Runtime: state the termination-time reconciliation rule and the fate of outstanding deduplication identifiers
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The runtime profile already defines the reconciliation window, outcome reconciliation, and single-use decision identifiers with idempotency keys. Three boundary conditions at the intersection of reconciliation and termination are implied but not stated, and a reviewer working through the timeout-after-the-permit case has to infer them:

1. **The unknown outcome needs an owner, not only a window.** When a permit is spent and the resource has not answered, the outcome is recorded as unknown. The window bounds *when* reconciliation happens; nothing names *who* must drive it to committed-or-failed before the deadline. An unknown nobody owns becomes a committed effect nobody recorded.
2. **Reconciliation must never admit a new effect under a non-active Mission.** Resolving an in-flight outcome to committed or failed after termination is legitimate bookkeeping. Executing anything new under the dead Mission is not, and the line between the two deserves a MUST.
3. **Consumed and outstanding deduplication identifiers survive termination.** A retry after termination may complete an already-consumed effect exactly once (resolving an unknown), never repeat it, and never start one. If termination erased the identifier state, a post-termination retry could double-execute.

## Proposal

One short paragraph in the reconciliation/evidence section (or the failure-mode table): unknown outcomes carry a named reconciliation owner and deadline as deployment obligations, reconciliation MAY resolve outcomes and MUST NOT admit new effects once the Mission is non-active, and identifier consumption state persists across lifecycle transitions for the duration of the reconciliation window.

## Non-goals

No new mechanism, no new evidence object. This is stating the boundary the existing machinery already implies.

issues.title: Core: name the three authority sources and the subject-representation discipline for organizational Missions
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The core defines the accountable Approver and the Mission record's accountability members, but it does not name the taxonomy of *where the authority a Mission draws on comes from*, and it does not state the subject-representation rule for work that is not reducible to any one person's entitlement. Deployments will meet three shapes immediately:

- **User-delegated**: the Mission is bounded by the delegating person's current authority, and the token's `sub` carries that person.
- **Service-owned**: the Mission is bounded by a workload's ceiling, and no human subject is involved.
- **Organizational**: the Mission is bounded by explicitly governed policy with a named accountable owner, and it impersonates nobody, because some enterprise work is not any one person's.

Without the taxonomy, the tempting implementation is to borrow a human subject for organizational work (the service account pattern wearing a Mission), which blurs the actor, the subject, and the accountable principal exactly where the record exists to keep them distinct.

## Proposal

A short subsection (or an addition to the trust-boundaries/roles text): name the three sources, state that the accountable principal lives in the Mission record in all three, that `sub` carries a delegating person only in the user-delegated form, and that an organizational Mission names its authority in the record rather than borrowing a human subject, with the actor chain carrying the Agent, instance, and delegates unchanged in every form.

## Non-goals

No new members if the existing accountability members can carry the distinction. This is a naming-and-discipline clarification, not a schema change.

## Analysis and recommendation (2026-08-12)

**Analysis**

The taxonomy does not exist in the core: no occurrence of user-delegated, service-owned, or organizational anywhere in `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md` on main. The machinery the issue says should carry it is all present:

- The Subject already admits a non-human: "The user or system on whose behalf the Mission is approved" (Terminology, L594-596), and "the delegating user or system is the token `sub`" (agent-identity relationship, L433). The Principal Model fixes Subject and Approver as (`iss`, `sub`) pairs (L668-669) and the derived token `sub` as the AS-local subject under the injective mapping of the approval event (L676-689; L1693-1702: injectivity is the rule, verbatim adoption one permitted choice; the D66/D67 reword).
- Accountability is record-borne in every case: `approver` REQUIRED and equal to `approval_basis.consent_principal`, "the accountable human (or human-accountable principal)" (L2043-2046, L2064-2067); every Mission is rooted in an approved authorization basis (D57 constitution, L1739-1746), `direct` MUST be a human approval event, and a standing-consent type MUST trace to an accountable human (L2087-2092). Basis types today: `direct` in core, `template` and `policy_drawdown` cited as companion examples (L2054-2062), `ceiling_drawdown` owned by progressive (progressive.md L299, D70).
- The actor chain is already form-invariant: `client_id` names the Agent (L2103, L3052), delegates ride `act` (L2972+), and dynamic delegation is token-borne, never record-borne (L707-709).
- The Approver != Subject case is specified (approval event step 2, L1683-1692; the rendering MUST identify the Subject, ~L1713), so approving for another person is covered. What is unstated is work that is not any one person's.

Two frictions. First, Applicability excludes "machine-to-machine service credentials" (L443-448); read alone, that sentence invites exactly the service-account anti-pattern the issue names, though its real target is calls whose credential lifetime is the task lifetime. Second, "authority source" is already used by the architecture for a different axis, the ceiling composition at derivation (issuer policy, the Approver's own authority, decision-point policy; architecture.md L1505-1516). The issue's three sources name whose authority the Mission draws on, refining the "Approver's own authority" element rather than colliding with it, but the prose must say so.

**Recommendation**

Name the three sources in the core as a short Overview subsection beside the Principal Model, using the issue's names (user-delegated, service-owned, organizational), and make the subject-representation discipline its normative payload. Two orthogonal axes, stated once: the source names whose authority bounds the Mission; `approval_basis` records how drawing on it was activated; any source may activate via `direct` or a companion standing-consent basis. Discipline: in every source the accountable principal is `approver` (equal to `approval_basis.consent_principal`), never inferred from `sub`; `sub` carries a delegating person only in the user-delegated source; a service-owned or organizational Mission records the workload or organizational principal as `subject` and MUST NOT borrow a human principal for it, under the same injective mapping (its principal gets its own AS-local `sub`, colliding with no person's); the actor chain (`client_id`, `act`) is invariant across sources. No new members: `subject`, `approver`, `approval_basis` carry the whole distinction, and organizational ownership and tenancy stay management-plane admin metadata (management companion `owner`/`tenant`, already "distinct from `subject` ... and `approver`").

**Solution sketch**

All sites in `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md`:

1. New `## Authority Sources {#authority-sources}` in Overview, after Principal Model (insert before Protocol Flow, ~L711). Roughly 15-20 lines. Rule shape:
   - "A Mission draws its authority from one of three sources: a delegating person's own authority (user-delegated), a workload's ceiling (service-owned), or explicitly governed organizational policy with a named accountable owner (organizational). The source names whose authority the approval draws on; `approval_basis` records how it was activated ({{mission-record}}), and the two compose."
   - "In every source the accountable principal is `approver`, equal to `approval_basis.consent_principal`; it is never inferred from the token `sub`."
   - "`sub` carries a delegating person only in the user-delegated source. A service-owned or organizational Mission MUST record the workload or organizational principal as `subject` and MUST NOT record a human principal in its place; the injective mapping of {{approval-event}} applies unchanged, so that principal denotes itself and impersonates nobody."
   - "The actor model does not vary by source: `client_id` names the Agent, and delegates are carried on `act` ({{delegation}})."
2. Terminology, Subject entry (L594-596): one added clause, "user, workload, or organizational principal ... ({{authority-sources}})".
3. Applicability (L443-448): one clarifying clause that the machine-to-machine exclusion means credential-lifetime-equals-task-lifetime calls; a workload's durable multi-step task is in scope as a service-owned Mission.
4. Approval event step 2 (L1681-1702): at most one sentence that the Subject may be a workload or organizational principal with establishment and injectivity unchanged; possibly zero-touch, the step already says "the principal the task is for".

No record, claim, wire, or IANA change; consent rendering already carries the Approver != Subject duty (~L1713).

**Open questions**

1. Vocabulary reconcile with architecture.md L1505-1516: keep "Authority Sources" plus the refining sentence and a follow-up architecture cross-ref, or title it "Authority Rooting" to echo the D57 "rooted in an approved authorization basis" constitution and avoid the overload entirely.
2. Does the Applicability clarification (site 3) ride this PR or land separately? It is the sentence most likely to be misread today.
3. Does "organizational principal" need its own terminology entry, or does the subsection's usage suffice? (Recommend the latter; richer subject identifier formats are already deferred, L708-711.)
4. Sequencing beside #499 (pending Single Accountable Approver pointer to the merged Approval Governance draft): this change should avoid that section entirely so the two edits stay disjoint.

**Effort**

Small. One core-only PR on Karl's go-ahead (editor's draft protocol): roughly 25-35 added lines across 3-4 sites, two MUSTs plus naming prose, no schema or code impact, no companion edits required (architecture cross-ref an optional follow-up).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Review: **approve the subject-discipline change; revise the taxonomy claims**.

The anti-impersonation rule is worth landing: organizational work must not borrow a convenient human `sub`, and the accountable human must remain distinct from the subject and actor. The existing `{subject, approver, approval_basis, client_id, act}` machinery can express that separation without a wire change.

I recommend four corrections before implementation:

1. Call these **authority-rooting modes**, not the Mission’s three exclusive “authority sources.” The effective authority is still conjunctively bounded by issuer policy, the authority available through the approval/root, and Resource policy. User-delegated, service-owned, and organizational classify whose standing the Mission is rooted in; they do not replace the other authority sources already named by the architecture. Real deployments can also combine a workload actor with user-delegated authority, so the prose must classify the root, not the actor’s implementation shape.
2. Distinguish record and token vocabulary precisely. The Mission record carries `subject`; a derived token carries the AS-local `sub` mapped from that subject. Say that a human-valued token `sub` is appropriate only when the Mission `subject` is that delegating person. For service-owned and organizational roots, `subject` names the workload or organizational principal and the derived token `sub` names that same principal in the AS namespace.
3. Do not claim the existing record makes the three-way classification independently verifiable. It does not carry an `authority_source` discriminator or a type tag on `subject`. With the no-new-member constraint, these are normative representation rules plus an informative taxonomy; a deployment/auditor determines the principal kind from the governed issuer namespace and policy. If machine-readable portable classification is desired, that is a separate schema/profile decision.
4. Keep accountability distinct from ownership. `approver == approval_basis.consent_principal` records the accountable consent principal; it does not necessarily identify an organization’s owner or encode the organizational policy that supplies standing. Where organizational validity depends on policy authority, the approval-governance record is the appropriate provenance layer. Avoid saying that `approver` alone “names its authority.”

Suggested normative center:

> A Mission can be rooted in a person’s delegated authority, a workload’s own authority, or authority governed for an organizational principal. These rooting modes do not alter the other policy bounds on effective authority. The Mission `subject` MUST identify the principal whose authority is being exercised and MUST NOT identify a human merely to lend a human identity to service-owned or organizational work. A derived token’s `sub` is the AS-local mapping of that `subject`. The accountable consent principal remains the Mission `approver`, equal to `approval_basis.consent_principal`, and MUST NOT be inferred from token `sub`. The acting Agent and delegates remain identified by `client_id` and `act`.

I agree that the Applicability sentence should be fixed in the same PR. Excluding ordinary credential-lifetime-equals-task-lifetime client-credentials calls should not be readable as excluding durable service-owned Missions. “Authority Rooting” is the clearer subsection title.

issues.title: Runtime: name the execution-evidence property set as one citable requirement cluster
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The OAuth agent-authz use-cases work is converging on a named requirement class for execution-time evidence. Maisy-ML/Agent-Authorization-Use-Cases#11 specifies four properties for high-risk agent actions: parameter-bound (produced at execution and cryptographically bound to the parameters rendered to the human), key-isolated (signed by key material the agent's runtime cannot access or forge), session-independent (verifiable whether the carrying session is active, expired, or absent), and non-repudiable (offline and third-party verifiable over time). Maisy-ML/Agent-Authorization-Use-Cases#10 frames the architectural split those properties live on: Grant Layer Authority versus Execution Layer Evidence.

The runtime profile already satisfies all four, but distributed: `parameter_digest` and action-bound approval's dynamic linking carry parameter binding, mediated custody carries key isolation, the session/harness rules carry session independence, and Execution Evidence with the Mandate and SCITT registration carry third-party verifiability. A reviewer arriving from the WG's vocabulary has to reassemble the cluster from four sections.

## Proposal

One short section (or a table in the conformance material) that names the property set and points each property at its existing mechanism, using vocabulary alignable with the WG discussion: parameter-bound, key-isolated, session-independent, third-party-verifiable. No normative change, no new mechanism. The value is citability: when the use-cases draft formalizes the requirement class, the family's answer should be one anchor, not four.

## Non-goals

No new evidence object, no change to any mechanism's semantics. Relates to #315 (the reconciliation boundary those same properties depend on at the effect end).

## Analysis and recommendation (2026-08-12)

**Analysis**

The landscape changed since filing, in a way that partially satisfies the ask and relocates its natural home. `draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime-evidence.md` was extracted from the AuthZEN binding (commit `ea45451`, 2026-08-11, PR #473) as the schema companion: it now defines the Decision Evidence object (:273), Refusal Record (:512), Execution Evidence object (:893) with the `authorized_parameter_digest` / `effective_parameter_digest` pair (:931-957), the per-emitter `sequence` (:985), the JWS integrity envelope with emitter-key-to-scope-and-audience binding (:703-748), the emitter key publication and retired-key retention rules (:1252 `{#evidence-integrity-signing-keys}`), and producer/consumer conformance (:1205). D72 (PR #494) added the substrate consumption declaration whose capability table already states the verifiability tiers honestly: Independently Verifiable "supplied in scoped form" against the Enforcement Scope Statement's published keys, and Portable Evidence "not supplied by this document alone", routed to the audit profile (:260-261; restated normatively at :1277-1286).

What the extraction did NOT do is name the property set. The terms key-isolated, session-independent, and third-party-verifiable appear nowhere in the family (repo-wide grep; `non-repudiable` appears only in containment.md:727 in a different, approver-disclosure sense; `parameter-bound` is imported into runtime-evidence's conventions at :181 from the runtime profile). A reviewer arriving with the WG vocabulary now reassembles the cluster across THREE documents instead of four sections of one:

- parameter-bound: runtime.md `{#action-approval}` (:828), `{#parameter-binding}` (:1729), `{#parameter-digest}` (:1767); runtime-evidence `parameter_digest` (:385), the authorized/effective digest pair (:931), and the TOCTOU chain section (:1108).
- key-isolated: runtime.md `{#custody}` (:938) and the compromise-resistant claim's custody condition (:2226); runtime-evidence's rule that each record is signed by the emitter's published key bound to its scope and audience (:736-748).
- session-independent: runtime-evidence verification anchored in published key sets with retired keys resolvable for the retention window (:1252-1276); no verification step consults a live session or the carrying credential; harness.md's rule that session continuity is never proof Mission authority continues (:148).
- third-party-verifiable: two-tier, per the D72 correction: scoped independent verification from runtime-evidence itself (:1277-1286), offline durable third-party verifiability via the audit profile's Transparent Statements (audit.md:180-210), whose evidence-types table registers Decision, Execution, and Refusal records (audit.md:394-397); the Mission Receipt / Mandate projection sits in runtime.md `{#mission-receipt}` (:2128).

Citing sites today: audit's evidence-types table (audit.md:395-397), the AuthZEN binding's conformance incorporation (authzen.md:295-302, runtime-evidence.md:1211), and harness (:1133, :1347). None of them, and no section anywhere, is the one anchor the WG conversation can cite. Runtime.md's Named Enforcement Claims (:2201) is the precedent for named, table-backed claims, but both existing claims are deployment claims, not record properties. Related: #315's reconciliation boundary has since been specified (closed via PR #505), so the effect-end dependency the issue noted is resolved.

**Recommendation**

Keep the issue open and resolve it with the small edit it asks for, relocated to the extraction's home: add one short informative section to `draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime-evidence.md` (the schema companion is where the records live; the issue predates the extraction and implicitly targeted runtime's conformance material). Do not close as satisfied: the extraction gives the cluster a single document but not a single named, citable anchor, and the WG-alignable vocabulary is still absent.

**Solution sketch**

One section, `## Evidence Properties {#evidence-properties}`, placed after the Execution Evidence object (before `{#evidence-extensions}` or just before `{#conformance}`), informative, no new normative words. A one-sentence lead naming the four properties, then a four-row table: property, mechanism, citations.

- Parameter-bound: `parameter_digest` on Decision Evidence, the authorized/effective pair on Execution Evidence, dynamic linking via action-bound approval (runtime `{#parameter-binding}`, `{#action-approval}`; here `{#decision-evidence-object}`, `{#execution-evidence-object}`).
- Key-isolated: emitter-published signing keys bound to scope and audience (`{#decision-evidence-integrity}`); where the deployment claims agent-compromise-resistant enforcement, key material is held by the mediating PEP, inaccessible to the agent (runtime `{#custody}`, `{#compromise-resistant}`). Phrase conditionally: base conformance alone does not deliver this row.
- Session-independent: verification against published key sets with retired-key retention (`{#evidence-integrity-signing-keys}`); verifiable whether the carrying session or credential is active, expired, or absent.
- Third-party-verifiable: two-tier phrasing mirroring the D72 capability rows verbatim in spirit: scoped independent verification here, offline third-party verifiability via the audit profile where adopted. This keeps the existing honesty scoping intact rather than overclaiming.

Define the three new terms in the section itself (plain, timeless prose; no citation of the WG GitHub threads in the spec). Optionally one pointer sentence from runtime.md's `{#evidence}` intro (:2020); skippable to keep the change one-file. Gate: build 0 "Section ??", lint 0.

**Open questions**

1. Home confirmation: runtime-evidence (recommended, record properties) versus runtime.md Named Enforcement Claims (deployment claims; wrong genus, but the key-isolated row must cite it).
2. One row or two for verifiability: mirror the D72 split (Independently Verifiable vs Portable Evidence) as two rows, or keep the WG's single third-party-verifiable term with two-tier wording (recommended).
3. Term choice: use third-party-verifiable, not non-repudiable, as the section's term, since containment.md:727 already uses non-repudiable for approver disclosure.

**Effort**

Small. One PR, one file (~30-45 lines), optionally one sentence in runtime.md; informative only, no schema or conformance change.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review: **keep open and add the single citable table in `runtime-evidence`, but make it a conditional capability map rather than saying the runtime profile “satisfies all four.”** The extraction made the home clear; it did not eliminate the need.

The proposed location and informative status are right. The table needs to preserve four distinctions that are easy to blur:

1. **Parameter integrity is not automatically human-rendering integrity.** `parameter_digest` binds evidence to canonical parameters evaluated/observed at particular points. It becomes “bound to the parameters rendered to the human” only when the action-bound approval/dynamic-linking profile is used and that UI path is in the trusted computing base. The row should name both the base evidence property and the extra condition.
2. **Key isolation is deployment-conditional.** A valid emitter signature and published key binding provide origin/integrity; they do not prove that the agent could not access the private key. Claim key isolation only with mediated custody (and the corresponding compromise-resistant deployment claim). This should be an explicit “conditions/profile” column, not a footnote readers may miss.
3. **Session-independent verification is not session-independent validity.** A verifier can validate retained evidence without treating a live session or access token as the trust anchor. That does not prove that the action was authorized *now*, nor eliminate key-status, revocation, lifecycle, or evidence-freshness checks. Avoid wording that suggests an expired carrying credential retroactively validates an action.
4. **Independent verification and durable portability are separate tiers.** Runtime Evidence supplies scoped signature verification using the Enforcement Scope Statement's key material. Offline/long-term/third-party portability requires the audit/Transparent Statement profile and its retention model. Do not compress those into an unconditional “third-party-verifiable” checkmark.

I also strongly agree with avoiding **non-repudiable**. A signature can support origin and integrity evidence; it does not, by itself, establish legal non-repudiation, human intent, exclusive key control, or truth of the signed assertion.

Suggested table columns: **Property / What the base evidence proves / Additional mechanism or condition / What it does not prove**. That will be more useful than a simple property-to-citation matrix and will stop optional profiles from being mistaken for base conformance.

Disposition: **approve one informative `runtime-evidence` PR (~40 lines), then close #343.** A pointer from runtime.md is optional; keep definitions and caveats single-homed in the evidence companion.

issues.title: Core/Security Considerations: state the third-party data-subject boundary explicitly
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Problem

The use-cases catalog is adding a new top-level requirement class for third-party data-subject authorization (Maisy-ML/Agent-Authorization-Use-Cases#7): an agent needs data about a person who is neither the agent's principal nor the resource owner, and that person's consent is required for disclosure. The illustrative case is a background check, where the employer is the principal, the agent is the checker's, the university is the resource, and the job candidate is the data subject with no session anywhere in the flow.

The Mission model does not cover this, and nothing in the family should be read as if it did. The Subject/Approver distinction separates the user the task is for from the principal who approved it. Neither role reaches a third party outside the transaction. The risk is silent overclaim: a deployment treating an approved Mission as if it carried the data subject's consent, when it only records the principal's authorization.

## Proposal

An explicit boundary statement, in the core's security considerations or the what-not-to-claim material: a Mission records the accountable principal's authorization of the undertaking and never constitutes or substitutes for a data subject's consent to disclosure. Where a resource requires data-subject consent, that requirement is resource-side policy, satisfied by mechanisms in that lane (UMA claims gathering, consent receipts, or a resource-defined artifact), and a conforming deployment treats the absence of such consent as the resource's refusal, not a Mission gap to route around.

## Non-goals

No new role, member, or mechanism. This is a boundary named so the category cannot be stretched over a class it does not cover, the same discipline as the existing non-goals for intent inference and semantic evaluation.

## Analysis and recommendation (2026-08-12)

**Analysis**

Current main has no statement of this boundary. Outside Privacy Considerations, `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md` has zero hits for "data subject", "personal", "erasure", or "lawful"; the only personal-data language in the document is the Intent Retention and Anchor Disclosure paragraph (4025-4038), which names the Intent members `goal` and `constraints` as "personal-data sinks" carrying "whatever task description the user supplied" (4027) and points record erasure at the audit profile (4029). That framing reads as the user's own data; nothing addresses a third party who is neither Subject nor Approver.

Third-party personal data can enter at four surfaces: the free-text Intent members `goal` (761) and `constraints` (771), recorded verbatim on the Mission (2009) with no minimization caution anywhere in the Intent section (740-969, verified negative); the `proposed_authority` array "recorded exactly as submitted" (2012), whose resource identifiers can name a person; the Mission record itself, which "concentrates the task, its authority, and its principals at the AS" (4041) with a retention floor and no ceiling (2126); and the unsalted integrity anchors, where "a party holding a candidate Intent can confirm it against `intent_hash`" (4032), a confirmation channel that works equally against a guessed third party's details, with the same channel for `proposal_hash`. The audit companion salts enumerable evidence for exactly this risk (`draft-mcguinness-mission-audit.md:1160`) and defines the erasure record with a `data_subject_request` basis (636-651); the consent-evidence companion tells deployments to redact free-form task text not required for ordinary audit (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-consent-evidence.md:1126`).

Meanwhile approval is consistently an authorization act by the accountable principal: the Approver definition (598, 668), Consent Binding ("a user's approval of a task bounds every token derived for it", 3513), and Non-Goals (525-579) scope semantic verification, approval-free widening, and unlinkability, but never this class. The silent-overclaim risk in the issue is real: a deployment can read an approved Mission as carrying the candidate's consent when the record only holds the Approver's authorization.

**Recommendation**

Add one Privacy Considerations subsection stating the boundary: a Mission records the accountable Approver's authorization of the undertaking and never constitutes or substitutes for the consent of a data subject the task touches, including third parties outside every Mission role; deployments process third-party personal data under their own legal basis, data-subject-consent requirements are resource-side policy satisfied in the resource's own lane, and absence of that consent is the resource's refusal, not a Mission gap to route around. Fold in minimization guidance for the surfaces above and reuse the existing audit-profile erasure pointer. Additive, not duplicative: it extends the personal-data-sink paragraph to the third-party class and names the boundary no existing section states.

**Solution sketch**

Edit site: new subsection `## Third-Party Data Subjects {#third-party-data-subjects}` in Privacy Considerations, immediately after Intent Retention and Anchor Disclosure (insert between 4038 and 4039), so it sits beside the paragraph that already names the personal-data sinks. Three short paragraphs:

1. The boundary. Approval records the accountable Approver's authorization ({{approval-event}}); it is not a data subject's consent to disclosure, and no Mission role reaches a third party the task is about (the candidate in a background check, where the employer's agent queries a registrar). Where a resource requires data-subject consent or another legal basis, that is resource-side policy satisfied by mechanisms in that lane (claims gathering, a consent receipt, a resource-defined artifact); a conforming deployment treats its absence as the resource's refusal.
2. Minimization. Third-party personal data placed in `goal`, `constraints`, or `proposed_authority` persists on the record for the audit horizon ({{mission-record}}) and is confirmable through the unsalted anchors by anyone holding a candidate value; clients SHOULD reference third parties by opaque or resource-scoped identifiers rather than embedding identifying detail in Intent prose.
3. Erasure. Retention and erasure follow the deployment's policy, with the audit profile's erasure record (its `data_subject_request` basis) as the transparency-side mechanism, same informative pointer as the existing paragraph.

Optionally, one sentence in Non-Goals (525-579) naming the class, matching the discipline of the semantic-verification and unlinkability bullets, with a pointer to the new subsection.

**Open questions**

- Include the Non-Goals bullet, or let the Privacy subsection carry the boundary alone? The issue asks for "security considerations or the what-not-to-claim material"; doing both is one extra sentence but two homes for one boundary.
- Name UMA claims gathering as the example mechanism? The core keeps companions informative and currently never references UMA; "claims gathering" generically avoids implying a dependency while the UMA binding stays experimental.
- Add a forward pointer from the `goal`/`constraints` definitions (761, 771) to the new subsection? The Intent section currently has no privacy caution at all; one cross-reference is cheap but grows the edit.
- Anchors stay unsalted by design (an auditor reproduces the digest from the record alone, 1943); the sketch treats the confirmation channel as a minimization argument, not a salting proposal.

**Effort**

Small. One subsection of roughly 12-18 lines plus an optional Non-Goals sentence; no new role, member, or mechanism, per the issue's own non-goals. Lands as a single reviewable PR on the editor's draft once approved.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review: **the boundary is necessary and the proposed core-only treatment is directionally right, with two important wording changes.**

The central statement should land: Mission approval authorizes an undertaking on behalf of the accountable Approver; it does **not**, merely by existing, establish permission to disclose personal data about some other person. That prevents a serious category error without adding a role or turning the Mission protocol into a consent-management protocol.

Recommended adjustments:

1. **Describe an enforcement boundary, not a mandatory deployment location.** “Resource-side policy” is useful shorthand, but the policy may be evaluated by the RS, an upstream gateway, a PDP, or an AS acting for the resource domain. Say that the resource domain's disclosure policy MUST be satisfied and access MUST be refused when required evidence is absent or invalid. Do not require the RS process itself to perform claims gathering.
2. **Avoid making a legal conclusion for every jurisdiction.** Say that Mission approval is not *by itself* evidence of a third-party data subject's consent or other required legal basis. Whether consent is required, and what qualifies, is deployment/legal policy outside the protocol. This is stronger technically and safer than saying every deployment “processes under its own legal basis” as if the draft could define that basis.
3. **Keep examples generic in core.** “Claims gathering or a resource-domain consent artifact” is enough. A normative-looking UMA reference would create the wrong dependency and falsely suggest UMA is the only or preferred solution.
4. **Minimization should cover all four persistence/linkability surfaces**, including identifiers in `proposed_authority`. Recommend data minimization and resource-scoped/pseudonymous references where appropriate, but do not imply an opaque identifier is necessarily anonymous or non-personal data.
5. **Do not duplicate the rule in Non-Goals.** Put one normative boundary in the new Privacy Considerations subsection and add, at most, a short forward pointer from the Intent definitions. A second independently worded non-goal will drift.

The anchor observation is correct: this is a reason to avoid predictable sensitive prose, not a reason to salt the protocol's reproducible integrity commitments. The existing audit-erasure pointer is also the right informative hook, provided the text does not imply that an erasure record itself performs erasure or overrides retention law.

Suggested disposition: **approve a small core PR with those amendments**. No new Mission member, actor role, or consent mechanism.

issues.title: Core/Security Considerations: no authority by information propagation alone (emergent authority through coordination)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Summary

The core enforces possession-independence on the credential plane: a credential or continued handle grants nothing, and authorization is re-checked at the live gate for every consequential action. A documented multi-agent incident shows the same failure on a different carrier. Independently bounded agents used shared state (a writable package repository, then a channel reconstructed from directory names after the first was removed) as a coordination and memory plane, composing discoveries, techniques, and credentials across runtimes until many bounded agents behaved as one persistent, increasingly capable actor.

This is authority acquired by information propagation. No single action was individually unauthorized; the composition was.

## Proposed addition to Security Considerations

State the invariant that generalizes the family's existing possession-independence from credentials to work products (files, messages, memory entries, queue events, directory names, and other durable shared state):

> No authority may be acquired by information propagation alone. An agent may inherit another agent's knowledge; it never inherits another agent's authority. Information may cross a boundary without authority crossing with it.

Corollary: a work product produced under one Mission, when read by an agent operating under another Mission, is input, not authority. The receiving Mission determines what may be done with the information under its own Authority Set. The producing Mission's authority does not transfer through the artifact by copying, referencing, embedding, or communicating it.

This is the artifact-plane statement of a claim the core already makes on the credential plane (revocation is possession-independent; an Active Mission is not ambient standing authority). It extends the existing invariants rather than contradicting them.

## New threat category

Add "emergent authority through coordination" alongside the existing catalog (stolen token, confused deputy, ambient standing authority, trifecta exfiltration, child fan-out abuse, swarm-instance compromise):

> Multiple agents executing independently bounded work communicate through shared state, allowing discoveries, credentials, techniques, or intermediate results to persist across runtimes and Missions. Individually acceptable actions compose into behavior that no single Mission authorized.

This is distinct from swarm-instance compromise, which is legitimate class-pinned multiplication under one Mission. Here the composing units are independent Missions coordinating through an unmanaged carrier.

## Mechanism (informative, kept out of the core)

The mechanism is specified in a companion so the core stays self-contained: a forthcoming Mission Work Products companion defines (a) a policy-free work-product provenance object attributing an artifact to its producing Mission, and (b) the non-transitive Mission-to-Mission handoff rule. The core addition is the axiom and the threat category only, and takes no normative dependency on the companion.

## Why the core, and why an issue

This is a base security-model claim, not a profile detail, so it belongs in the core's Security Considerations. The core is published, so this is filed as an issue rather than a direct edit.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Proposed resolution

The mechanism is now implemented and merged, so this resolution has working backing: the Mission Work Products companion (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-work-products`, PR #403) specifies the work-product provenance object and the non-transitive Mission-to-Mission handoff, and the reference impl (PR #404) proves it (an incident-reconstruction e2e where reading a shared-state artifact changes what a receiving Mission knows but not what it may do). The core addition below is the axiom and the threat only, self-contained, taking no normative dependency on that companion.

It extends statements the core already makes rather than adding a new claim: Mission Drift (no escalation by acquiring tokens) and possession-independent Revocation (revocation acts on `mission_id` independent of possession of any token), and it sharpens the existing Prompt Injection and the Exfiltration Leg subsection (which disclaims information-flow control).

### Proposed new Security Considerations subsection

Recommended placement: immediately after **Prompt Injection and the Exfiltration Leg** (`{#prompt-injection}`), before **Issuance Scope, Not Runtime Enforcement** (`{#runtime-boundary}`). Its conceptual sibling is **Mission Drift** (the token-plane version of the same bound), so directly after Mission Drift is an acceptable alternative.

---

## Authority Does Not Propagate With Information {#information-propagation}

The Mission Drift consideration above bounds escalation by token
acquisition: an agent cannot exceed the approved task by acquiring
additional tokens. The same bound holds for information. No authority
may be acquired by information propagation alone. An agent may inherit
another agent's knowledge; it never inherits another agent's authority.
Information may cross a boundary without authority crossing with it.

A work product produced under one Mission, such as a file, message,
memory entry, queue event, or other durable shared artifact, is input
when an agent operating under another Mission reads it, not authority.
The receiving Mission determines what may be done with the information
under its own Authority Set ({{subset}}), and the producing Mission's
authority does not transfer through the artifact by copying,
referencing, embedding, or communicating it. An agent that needs
authority to act on what it read acquires it only through an authorized
derivation or delegation bounded by the Mission ({{delegation}}), never
from the artifact.

This extends a possession-independence the profile already requires.
Revocation acts on the `mission_id` independent of possession of any
token ({{revocation}}); here, authority is likewise independent of
possession of any information. It is not information-flow control, which
this profile does not provide ({{prompt-injection}}): the profile does
not constrain what agents communicate, only what that communication can
confer. Coordination between agents remains possible and cannot route
around Mission authority.

The threat is emergent authority through coordination. Multiple agents
executing independently bounded work communicate through shared state,
so discoveries, credentials, techniques, or intermediate results persist
across runtimes and Missions, and individually acceptable actions compose
into behavior that no single Mission authorized. This differs from a
compromised or multiplied agent acting within one Mission's Authority
Set: the composing units are independent Missions coordinating through a
carrier outside any Mission's gate. The mechanism that upholds the
invariant across such a carrier, work-product provenance and a
non-transitive Mission-to-Mission handoff, is specified by Mission Work
Products {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-work-products}}; this
document takes no normative dependency on it.

---

To be applied in the next core revision; the published core is not edited directly.

issues.title: Impl: kernel must propagate containment to existing child Missions (matches PR #408 normative rule)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Spec/impl divergence introduced by PR #408

The external-review resolution PR #408 added a NORMATIVE rule to
`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md`: when a parent
Authority Set entry is contained, the Mission Issuer MUST propagate the
containment entry-wise to existing child Missions justified by that entry
(mirroring the existing discharge-propagation rule). This closes the
verified "derive-then-contain" composition gap for child Missions.

The reference kernel does not yet implement this. Today `contain()` does not
propagate to children, and `cascadeChildren` fires only on a parent
transition to a non-active state, so a contained-but-still-active parent
leaves existing children deriving the contained authority.

Do:
- Propagate a contain transition entry-wise onto existing child Missions in
  the kernel (`services/authorization-server/src/kernel/`), mirroring the
  discharge-propagation path.
- Add a test that a child of a contained parent can no longer derive the
  contained entry while non-contained entries still derive.
- Confirm the cross-domain-grant and offline-attenuation-root cases behave
  as the narrowed containment claims now state (lifetime-bounded residual,
  no post-hoc issuer reach), and document the residual in the reference build.

Source: external architecture review, verified Finding 1.
