issues.title: Convergence 2a: normative Deployment Profile schema, claim identifiers, and validation rules
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Context

The architecture-convergence review found that the family's assurance labels are not yet reliable comparison points. The levels (Baseline Issuance, Runtime-Enforced, Governed Agent, High-Assurance Agent) are described as guidance whose meaning varies by binding, and the Deployment Profile that would make a claim checkable has no normative serialization, no stable identifiers, and no validation rules. Consequently two parties cannot interoperably compare "Runtime-Enforced" or "High-Assurance Agent."

The review also gave a sequencing constraint: publish the Deployment Profile schema before adding more assurance vocabulary.

This issue tracks that work (convergence Phase 2, item 2a). It is filed for deliberation rather than resolved inline, because it introduces new normative content and a placement decision that should be settled before drafting.

## What is needed

1. A normative, machine-readable serialization for the Deployment Profile (a schema), so a deployment's declared capabilities and claims are structured and validatable.
2. Stable claim identifiers, separated along the three axes the review named:
   - binding capabilities: record-only, joined, credential-carried, state-observable;
   - enforcement assurance: recorded, state-aware, action-enforced, compromise-resistant;
   - named claims, each with normative validation criteria (which mechanisms MUST be present for the claim to hold).
3. Validation rules a relying party can apply to decide whether a declared claim is satisfied by the declared capabilities.

These should compose with the two substrate capabilities now defined (lifecycle-gated vs state-observable, PR #420) and with the machine-readable family manifest and CI guardrails (PR #423).

## Placement decision (to settle first)

The architecture document is Informational, so it cannot be the normative home. Two options:

- (a) A normative section in `draft-mcguinness-mission-substrate.md`. Substrate is already the cross-binding conformance document and now carries the two substrate capabilities, so the Deployment Profile (declaring capabilities and claims) fits there, and this avoids adding a new profile during the convergence freeze. Recommended.
- (b) A dedicated `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-deployment-profile` companion. Cleaner separation, but one more draft while the family is consolidating.

## Notes

- Honor the convergence freeze: prefer folding into an existing normative document over a new companion unless the material clearly warrants its own draft.
- Once the schema exists, the family manifest / CI (PR #423) can additionally validate that declared claims reference only registered claim identifiers.
- Source: architecture-convergence review, structural weakness "Assurance labels are not yet reliable comparison points."

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Deferred: not needed yet (maintainer call). The assurance-claim model was just reshaped by the convergence cycle (the two substrate capabilities in #420, the approval_basis constitution in #418/#419, and the containment two-property split in #421), so a Deployment Profile claim vocabulary should stabilize before it is drafted; locking it now would be premature-vocabulary lock-in.

PR #281 (open since 2026-07-14, deliberately parked) is a prototype of the standalone-companion approach; this issue and #281 track the same deferred work. No action until the assurance model has settled and the need is concrete. Keeping this open only as a deferred tracker.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
A question surfaced by the 2026-08-16 fresh architecture review (see #563 for the sibling core/architecture findings). Citations checked: both match current text.

Core reads: "The declaration's home is the deployment's published statement of what it enforces (the Mission Deployment Profile of {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture}})" (oauth-mission.md:2107-2120). Grammatically, the stated home is "the deployment's published statement"; the Deployment Profile sits in a parenthetical gloss on it. The architecture doc says of that same artifact: "this document fixes no serialization... until it exists [a machine-readable manifest schema], the shape below is illustrative and the per-profile statements are the checkable form" (mission-architecture.md:2455-2458).

Whether this is a conflict turns on how the parenthetical reads:

- (a) If the parenthetical is definitional (the Deployment Profile *is* the home), reword core's pointer so the MUST is checkable against a deployment's own published statement without naming the Deployment Profile as its home. Small core PR; keeps #424 parked.
- (b) Unpark #424 and give the Deployment Profile a checkable schema (stable claim identifiers, validation rules). Larger effort, was deliberately deferred.
- (c) Leave both texts as they are. This rests on reading the parenthetical as an example rather than the sole home, so the MUST stays satisfiable by any published statement and the Deployment Profile reference stays informative.

Which course would you like, or should this stay parked as is?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
I recommend **course (a): clarify core and keep #424 parked**.

The present sentences are arguably satisfiable—the grammatical home is “the deployment's published statement”—but the parenthetical makes a normative core MUST look as though its sole conformance artifact is the schema-free, Informational Deployment Profile. That ambiguity is cheap to remove.

This requirement does not yet need another OAuth protocol surface. `controls.acr` already has deployment-policy-defined semantics and no global strength ordering. The AS needs a published local floor and must verify that approval authentication satisfies both that floor and any submitted `controls.acr`; it does not need a registered JSON schema, discovery endpoint, or new metadata to do so.

Suggested core shape:

> A deployment MUST publish a statement declaring the minimum approval-authentication strength it enforces for Missions whose derived Authority Set carries the identified high-risk authority, and the deployment scope to which that declaration applies. Approval authentication for such a Mission MUST satisfy both the published floor and, when present, `controls.acr`, under the deployment's policy mapping; this document defines no global ordering of `acr` values. The Informational architecture calls the system-level composition of such statements the Mission Deployment Profile; this specification requires no particular serialization.

Normative consequences:

- the existing published-floor MUST remains;
- the statement's applicable deployment scope becomes explicit;
- satisfaction is the conjunction of the floor and `controls.acr` without implying a universal ACR ordering;
- the Architecture reference is informative terminology, not the normative home; and
- no new wire member, metadata, IANA registration, or schema is introduced.

Keep #424 parked until a concrete automated consumer must discover or compare these claims. At that trigger, the current Mission Substrate Statement should be the starting point: it now owns capability scope, activation, temporal elements, failure behavior, and extensions. Parked PR #281 predates that model and would need redesign rather than a mechanical rebase.

issues.title: Delegation identity: model the RFC 8693 act chain across all flows (subsumes approved_client)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Delegation identity: model the RFC 8693 act chain across all flows

Per the standards review's client_id finding and the follow-on design discussion: the correct on-token representation of delegation identity is the RFC 8693 actor (`act`) chain, not a family-specific single-client claim.

**Model:**
- `client_id` (top-level): the client requesting THIS token (RFC 8693 / RFC 9068). (Already the case in code; P0 fixes the draft prose.)
- `act`: the current delegate/actor; each prior hop nests via `act.act`.
- The **root of the act chain is the originally-approved agent.** The approved agent therefore falls out of the chain and needs no separate claim.
- Introspection and the Mission Mandate expose the chain and identify its root as the approved agent.

**Why this over a `mission.approved_client` claim (withdrawn):** the act chain travels on the token, so it works cross-domain (a partner Resource AS that cannot call the origin issuer's introspection can still read the chain root); it is the standard delegation representation; and it captures the full lineage, not just one endpoint.

**Work (the plumbing that does not exist yet):** today only the continuation flow builds an `act` chain (`kernel/continuation-grant.ts` via `extendChain`). Model it consistently across the delegation flows that currently do not nest one:
- child creation / child jwt-bearer redemption (`child-delegation.ts`, provider handlers),
- template dispatch (`handleMissionDispatchGrant`),
- cross-domain projection (`kernel/cross-domain.ts`, so the chain root travels to the partner domain),
- and confirm continuation stays consistent.
Nesting convention: outermost = current actor, innermost = approved agent. Add a wired multi-hop test where a genuinely divergent requesting client and a 2+-level chain occur together (the P0 code PR could only unit-test this against the emitter API, since no such wired flow exists yet).

Depends on: the P0 `client_id` interop fix landing first. Spec: the mission-claim / delegation sections (core) + cross-domain + introspection + mandate. Priority: P1.


## Analysis and recommendation

(Architect analysis, 2026-08-13. Supersedes nothing in the 2026-08-11 re-scope comment; it resolves the issue's remaining open state into a rulable proposal. All citations verified at HEAD.)

### What changed since the D63 re-scope

Three consumers arrived: #538, #539, and #540 all cite this issue as owning "one actor-chain convention." What they need is new, and it is **not** the deferred Concern 2:

- **The attenuation chain carries no `act` today.** The substrate identifies parties by key possession only (`cnf` per hop); its sole mention of `act` is the contrast section placing issuer-mediated delegation *beside* offline attenuation. #538's hop-field list ("the RFC 8693 `act` chain specified by #433") assumes a convention that does not exist yet. That convention is this issue's remaining work.
- **Org boundary vs lineage boundary is unstated.** D63's rule is nest-in-Mission / restart-at-new-approval. An attenuation hop is in-Mission delegation, so crossing an organization extends lineage (#538: "an organization change is not a new root and does not reset depth"). Consistent, but the corollary (restart keys on approval basis, not topology) is written nowhere.
- **The actor-profile suite is further along than the family's citations suggest.** Beside the base OAuth Actor Profile for Delegation (profile-conformant actor objects REQUIRE `act.iss`, so `act.iss` + `act.sub` is a canonical issuer-qualified actor identifier; `sub_profile`; Transaction Tokens covered), the sibling repo defines Actor Receipts (issuer-signed per-hop provenance, hash-chained via `prh`, per-issuer non-transitive trust, historical top-level `cnf` preserved at the receipt level with `act.cnf` prohibited), Actor Proofs (the *added actor* signs its own participation and the target binding it authorized, keys resolved from `(act.iss, act.sub)` through pre-established trust), and Actor Chain Authority Bounds (recorded per-hop authority, monotonic except at signed re-authorization events).
- **The family already cites that suite at the two seams that matter.** Runtime consumes proofs/receipts "as token-derived facts where present" (runtime draft, out-of-scope list). Cross-Domain already says a consumer needing independently verifiable provenance of hops upstream of a re-mint MAY require issuer-signed hop receipts (~L894-899). Those two citations pre-answer questions this ruling would otherwise open.

### Two delegation lanes (the structural finding)

The actor suite is the evidence layer of **issuer-mediated** chaining: every hop is added by an AS, so receipts (issuer-signed) and proofs (actor-signed) reconstruct provenance. The attenuation chain is **holder-mediated** and already *is* proofs-and-bounds fused structurally: each hop is delegator-signed, carries its `authorization_details` narrowing, `aud`, `exp`, and the next presenter's `cnf`, and the verifier recomputes every subset relation. The chain needs neither receipts nor bounds; it is self-proving. #538's "issuer-mediated chain as a future standards-track alternative" now has a named evidence layer: the actor suite. First revision stays one wire format (holder-mediated), per #538's own interop rationale.

### Proposed ruling

1. **Reaffirm D63 unchanged**, plus the corollary: the restart rule keys on **approval basis, not organizational topology**. In-Mission delegation nests (`act.act`); lineage boundaries (child, successor: new approval basis) restart; an offline attenuation hop is in-Mission and therefore **extends**, including across organizations.
2. **The substrate hosts the attribution mechanics.** Offline Attenuation gains an OPTIONAL per-hop actor-attribution member: shape is a **profile-conformant actor object** (Actor Profile for Delegation: `iss` REQUIRED, so issuer-qualification comes free; `sub_profile` as profiled), nesting per RFC 8693 (outermost = current actor), **extend-never-truncate**. Its trust class is stated explicitly: **delegator-attested** (the parent's signature is the parent naming its delegate, never an issuer assertion); the entry-to-key binding (`act` entry vs hop `cnf`) is checkable only through the deployment's workload-attestation mapping. Absent member = key-based identity only, today's behavior, the unchanged default. #538's companion then profiles the member REQUIRED for cross-org conformance. **Actor Proofs is the named optional upgrade** where actor-side pre-issuance non-repudiation is needed (the added actor signs its own participation + target binding); it is not a chain requirement.
3. **The root identifies the approved agent.** The chain's approved-agent identity is the issuer-signed root (sender-constrained to the approved agent's key, correlated to the Mission Record), never an `act` entry, and never a resurrected `approved_client`. A chain-verifying RP recovers the approved agent from the verified root.
4. **Projection keeps restarting.** A destination-minted local token restarts `act` at the local delegate (existing cross-domain rule). Chain lineage survives on the evidence plane (derivation evidence: chain digest, actor lineage) and via the destination AS's own introspection; it is never imported into local `act` (which would carry unverifiable foreign actors and non-portable identifiers into a local claim).
5. **Concern 2 stays deferred, and its eventual shape is now named.** When a consumer materializes (an RP that is neither chain-verifying nor able to reach its own Resource AS's records), the resolution is **profiling Actor Receipts on the projection**, exactly the MAY Cross-Domain already carries. The bespoke "distinguished attribution claim" option is retired: receipts are standards-track-adjacent, already cited, preserve historical per-hop `cnf` without touching `act`, and require no new family member.
6. **Authority Bounds caution (composition rule).** Bounds' monotonicity duplicates what the attenuation chain proves structurally, so it belongs only on the issuer-mediated lane. Its `reauthorized`/`bounds_events` affordance (in-chain, signed authority widening) conflicts with the family's Expansion discipline: re-authorization is never an in-chain event; it is a successor Mission with fresh consent (successor-or-refusal). Any family profiling of Authority Bounds MUST prohibit `reauthorized`/`bounds_events` and route widening to Expansion.
7. **Housekeeping.** AAuth -11 removed `act` and the agent identifier from AAuth auth tokens (per the upstream note on this issue). Check `draft-mcguinness-mission-aam` and the AAuth binding for stale references; the family's carry-the-chain rationale is topology-specific (a partner that cannot call the origin's introspection) and stands without an AAuth citation.

### Solution sketch

- **attenuation.md (substrate, ~S):** one subsection in the chain-token definition: the OPTIONAL `act` member per hop; profile-conformant actor-object shape; extend-never-truncate; delegator-attested trust class stated; entry-to-`cnf` cross-check via workload attestation where the deployment maps it; privacy note (issuer-qualified actor identifiers are correlation handles; the pairwise-identifier guidance applies as for `mission.subject`).
- **core (delegation section, ~XS):** one corollary paragraph: restart keys on approval basis, not topology; pointer to the substrate for the offline in-Mission case. Citation posture unchanged (Actor Profile stays informative, confined to the Delegation capability).
- **cross-domain.md:** the scope correction already in #538's deliverables (chain depth is global; projection-local depth begins after chain verification; a projected token never re-enters a chain). The existing receipts MAY (~L899) stands and becomes Concern 2's named resolution shape.
- **#538's companion (at build):** REQUIRED profile-conformant `act` entries per hop; the root-identifies-approved-agent rule; Actor Proofs as optional composition; its existing vectors (actor-chain truncation, actor/leaf-key mismatch) bind to this convention.
- **#540 (at build):** transaction token carries `act` per the base profile (which covers Transaction Tokens); proofs/receipts stay off the token and ride the input credential the Transaction Authorization Server verifies at redemption, consistent with its no-evidence-bags rule.
- **Reference implementation:** nothing now; the substrate member is spec-only until #538 builds.

### Tradeoffs

- **`act` on offline hops (delegator-attested) vs key-only chains.** Attribution becomes readable by verifiers and auditors without resolving workload attestation at every hop; the costs are per-hop token growth, a correlation surface (mitigated by pairwise identifiers and audience narrowing), and the risk that a verifier reads chain `act` with issuer-grade trust, which is why the trust class is stated normatively and cross-checked against `cnf`.
- **OPTIONAL at the substrate vs REQUIRED.** Single-domain offline chains may not need attribution (keys suffice; audit lives at the issuer); forcing it burdens the simplest deployments. Profile-gating matches the family's overlay discipline; #538 makes it REQUIRED where it is load-bearing.
- **Reusing the name `act` vs a distinct member.** Reuse keeps one vocabulary (#539's three-identity separation depends on it) and the exact RFC 8693/Actor Profile shape; the trust-class difference is carried in prose and in the profile's conformance statement. A second name would fork the vocabulary to encode one sentence.
- **Actor Receipts as Concern 2's shape vs a family claim.** No new family member, already cited by Cross-Domain, per-issuer trust explicit; the cost is a dependency on an in-progress external suite, held at MAY/profile-gated posture, the same risk class as the existing informative Actor Profile citation.
- **Two lanes vs one.** Maintaining both eventually costs interop surface; but the first revision stays one wire format (holder-mediated), and the issuer-mediated lane is documentation of where its evidence layer will come from, not a second format now.

### Sequencing

This ruling unblocks #538 (hop rule 8), #539 (relies on `act` staying actor-only identity), and #540 (act carriage). Order: #433 ruling, then #539, then #538 in parallel with #540. The core corollary paragraph and the substrate subsection can ride #538's build PR; nothing depends on them landing earlier.

### Open questions for the ruling

1. Substrate hosts the OPTIONAL member (recommended, so single-domain offline chains get the same audit lineage and #538 stays a true profile) vs defining it only in #538's companion?
2. Confirm reuse of the `act` name with trust-class prose (recommended) vs a distinct member name?
3. Land the core corollary + substrate subsection with #538's build (recommended) vs as a separate prior PR?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Re-scoped (2026-08-11): #433 splits into two concerns; the act-chain "plumbing" list is superseded

Design exploration (see PLAN.md D62 and the "continuity is not one thing" analysis) concluded that this issue conflated two distinct things, and that most of the original **Work** list no longer applies.

**Superseded.** The original plan (model the act chain across child creation / template dispatch / cross-domain projection, so one continuous chain carries the approved-agent root everywhere) is rejected by the family's own invariants. A Child Mission has its own approval basis (`policy_drawdown`), and "information may propagate, authority may not": a child/successor acts under its **own** approval, not the parent actor's delegated authority. The drafts already encode this correctly as **restart-at-lineage** — child-delegation.md `{#child-vs-act}` and its `actor_token` definition ("a new work-continuity unit whose own `act` chain restarts at the child actor"), expansion.md ("begins its own act chain afresh under its own approval"), and cross-domain (restarts at depth 0). In-mission delegation nests (`act.act`); lineage boundaries restart. No change needed there.

**Concern 1 — actor-gating ENFORCEMENT unification (in progress).** The real, groundable gap this issue exposes is not the act chain but the eligibility matcher:
- Core `allowed_delegates` (the `may_act` gate, draft 2955-2991) is **specified but has no runtime matcher in code** (`delegation.ts` does depth + structural checks only).
- The child `actorAllowed` (the only runtime matcher) is **non-conformant to both drafts**: it matches `sub_profile` by raw string equality instead of space-separated membership, and its absent-list default is blanket-allow, contradicting the core's "an absent matcher list is deferred to policy, never a blanket grant."
- The published RAR metadata schema omits `allowed_child_actors`.

Scope of the fix: one shared eligibility helper conforming to the drafts (`sub_profile` membership; **absent list => fail-closed deny** as the reference impl's realization of "deferred to policy"; self-asserted profile never satisfies a matcher), used by BOTH the core delegation path (implementing the missing gate) and the child path (fixing it); `allowed_child_actors` added to the schema. Code-only conformance; the drafts already state the target semantics. Note this is a conformance defect (governs *who* may act; derived authority stays strict-subset-bounded), not an authority-escalation path.

**Concern 2 — approved-agent / lineage-root recovery (DEFERRED).** The legitimate requirement behind retiring `mission.approved_client` is real, but within a domain the approved agent is already the Mission's `client_id` on the record (recoverable via introspection), and across lineage via the `parent`/`predecessor` record links. Only **cross-domain** (partner can't introspect) would need it on-token — and cross-domain projection carries no actor today, with delegate-crossing explicitly out of scope, so there is likely **no consumer yet**. When built, it must be a **distinguished attribution claim, NOT the `act` chain** (`act` is authorization-bearing and cross-domain narrows out non-portable `sub` client identifiers; putting the approved agent in `act` would re-conflate the two concerns). Deferred until a real cross-domain consumer exists.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Context rather than a correction, since this is your substrate's own delegation model — but it may matter for anything in the binding that leans on AAuth's `act`.

**dickhardt/AAuth#73 removes `act` from AAuth auth tokens entirely**, along with the agent identifier. The reasoning:

In call chaining the intermediary signs the downstream request with its own key and presents its own credentials, so a downstream resource already knows who is calling. `act` named the parties one and two hops further up — parties the recipient has no relationship with and cannot evaluate, and which are also the person's tooling, disclosed to a resource that had no use for them. The chain is held by the person server, which authorizes every hop and holds the mission log.

There was also no interop to preserve: RFC 8693's `act` names the *current* actor, whereas AAuth put the *upstream* party there and used `agent` rather than `sub` inside each node. It was a different claim wearing the same name.

**Your rationale here doesn't transfer, and I don't think it should.** You want the chain on the token because a partner Resource AS that cannot call the origin issuer's introspection still needs to read the chain root. AAuth doesn't have that case — the person server is in the loop on every hop by construction, so nothing needs to travel for a party that can't ask. Your model looks right for your topology; it just no longer has an AAuth analogue to cite.

Worth checking whether `draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth` references AAuth's `act` or the auth token's `agent` claim anywhere, since both are gone in -11. Sub-agent structure is likewise no longer visible downstream — the person server issued both tokens and holds the `parent_agent` binding.

Fuller -11 summary on #445.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## External review independently corroborates Concern 2

A fresh OAuth architecture review (finding 8, "the approved agent disappears from delegated tokens") independently re-derived this issue's **Concern 2**. Verified against current `main`: the core states its own gap plainly — the originally-approved agent is not carried on the token, only in the Mission Record, and an RS `MUST NOT` infer it from `client_id` (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md` ~L2365-2368, L3575-3579). So an RS holding a delegated token cannot correlate the executing delegate back to the approved client without another artifact.

The reviewer's proposed remedy — a stable, **non-authoritative** `mission.approved_client_id` for correlation / policy-input / audit, explicitly **not** an authorization grant — is exactly the shape D63 already concluded: a **distinguished attribution claim, not the `act` chain** (`act` is authorization-bearing and cross-domain narrows out non-portable `sub` client identifiers, so putting the approved agent in `act` re-conflates the two concerns). It even echoes the dropped `mission.approved_client` name.

**Status unchanged: still deferred.** The scenario remains unreachable cross-domain today — delegate-crossing is out of scope (`cross-domain` ~L544-549) and the cross-domain grant carries no `act` chain, so "no consumer yet" (the D63 gating premise) still holds.

**One live edge to watch as the trigger for un-deferring:** a target-domain Resource AS that mints its *own* delegated tokens (whose `act` root is the local delegate at depth 0) still cannot recover the *original* approved agent — the `mission` claim correlates to the Mission, not to the approved client. If a real deployment needs that cross-domain approved-agent correlation, that's the concrete Concern-2 consumer that would justify building the distinguished attribution claim.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Architecture review — revise before implementation

The updated direction is substantially better, especially the separation between issuer-mediated delegation and holder-mediated attenuation and the D63 corollary that authorization continuity, not organizational topology, determines whether history extends or restarts. I recommend revising the proposed wire model before implementation, however. It does not yet establish the portable identity guarantees required by #538.

### P1 — The attenuation root still does not identify the approved agent

The proposed ruling says the issuer-signed root, its `cnf`, and Mission-record correlation identify the originally approved agent. That is not sufficient for a portable chain:

* `client_id` identifies the immediate OAuth client, not an actor identity.
* `cnf` identifies a key, not the person or workload controlling it.
* The approved agent remains only in the Mission Record, which a downstream or cross-organization verifier may not possess.
* Offline Attenuation does not normatively require root `client_id` to equal the Mission's originally approved client.

Make the root carry an issuer-attested actor identity bound to its `cnf`. A root `act` naming the approved agent is the cleanest model because the root represents the initial subject-to-agent delegation. A distinguished origin-actor statement is another possibility, but a bare key plus an inaccessible Mission Record is not portable actor identity.

### P1 — Holder-minted `act` values are not authenticated identities

A parent signature proves that the parent delegated to the child key. It does not prove that arbitrary `act.iss`, `act.sub`, or `sub_profile` values identify the controller of that key. The OAuth Actor Profile normally gets this property from the AS authenticating the actor and constructing the actor object; `(act.iss, act.sub)` is the canonical identity and top-level `cnf` binds the current presenter.

Holder-mediated attribution therefore needs an explicit trust rule:

* For cross-organization use, require a validated workload credential or attestation binding `(act.iss, act.sub)` to the child token's `cnf`.
* Fail closed if a named actor is required and that binding is absent or invalid.
* An unverified actor object may be retained as informational provenance, but MUST NOT satisfy `allowed_delegates`, `sub_profile`, or any authorization rule.
* Actor Proofs can add actor participation/non-repudiation, but do not by themselves establish the identity-to-`cnf` binding unless that composition is specified explicitly.

The proposed key-only default is reasonable only where authorization does not depend on a named actor. It cannot satisfy #538's cross-organization case.

### P1 — Do not repeat the complete nested `act` chain in every AAT artifact

AAT already requires the complete signed root-to-leaf token chain. Each child is linked to its parent, signed by the parent key, and binds the next holder through `cnf`. Adding an ever-growing nested `act` history to every artifact duplicates the same history, creates quadratic growth, adds consistency rules, increases privacy exposure, and enlarges denial-of-service inputs.

RFC 8693 nesting is useful when an AS issues one replacement token and the prior tokens disappear. That is not the AAT representation.

Instead, each AAT artifact should carry only the actor for that hop. Reconstruct the ordered actor history from the validated artifact chain, and materialize a conventional nested RFC 8693 `act` projection once at a PDP, introspection, or destination-AS boundary when needed.

The verification algorithm should:

1. Validate the root and its issuer-attested root actor.
2. Validate each parent signature, parent hash, attenuation, depth, expiry, and audience.
3. Validate each current-hop actor's binding to the child `cnf`.
4. Reconstruct the actor chain from the validated artifacts.
5. Reject conflicting or duplicated representations.

### P1 — Actor Receipts do not directly solve holder-mediated projection provenance

Actor Receipts fit issuer-mediated delegation, where an AS or token translation service adds a visible `act` entry and signs a receipt for that hop. AAT hops are holder-created, while the proposed destination projection deliberately restarts and removes the upstream `act` chain. A destination AS cannot retroactively manufacture issuer receipts for historical holder-created hops without changing the meaning of those receipts.

Keep Actor Receipts in the issuer-mediated lane. For an AAT-to-local-token bridge, select one of:

* carry the validated AAT chain alongside the local token;
* expose the validated chain through introspection or evidence resolution; or
* issue a destination-AS chain-verification attestation committing to the complete AAT chain and verification result.

The last option is an AS attestation about verification, not an Actor Receipt claiming that an AS created each historical delegation hop.

### P2 — The Authority Bounds restriction is incomplete

Prohibiting only `reauthorized` and `bounds_events` does not preserve Mission monotonicity. Actor Authority Bounds also permits a `domain_transition` basis reset, and its audience behavior is not monotonically narrowing by default.

A Mission profile should prohibit every basis-reset or widening mechanism within the same Mission, including `domain_transition`. Cross-domain vocabulary translation needs an explicit verified subset/projection rule. A new authority basis belongs in Expansion, successor creation, or another fresh approval boundary. Keep the detailed Authority Bounds profile in a separate issue rather than growing #433 further.

### Scope and sequencing

Concern 1, the shared actor-eligibility matcher, is implemented for core and child delegation. Mark it complete and remove it from this issue's active scope. Keep AAuth cleanup in #445.

Recommended answers to the open questions:

1. Specify the actor field through #538 first, because that is the first consumer requiring authenticated named-actor identity; generalize it into base Attenuation after those verification semantics are concrete.
2. Reuse `act` for the current actor on each signed AAT artifact, not for a complete duplicated nested history. Reconstruct/materialize the RFC 8693 chain at projection time.
3. Land the normative wire and verification changes with #538. #433 should record the architectural ruling. #539 only needs the rule that `act` is attribution rather than authority and need not wait for the wire change.

### Suggested ruling

> Delegation history follows authorization continuity, not organizational topology. Issuer-mediated delegation represents the current actor using RFC 8693 `act` and extends the nested chain while authority remains within the same approved Mission. A new approval, successor, child Mission, or authority expansion starts a new delegation basis.
>
> Holder-mediated offline attenuation represents the actor for each hop in that hop's signed artifact. The root actor is asserted by the Mission issuer and bound to the root presenter key. Every subsequent named actor MUST be independently bound to the child `cnf`; otherwise the hop is key-only and its asserted identity MUST NOT influence authorization. The complete actor history is reconstructed from the validated root-to-leaf artifact chain.
>
> A destination-domain projection starts a local RFC 8693 `act` chain. Upstream holder-mediated history remains derivation evidence and MUST remain verifiably available if provenance is claimed.

This preserves the sound parts of D63, gives #538 an implementable identity model, and avoids turning `act` into a redundant second attenuation chain.

The PR closes this issue on merge.

Disposition of everything else, for the record:
- **Concern 1** (shared eligibility matcher): implemented for core and child delegation; complete, out of scope here.
- **Concern 2** (approved-agent recovery): stays deferred; its named shape is profiling the hop-receipts MAY Cross-Domain already carries, and its trigger is a real cross-domain consumer needing approved-agent correlation (the target-domain-minted-token edge recorded above).

issues.title: Core: stale description of the substrate companion after the kernel refactor
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
The published core describes the substrate companion as a generalization of the Mission model:

> A substrate-neutral statement of the Mission model, generalizing it across non-OAuth authorization substrates, is specified separately and is out of scope for this document. (draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md:487-489; a related informative mention at :361-365 calls the Mission model "a candidate binding onto that substrate" for GNAP.)

After the substrate's capability refactor (#428) and the follow-ups (#438 Bounded Reliance, #439 standalone posture + family bridge), that description inverts the actual relationship: the substrate is now a standalone contextual-governance kernel adoptable outside the family, and this document's Mission model is its OAuth-native instantiation. The substrate's family appendix carries the vocabulary mapping and a scoped precedence rule (the core governs the OAuth-native mapping; the substrate governs kernel and capability vocabulary; no normative dependency either way).

Proposed for the core's next revision (no normative change, informative description only): replace the sentence at :487-489 with wording along the lines of:

> A binding-neutral contextual-governance kernel, of which this document's Mission model is the OAuth-native instantiation, is specified separately and is out of scope for this document.

Both informative mentions should be checked together so the GNAP paragraph's "binding onto that substrate" phrasing stays consistent with the kernel/capability vocabulary.

Per family process the core is published and is not edited directly; this issue records the reconciliation for the next revision.

issues.title: Tracking: upstream AAuth coordination backlog (extension points)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
Living tracker for coordination with the AAuth author. Policy: bank asks here, engage upstream once when the list is stable, in the repo's extension-proposal style (their #10/#48/#71 precedent). **This body is the canonical list; the comment trail is history.** Resolved items are pruned (see the trail for the record); the base protocol referenced is the AAuth editor's copy as of the merged person-token revision (upstream PR #73), which the family aligned to in #472.

## Active asks

- [ ] **Clock-skew documentation for `expires_at`.**
  *Problem:* the base protocol enforces `expires_at` on every PS decision path and caps every token carrying `mission_s256`, but says nothing about clock synchronization, comparison precision, or tolerated skew.
  *Proposal:* one deployment-documentation sentence, per the expiry profile's Security Considerations (draft-mcguinness-aauth-mission-expiry, which retains this as a delta). Raise opportunistically.

## Family follow-on (ours, not an upstream ask)

- [ ] **Relocate management's operations to `mission_control_endpoint`.** The base protocol defines it as the PS's mission control plane for parties other than the owning agent and charters its operations to a companion specification — this document's scope (draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth-management). The relocation adopts the per-mission URL and `action` discriminator conventions and defines the non-agent authentication model the base protocol leaves to the companion. #472 records the split and schedules this as the management draft's next revision.

## Coordination (not asks)

- **Mission events profile:** if drafted, a profile of `draft-hardt-aauth-events` (subscribe tokens, AP-inboxed signed JWTs), never a new transport; candidate events `mission.terminated`, `mission.expiring`, `mission.policy_changed`, `mission.compromise_suspected`; coordinate with upstream #71 first.
- **Log completeness / offline activity integrity:** coordinate with upstream #49; the binding discloses the honest scope (PS-observed vs agent-reported); any future audit-receipts extension distinguishes PS-observed decisions, agent-reported actions, and harness-attested evidence, and its receipts are evidence, never reusable authorization.
- **Delegation visibility:** the base protocol carries no `act` chain in tokens; the chain is PS-held, and the management companion's delegation-tree operation is its interoperable view. Keep that scope stable while upstream #25 is unsettled.

## Not planned

- Another structured Authority Set for AAuth: R3 owns resource-owned structured semantics; an AAuth+R3 composition statement is the most the family should add.
- Delegation-tree scope changes while upstream #25 is unsettled.

comments.author: mcguinness

The upstream ask itself (reserve the name / add the extensibility sentence) remains open.

comments.body:
Additions from the external review (verified against upstream sources):

- [ ] **AAuth Mission Events profile.** Upstream `draft-hardt-aauth-events` exists (Standards Track: subscribe tokens, signed-JWT delivery via the Agent Provider inbox). A mission events profile (`mission.terminated`, `mission.expiring`, `mission.policy_changed`, `mission.compromise_suspected`) should be a profile of that transport, not a new one, and should coordinate with upstream #71 (activity/compromise signal sharing) before drafting.
- [ ] **Upstream the lifecycle status semantics.** The mission-status operation's semantics (and an operation registry for `mission_endpoint`) would ideally live in base AAuth rather than only in the family's management companion. Note: AAuth-10 §8.5 already charters exactly our companion's scope ("revocation, delegation tree queries, and administrative interfaces... will be defined in a companion specification"), so the ask is blessing/adoption, not permission. The management draft now reuses the base `mission_status` member name (#456).
- [ ] **Coordinate log-completeness work with upstream #49** (mission-log completeness under agent-PS partition). The binding now discloses the honest scope (PS-observed vs agent-reported, #456); a future Offline Activity Integrity / audit-receipts extension, if offline `approved_tools` governance comes into scope, should distinguish PS-observed decisions, agent-reported actions, harness-attested evidence, and tamper-evidence vs completeness, and its receipts must be evidence, not reusable authorization.

Explicitly not planned: another structured Authority Set for AAuth (R3 already owns resource-owned structured semantics; an AAuth+R3 composition statement is the most the family should ever add), and delegation-tree scope changes while upstream #25 is unsettled.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
New upstream ask from the third-round review (verified against protocol §9.1.1):

- [ ] **Mission-propagation downgrade protection.** The PS-to-AS token request carries the mission only inside the presented resource token (`resource_token`, `agent_token`, `subagent_token`, `upstream_token`; no independent mission parameter), so a mission-unaware resource that ignores `AAuth-Mission` silently yields a missionless token request the PS cannot attribute to the mission. Ask: an independent mission-reference parameter on the token request (or an explicit rule that a PS may require one), plus a resource-side requirement or signal for echoing the reference into the resource token, so mission governance cannot be stripped by an intermediary. The Mission binding now bounds the downgrade locally (agent verifies the echo; a governance-bound agent's missionless token requests are rejected) but the structural fix belongs upstream.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Body consolidated into the canonical problem/proposal list (six active asks, three coordination notes, resolved and not-planned sections), folding in the original three items, the three comments above, and the PR #73 reshaping. Earlier comments are superseded by the body.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Thanks for keeping this list — it's been useful. Status against **dickhardt/AAuth#73**, which is open on the `person-token` branch and becomes `draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11`. Not merged yet, so nothing here is final.

## Resolved

**Mission-propagation downgrade protection** (your third-round ask) — solved, though not the way you proposed. Rather than an independent mission parameter on the token request, the mission now travels inside a new **person token**: a PS-issued JWT, audience-restricted to one resource, that the agent presents in `Signature-Key` in place of its agent token. The PS validates the mission when it issues that token, the resource MUST copy `mission_s256` into the resource token, and the resource token carries `person_token_jti` naming the person token it was derived from — so the PS resolves what it actually issued and compares.

That makes stripping **detectable** rather than merely prohibited. Worth noting why claim comparison alone wouldn't have been enough: an agent running concurrent missions holds several person tokens for the same resource, so "the person token issued for this agent and resource" doesn't identify one.

`AAuth-Mission` is removed entirely. A mission-unaware resource ignoring the header is no longer a reachable state.

**`expires_at` adopted natively** — your stretch goal. The mission blob MAY carry it, no token carrying `mission_s256` may have an `exp` later than it, every PS decision path compares current time against it, and a new `mission_expired` status distinguishes a mission that ran out from one that was revoked.

**Mission-blob member extensibility** — the member lists are now stated to be a floor, not a closed set. A PS MAY add members, readers MUST ignore what they don't recognize, and a blob carrying an extra member has a different `s256` because it is a different mission.

**`mission_control_endpoint`** — now described as the human-facing administrative surface, explicitly distinct from the interoperable lifecycle operations at `mission_endpoint`, and marked work-in-progress with a separate specification expected. Companion specs shouldn't build interoperable behavior on it meanwhile.

## Still open — and I'd like your view

**Operation discrimination at `mission_endpoint`.** Agreed this is a real gap, and it's an inconsistency in our own document before it's an accommodation: the deferred-response pattern already solved the identical problem with a REQUIRED `action` member on POSTs to the pending URL.

The shape I'm leaning toward is a sub-resource rather than a body discriminator:

```
POST   {mission_endpoint}                  create
GET    {mission_endpoint}/{mission_s256}   status
DELETE {mission_endpoint}/{mission_s256}   terminate
```

Two reasons. AAuth signs `@method`, `@authority`, and `@path` on every request but does not require `content-digest` — so a body discriminator isn't necessarily integrity-protected while method and path always are. And a PS that doesn't implement an operation returns `405`, which is defined HTTP behavior rather than new spec text.

There's precedent: pending URLs already use `GET` to poll, `POST` to respond, `DELETE` to cancel.

My inclination is to **reserve the shape and not define the operations** — the §8.5 charter is yours and specifying status and terminate here would take the work rather than unblock it. But that's your call as much as ours; tell me if a body discriminator suits your drafts better, or if you'd rather AAuth define the operations after all.

## Two premises under #447 moved

Flagging these because #447 landed on the 10th and -11 changes the ground it stands on.

- **Byte-exact agent storage is gone.** Agents no longer store the approval response bytes verbatim. The blob is returned base64url-encoded in an envelope alongside `s256`, the PS hashes the bytes it persists, and agent verification is a SHOULD. Encoding it was what gave the digest an unambiguous byte sequence once the envelope needed room for other members.
- **`capabilities` moved out of the blob**, to the envelope — specifically because session-varying data doesn't belong in an immutable hashed record and shouldn't perturb the digest of two otherwise identical missions. It was cited in #447 as precedent for PS-determined session-specific information inside the committed bytes, and that reasoning now runs the other way.

Neither disturbs the conclusion that the member list is open — that's now stated directly.

## Other -11 changes affecting pins

The family is pinned to -10. Beyond the above:

- The `{approver, s256}` mission reference becomes a bare **`mission_s256`** string; `approver` is dropped everywhere but the blob, since `ps` identifies the person server.
- Auth tokens no longer carry `agent`, and **`act` is removed entirely** — see the note on #433.
- `token_endpoint` becomes **`auth_token_endpoint`** in PS and AS metadata.
- Five resource access modes rather than four, with **person identity** as a distinct mode.
- The mission blob gained `approved_resources`; a proposal MAY name `resources` and receive a person token for each.
- The opaque credential in `AAuth-Access` is now named the **session token**.

Unchanged and still yours: the §8.5 sentence chartering revocation, delegation-tree queries, and administrative interfaces to a companion specification, and the `mission_status` member name.

comments.body:

- Operation extension point: the base protocol adopted a REQUIRED `action` discriminator at per-mission URLs and explicitly charters non-owning-agent operations (status, terminate, delegation queries) to a companion specification at `mission_control_endpoint` — an anchor literally named #mission-management.

issues.title: Child creation + peer create-or-mutate exchanges need business-level idempotency
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Child creation (and peer create-or-mutate token exchanges) need business-level idempotency

From the fresh architecture review; verified against current `main`.

**Gap.** Child Mission creation relies on DPoP `jti` single-use for replay protection (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md` request-processing, ~L623-624 / L668). That prevents reuse of *one* proof, but it does not prevent a **duplicate child** when:

1. the AS creates the child,
2. the success response is lost in transit,
3. the client retries with a **fresh** DPoP proof (new `jti`, which passes replay protection) → a second Child Mission.

Verified there is no other dedup in the flow: no `idempotency_key`/`delegation_request_id`/dedup constraint anywhere in the draft body; `intent_hash` is only a Child-Evidence anchor input, not a uniqueness constraint; `{{creation-race}}` handles parent *state* races, not duplicate creation. The gap is sharpest in the **synchronous** completion mode, which the draft itself calls "the common case" (the response *is* the child grant). Deferred and Interactive modes are more naturally handle/ceremony-scoped, though the initial deferred request is also not declared idempotent on a business key.

**Proposed shape (for discussion — scope/placement TBD).** A stable `delegation_request_id` / `idempotency_key`, scoped to the parent Mission + requesting client:
- same key + same normalized request → return the original result;
- same key + different request → reject;
- retain the mapping for at least the retry horizon.

The same pattern should cover **template dispatch** (`mission-dispatch`) and the peer **expansion** token exchange — i.e. all create-or-mutate Mission token exchanges. This is new normative content spanning child-delegation / template / expansion, so it wants a deliberate scope + placement decision rather than an inline edit.

Disposition from the review triage: real gap, no prior decision, **file** (not fix-now).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Shipped (auto-closed by the PR merge; completing the record). #488 (spec): creation_request_id REQUIRED on child-creation and expansion across all completion modes, expansion-owned + IANA-registered; typed operation fingerprint (mission-creation-fingerprint anchor); durable reserved->completed|failed reservation committed atomically with creation; recovery-as-delivery (expired delivery credentials re-minted for the already-created Mission under issuance-only accounting); the superseded-predecessor lookup-order rule; tombstone retention. #487 (code): the store, both paths, and three adjacent verified gaps fixed (proof-jti replay cache on all token-endpoint DPoP blocks, dispatch randomUUID fallback removed, deferral dedup client-scoped) plus the predecessor cross-check refusal. Gate 66 files / 594 tests / 0 skipped. Follow-ons: #485 (async-delegation retry safety), #486 (sync-successor divergence, decide). Decision log D69.

issues.title: Core: carry the authority proposal on the standard authorization_details parameter (retire proposed_authority-in-intent)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Core: carry the authority proposal on the standard `authorization_details` parameter

**Status: decided (2026-08-11), amendments incorporated; implementation proceeding issue-first per the core edit protocol.** This issue is the decision record and the breaking-change disclosure.

### Problem

Concrete authority is proposed inside `mission_intent` as the `proposed_authority` member (an array of objects each shaped as an RFC 9396 `authorization_details` entry), and the standard top-level `authorization_details` parameter is refused alongside `mission_intent` (`invalid_request`). Three defects follow:

1. **Custom carriage of standard semantics.** In narrowing mode (RECOMMENDED), derivation MUST produce same-type subsets of the proposed entries. Request, policy-narrow, grant is exactly RFC 9396's model, same object shape, same subset relation, same granted echo. The custom member adds no semantic capability; it relocates bytes.
2. **Internal inconsistency.** `scope` and `resource` are accepted top-level as requested subsets; only `authorization_details` is refused. And the family's adopted remediation grain (`authorization_remediation`, draft-zehavi) returns `authorization_details` objects the client must re-wrap into the custom member: the family's output vocabulary is forbidden as its input.
3. **A conformant-client trap.** Discovery advertises `mission_resource_access` in `authorization_details_types_supported` (SHOULD) and mandates its JSON Schema (MUST), but nowhere says the type is not client-submittable. A conformant RFC 9396 client reading that metadata builds a request that is guaranteed to be refused.

Three independent external review rounds converged on this point after updating on factual corrections elsewhere; the OAuth WG will raise the same objection.

**Calibration (what is NOT wrong):** enforcement is already pure RFC 9396 (the granted echo on tokens is standard); the task/authority commitment split already exists (`intent_hash` vs `authority_hash`); "a proposal, never authority" is untouched. This is carriage and packaging, not trust model.

### Decision

`mission_intent` becomes pure task context; the authority proposal rides the standard top-level `authorization_details` parameter, pushed through PAR alongside it. Semantics unchanged: the submitted details are a proposal, never authority; the AS derives and bounds by policy; narrowing mode still derives same-type subsets; template mode (no proposal; intent-only derivation) is untouched. The prohibition inverts: `mission_intent` carries no authority members.

**Commitment (domain separation, extending D57):**

| Question | Artifact | Commitment |
|---|---|---|
| What is the work? | `mission_intent` (task only) | `intent_hash` (`typ: mission-intent`) |
| What did the agent ask for? | submitted `authorization_details` | `proposal_hash` (`typ: mission-proposed-authority`), present iff a proposal was submitted |
| What was granted? | derived Authority Set | `authority_hash` (unchanged) |
| Under what basis? | `approval_basis` | record metadata (unchanged) |

`proposal_hash` is Mission-record metadata surfaced through introspection and the record schema; it is not carried on the `mission` token claim (approval-time provenance, not enforcement input, matching the `approval_basis` treatment).

**TOCTOU across the split anchors:** a change to any of task, proposal, or derived set between approval rendering and decision recomputes all three commitments; no Mission is created without consent to the changed context (per the substrate approval-event rule). Stated normatively so a swapped proposal under an unchanged `intent_hash` cannot equivocate.

**Anti-downgrade, both sides:** the existing client-side MUST NOT (a client holding an Intent must not strip it to obtain ungoverned tokens) gains an AS-side enforcement hook: a deployment that places a client under Mission governance rejects bare `authorization_details` from that client, mirroring the AAuth missionless-request pattern (#459).

**Consequential cleanups:** the discovery trap dissolves (the type is advertised and legitimately submittable as a proposal); the remediation loop closes natively (returned `authorization_details` feed the standard parameter directly); the partial-derivation echo-diff rationale re-anchors to `proposal_hash`.

### Breaking change (disclosed)

This changes the `intent_hash` input for any Intent that previously carried `proposed_authority`: existing integrity-anchor test vectors that include a proposal will no longer reproduce. The core is the editor's draft (`-latest`) with no known implementers beyond the reference implementation, but the datatracker-published artifact's anchor semantics change. The core Document History will carry an explicit entry ("anchor inputs changed: `intent_hash` no longer covers the authority proposal; `proposal_hash` added"), and `src/SPEC_VERSIONS.md` will record the supersession. All worked examples and JCS test vectors are recomputed and independently re-verified as part of the change.

### Plan

- **Phase 1 (core spec, one PR):** carriage swap, prohibition inversion, `proposal_hash` + TOCTOU rule + AS-side downgrade hook, discovery and remediation-grain alignment, vectors recomputed, Document History entry. Folds the two small round-3 items (subject-mapping sentence; discovery clarification).
- **Phase 2 (companion sweep, one PR):** grep-derived family-wide sweep, not a fixed list; seeded candidates: shaping, authzen, architecture (integrity-anchor envelope enumeration), substrate (family-vocabulary "Approved Context" row), consent-evidence (disclosure-rendering mirror), mandate and approval-revision (anchor enumeration / revision flows), audit (approval-event canonical bytes note).
- **Phase 3 (reference impl, one PR):** accept client-submitted `authorization_details` on PAR as kernel proposal input (issued details stay issuer-derived), record + anchor plumbing, D60 intake validation moves to the new path, tests incl. governed-client bare-details rejection and vector recomputation.
- Each phase independently verified before merge; D-entry on completion.

issues.title: Tracking: AuthZEN WG coordination backlog
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
Living tracker for asks to raise with the OpenID AuthZEN working group, accumulated across the runtime/authzen review rounds (PRs #460, #462, #465, #473, #474, #480). Same conventions as the AAuth tracker (#445): bank asks here, propose once when the list stabilizes, and draft any outward-facing text for review before posting. Add new asks as comments; check items off when resolved upstream.

- [ ] **Tier 1: a `critical` (must-understand) response-context marker** — the JOSE `crit` pattern (RFC 7515) applied to the evaluation response: `context.critical` names members the PEP MUST recognize and process to rely on the decision, else effective deny. Today the obligations array is AuthZEN's only must-understand mechanism, so profiles attaching decision-scoped constraints must either mis-model them as obligations or lose fail-closed against older PEPs. One-paragraph addition to core or the obligations profile; generic for every profile. Running code: draft-mcguinness-mission-authzen profiles the member in exactly this shape and defers to a standardized mechanism once defined.
- [ ] **Tier 2: a decision `conditions` class** — completing the XACML-lineage triad the obligations profile two-thirds adopts: obligations (MUST do), advice (MAY do), and conditions (only-valid-if): declarative constraints on relying on a decision, evaluated at every use rather than executed once, with unrecognized-condition = decision unusable, a seed registry (`valid_until`, `use_limit`, a request-binding digest, audience binding), and `supported_conditions` discovery symmetric to `supported_obligations`. Also fixes core's silence on decision reuse/caching (`valid_until` alone would). Running code: the Mission AuthZEN binding's `permit` member carries exactly these conditions with these semantics.
- [ ] **Obligations profile example cleanup** — the "Requesting Human Approval" obligation example collides with ARAP's model: a human approval that creates governance/approval state is ARAP's lane, not a PEP obligation; a PEP-local confirmation with no governance state could remain an obligation example.
- [ ] **ARAP: generalize `next_action`** — ARAP defines `next_action`/`retry_after` for the denial of a re-evaluation that presented an approval; the semantics are equally useful on any denial (transient conditions, terminal refusals, requestable denials). The Mission binding extends it with identical semantics and acknowledges the extension; upstream blessing would remove the extension note.

Context: the Mission profile's dependency posture already tracks ARAP and the Obligations Profile normatively (working-group drafts), so these asks refine documents the family has committed to.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Naming closure on tier 2's running code: the Mission AuthZEN binding's member is `context.conditions` (not `permit`), coined in exactly the shape proposed for standardization, with `critical: ["conditions"]` and contents `request_digest`/`valid_until`/`use_limit`. A standardized `context.conditions`, if adopted, is a no-op migration for the profile.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Strengthened rationale for the tier-1 `critical` ask, from PR #480's round-4 review: a profile cannot bootstrap must-understand semantics from inside the response — a PEP that predates the marker ignores the marker itself and proceeds on `decision: true`. Only the core specification (or a profile every implementation is required to process) can establish it. The Mission profile has accordingly REMOVED its profiled `critical` member and falls back to deployment-established PEP conformance gating; the member returns the moment the WG standardizes the mechanism. This makes the ask sharper: it is not a convenience, it is the only place the guarantee can live.

issues.title: Family: consumer-side substrate capability declarations (runtime is the exemplar)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Family: consumer-side substrate capability declarations (runtime is the exemplar)

The substrate's capability model requires that "a substrate-neutral profile MUST declare the kernel functions and optional capabilities it consumes" and forbids inferring an undeclared capability from a generic Missions-support statement. Today only the SUPPLY side exists: the UMA, AAuth, and MAS bindings carry Mission Substrate Statements declaring what they provide. No consumer profile declares what it consumes.

The runtime profile is being aligned first as the exemplar (a fresh external review's F8 finding; runtime is the consumer both the substrate and the architecture already point at). Its Mission Substrate section becomes a consumption declaration: kernel functions consumed plus a capability table (required / conditional with the condition stated), mirroring the supply-side Statement table idiom so provision and consumption pair visually, and its unqualified "another substrate can host this profile unchanged" claim narrows to the declared capability set.

**Remaining consumers to align to the same idiom** (substrate-draft citation counts on current main, a rough proxy for coupling):

- `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-containment.md` (4)
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-metering.md` (4)
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-security-model.md` (5)
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-harness.md` (1)
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-orchestration.md` (1)
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime-evidence.md` (0 citations today; the newly extracted draft should declare its consumption, likely including Portable Evidence / Independently Verifiable, which the runtime profile itself does not consume)

Each gets: a Mission Substrate (consumption) section in the runtime-established idiom, a normative reference to the substrate where capability definitions are consumed (the substrate's references to consumers are informative, so no normative cycles), and a `family-manifest.json` dep. Where a profile's portability prose overclaims, narrow it to the declared set, citing the substrate's Capability Confusion consideration.

Sequencing: after the runtime exemplar merges, these are a mostly mechanical pass per draft; the design decision in each is only the required/conditional split, which should follow each profile's own existing conditional language where it exists.

comments.body: Completing the record (auto-closed by the merge): PR #494 shipped five consumer declarations in the runtime (D68) idiom, the security-model Informational carve-out, both portability overclaims capability-scoped, and the five-finding review round incl. the Approved-Context kernel correction (also fixing the D68 exemplar), the runtime-evidence produce-vs-consume corrections, the IV/PE row split, and metering's exclusive-selector condition. Decision log D72.

issues.title: Async-delegation exchange: retry safety (creation_request_id follow-on)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Async-delegation exchange: retry safety (follow-on to the creation_request_id work)

The `creation_request_id` idempotency mechanism (from #467) covers child-creation, expansion, and (via the existing `dispatch_event_id`) template dispatch. The async-delegation token exchange was deliberately excluded from that pass.

The exclusion is a scoping choice, not a claim that no problem exists: a lost-response retry of the async-delegation exchange can mint a **second delegated refresh-token family** — a second live credential family. The consequence is lower than a duplicate Mission (each family is subset-confined to the grant's `rar` and independently revocable, and no Mission-creation accounting is affected), but it is not retry-safe.

When picked up: apply the same pattern (client-scoped operation identifier + semantic fingerprint + durable reservation + recovery-as-delivery), reusing the definitions the expansion profile owns. The fingerprint members would be the exchange's own inputs (base Mission, confined subset, target resource, presenter cnf).

comments.body: Completing the record (auto-closed by the merge): PR #497 shipped creation_request_id REQUIRED on the async-delegation exchange (D69 primitives by reference; family delivery/recovery defined in continuation.md itself); reserved->family-created->completed reservation preceding all side effects; consumption-proves-delivery with RFC 9700 single-lineage recovery (no sibling RTs); concurrency/crash/post-rotation interleavings tested. Gate 66/600/0-skipped. Decision log D73.

issues.title: Expansion: synchronous mode spec/impl divergence (successor vs confined derivation)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
## Expansion: synchronous mode spec/impl divergence (successor vs confined derivation)

Found during the #467 idempotency review (advisor finding, verified against main).

**Spec** (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-expansion.md`, completion modes): in the synchronous mode "the Mission Issuer issues the **successor's** access token in the token exchange response" — a successor Mission, reachable where a companion pre-consents an authority ceiling (progressive authorization) so the expansion is a drawdown.

**Impl** (`continuation-grant.ts`, expansion handler header): the synchronous branch is "an ordinary confined derivation, **NO successor**" — it mints a subset-confined token against the predecessor and creates nothing.

So the spec's synchronous mode describes Mission creation the reference implementation does not perform. Either:
1. implement the synchronous successor (create the successor record + supersede the predecessor atomically at the exchange, under the pre-consented ceiling), or
2. re-describe the spec's synchronous mode as a confined derivation (no successor) and reserve successor creation for the deferred/interactive modes.

Option 1 matches the drawdown/progressive-authorization design; option 2 matches the shipped code. Needs a deliberate call. Note: the #467 idempotency code scoped itself to actual creation paths, so whichever way this resolves, the sync path inherits the `creation_request_id` machinery only if it becomes a creation path (option 1).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Decided (option B-prime, 2026-08-12): expansion under the std-track document always widens and always requires fresh consent, so the synchronous completion mode is REMOVED (two modes remain: deferred, interactive); a non-widening request is refused with a dedicated denial reason rather than silently served as a confined derivation (which burned derivation budget and escaped the idempotency reservation). The ceiling-drawdown fast-path idea moves to its owner: the experimental progressive companion already completes policy-adjudicated drawdowns via the interactive path with the prompt skipped, and gains a paragraph specifying the drawdown successor's standing-consent approval_basis shape (root_commitment = ceiling_hash). Fact base: the spec's sync mode was unreachable (no ceiling exists in any code), disowned by its trigger (progressive never uses the token exchange), and basis-unspecified; the code's sync branch fired on exactly the input class the spec excluded. Implementation in flight: spec fix/486-sync-successor-spec, code fix/486-sync-successor-code.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Re-triaged decide→now: the option B-prime ruling (2026-08-12) is recorded in-thread but expansion.md still describes the synchronous completion mode verbatim (~:273, :295, :595, :638). This is now an execution task, and as recorded-decision drift it sits at the top of the now lane.

Expansion: two completion modes (deferred, interactive); non-widening requests refused with mandatory nothing_to_expand under invalid_request; 'effective Authority Set' defined (contained/discharged authority is expansion-restorable via fresh consent with disclosed history, never nothing_to_expand).
