- (a) Architecture doc's Mission Substrate section ({{substrate}}, mission-architecture.md). Central, but restates substrate's capability semantics a third time, risking a fourth lockstep-drift pair between the architecture doc and substrate.md.
- (b) Substrate-hosted OAuth Mission Binding Statement (substrate.md, {{oauth-statement}}). That section already carries all eight capability claims in the supplied/activation form and states it is "hosted here so the core remains self-contained with no companion normative dependency" (substrate.md:1132-1134). Adding the crosswalk there colocates it with the authoritative table, rides #551's planned core pointer, and touches core not at all.
- (c) Core's conformance section (oauth-mission.md). Direct, but is a core PR requiring explicit go-ahead.

Recommend (b): zero core touch, no new duplication, and it sits exactly where #551 already plans to point.

### Finding 2: drift tripwires for the lockstep pairs

Three mechanisms are available per pair: shared test vectors (a concrete byte-level artifact both sides can check); a reciprocal in-text sync note naming the counterpart section (cheap, textual); a repo-side script hashing or grepping both copies against a pinned marker (mechanical, but brittle against line-number drift unless keyed to a stable anchor rather than a line range, which is more machinery than these pairs currently warrant).

- **Commitment construction** (oauth-mission.md:2326-2399 vs substrate.md:390-428): recommend a reciprocal pointer to core's existing Integrity Anchor Test Vectors ({{test-vectors}}), added on the substrate.md side. Scope honestly: this pins only the envelope-anchor species over one worked example (`intent_hash` and friends). The canonical-object and raw-octet species, the parse-time duplicate-detection rule, the I-JSON numeric domain, and the reject-unknown-prefix/no-downgrade agility rules stay prose-only, unpinned by any vector. Core already carries the forward pointer ("This section instantiates the substrate's default commitment construction," oauth-mission.md:2378-2380); the reciprocal backward pointer in substrate.md is the only edit needed. Zero core touch.
- **Composition and the Effective Ceiling** (oauth-mission.md:4602-4625 vs mission-architecture.md:834-847): recommend a reciprocal in-text sync note, added on the mission-architecture.md side only, naming the core section by title. No computable bytes here, so a test vector does not apply.
- **Work-product rule** (oauth-mission.md:4318-4358 vs mission-architecture.md:826-832): same treatment, mission-architecture.md-side sync note. Both currently point outward to the Mission Work Products companion but not at each other; the note closes that gap without a core edit.

### Finding 3: architecture-doc nits

- The four-rung ladder (mission-architecture.md:524-554 vs :2234-2392): three of the four rungs carry their Assurance Level tag in a trailing parenthetical (Runtime-Enforced, Governed Agent, High-Assurance Agent); "Protocol core" at :530 does not. Fix: append "(the Baseline Issuance level, {{assurance-levels}})" to match the other three.
- The three-authorization-bases overstatement (mission-architecture.md:812-819): core (oauth-mission.md:2549-2557) fully defines only `direct`; `template` and `policy_drawdown` are companion-profile-defined values of the extensible `type` string. Fix: reword so the sentence says core defines `direct` and reserves the extension point the template and child-delegation companions use for the other two, rather than stating core itself names all three.
- Extra, spotted during citation-check, not one of the two the issue filed: mission-architecture.md:1192-1195 says "seven optional capabilities" and lists seven names, omitting Authorized Context Correlation, the eighth claim substrate.md defines and includes in the OAuth capability table (substrate.md:1198). Fix: correct "seven" to "eight" and add the missing name. Folds into the same architecture-side edit as the two nits above; no separate PR needed.

### Blast radius

| Item | Chosen approach | File(s) touched | Touches core? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Finding 1, recommended (b) | Add crosswalk subsection to the OAuth Mission Binding Statement | draft-mcguinness-mission-substrate.md | No |
| Finding 1, alt (a) | Add crosswalk to Mission Substrate section | draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md | No |
| Finding 1, alt (c) | Add crosswalk to conformance section | draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md | Yes, core PR |
| Finding 2, commitment construction | Reciprocal test-vector pointer | draft-mcguinness-mission-substrate.md | No |
| Finding 2, composition/ceiling | Reciprocal sync note | draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md | No |
| Finding 2, work-product rule | Reciprocal sync note | draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md | No |
| Finding 3, ladder tag + overstatement + count | Three small rewordings, one PR | draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md | No |

## Open questions

- For Finding 1: does the substrate.md crosswalk addition ride on #554 even though the OAuth Statement already uses the target supplied/activation format, or land as its own substrate.md PR that cites #563?
- For Finding 2: is one combined substrate.md and mission-architecture.md PR acceptable for all three tripwires, or should the commitment-construction pointer (substrate.md) and the two sync notes (mission-architecture.md) ship separately?
- For Finding 3: does the seven-to-eight count correction get folded into the same PR as the two filed nits, as sketched above, or tracked separately?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh-main review: **accept with revisions; non-core scope confirmed.**

The crosswalk should not equate the vocabularies. Core's three OPTIONAL items are implementation/conformance roles; the substrate's eight capabilities are scoped guarantee claims. Title and introduce the table accordingly.

The Delegation row needs correction. Core delegation subset-checks `authorization_details`, preserves the `mission` claim, sender-constrains the delegated credential, and refuses issuance unless the Mission is active. It therefore exercises Lifecycle-Gated Authorization, Structured Authority, Monotonic Derivation, and Credential-Bound. The `act` chain itself supplies none of those—it is attribution, never authority. Authorized Context Correlation belongs only if the OAuth Statement explicitly scopes its native association to delegated token exchange.

Introspection primarily activates State-Observable. Cross-Domain adds an interoperable projection surface but exercises existing Lifecycle-Gated, Structured Authority, Monotonic Derivation, and Credential-Bound guarantees; it does not become Portable Evidence merely by crossing a domain. Neither OPTIONAL surface creates a new substrate capability.

The proposed reciprocal links are useful, but call them synchronization or normative-home pointers rather than drift tripwires: a prose pointer detects no drift. Commitment construction can gain a reciprocal pointer to the existing vectors; a real tripwire requires a shared vector or CI assertion. The effective-ceiling and work-product passages are architecture summaries, not exact normative copies.

The architecture nits are confirmed, with these precise corrections:

- change seven capabilities to eight and add Authorized Context Correlation;
- state that core fully defines `direct` and provides the extension point used by companion-defined `template` and `policy_drawdown`; and
- label Protocol core as **the OAuth realization of Baseline Issuance**, preserving the architecture's rule that a binding is not itself an assurance level.

I recommend one standalone #563 PR touching only Substrate and Architecture. Do not fold this semantic work into #554's retired-table-format migration, and do not touch core.

issues.title: Family: convention stragglers from the August 2026 architecture review
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-16 fresh architecture review. Small mechanical convention gaps, batched.

1. **mandate.md lacks the capability-declaration table.** `mandate.md:217` opens with the same substrate-neutral trigger sentence as `runtime.md:530` and `runtime-evidence.md:253-254`, which per `substrate.md:779-782` obligates a declaration. `runtime.md:547-558` and `runtime-evidence.md:273-284` provide tables; mandate.md never does, even though `substrate.md:772-775` names Mandates as a Portable Evidence supplier.
2. **aauth-mission-expiry has no Conformance section.** Every other binding/extension has one; the same-size sibling folds expiry's deltas in by reference (`aauth-management.md:903`, `:927-931`), so the pattern was available.
3. **Substrate Statement placement is inconsistent.** `authority-server.md` front-loads it after Conventions (`:348`); `aauth` (`:758`) and `uma` (`:846`) back-load it after Conformance/Security/Privacy.
4. **transaction-authorization.md never declares its continuity home.** `work-products.md:347-350` places itself against the three-continuities taxonomy explicitly at the same structural point; txn-authz has zero hits for continuity/continuation despite handling execution-time evidence (`transaction-authorization.md:612-628`).
5. **approval-revision.md and approval-governance.md never cross-reference each other** despite extending the same deferred-approval state machine (`approval.md:315-328`); whether a `revision_required` interim outcome needs its own AGR evaluation is left implicit.
6. **"Mission Discovery" heading collision.** `authority-server.md:1030` titles its RFC 8414-style metadata section "Mission Discovery", unrelated to `draft-mcguinness-mission-discovery`; no disambiguating cross-reference exists in either direction.

Sketch and tradeoffs follow in a comment.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Sketch and tradeoffs

Every citation verified against the current text. Two corrections, noted in place: item 3's citations mix two distinct section types (the "Mission Substrate" consumption declaration vs the "Mission Substrate Statement" binding artifact), and item 4's continuation.md citation is :212-224 (the "Three Continuities" section bounds), not :223.

### 1. mandate.md capability table

Target: `draft-mcguinness-mission-mandate.md`, `# Mission Substrate {#mission-substrate}` (215-238), appended after the existing bullet list.

Edit plan: keep the existing primitives list as is and add a "Its declaration against the optional capabilities" paragraph plus table, mirroring runtime.md (549-558) and runtime-evidence.md (275-284). Read against Mandate Verification (637-705), the Failure Taxonomy (705-764), and Mission Evidence (844-874): the Mandate carries `authority_set` as a committed fact a verifier recomputes, never evaluates, is unbound and freely copyable, and is itself the verification artifact and the registrable evidence substrate.md:772-775 names it as. Use `produced` for the Consumption column, the vocabulary transaction-authorization.md's table (813-822, the newest of the three models) already uses; reserve `supplied`/`not supplied` for a future Mission Substrate Statement, a separate, larger artifact this item does not propose adding. Drop `conditional`: substrate.md:833 retires that state for Statements, and the State-Observable row below expresses the same fact as an activation condition in the Scope cell instead.

Draft rows:

| Capability | Consumption | Scope of consumption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structured Authority | not consumed | `authority_set`/`authority_hash` are committed facts a verifier recomputes for correlation (step 6 of {{verification}}); a consumer MUST NOT derive authority from any claim member ({{claims}}) |
| Lifecycle-Gated Authorization | not consumed | A Mandate authorizes no action and gates no decision; reliance on a currently active Mission is the freshness check below, not a gate this document performs |
| State-Observable | consumed | Consumed whenever reliance requires a currently active Mission (step 7 of {{verification}}); `state_at_issuance` never substitutes, and the stale class of {{failures}} applies until current state is obtained |
| Monotonic Derivation | not consumed | A Mandate narrows nothing; a rail's vertical derivation ({{vertical-derivation}}) is that rail's own governance, never this document's narrowing of the Authority Set |
| Credential-Bound | not consumed | A Mandate binds no holder and is freely copyable ({{non-goals}}); a deriving rail MUST independently authenticate the presenter through its own channel ({{vertical-derivation}}) |
| Authorized Context Correlation | not consumed | Presenter correlation is the deriving rail's own independent authentication, never a joining association this document establishes ({{vertical-derivation}}) |
| Independently Verifiable | produced | The Mandate is its own verification artifact: {{verification}} defines canonical input, trust anchor and key discovery (`kid` resolution, {{mission-substrate}}), algorithm agility (step 8), and validity interval (`mandate_exp`, {{state-at-issuance}}) |
| Portable Evidence | produced | Registrable Mission evidence under the audit profile's evidence-type pattern ({{audit-evidence}}); selective disclosure ({{selective-disclosure}}) supplies the minimization the capability requires; already the condition two base bindings' own Statements name ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server}}:415, {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-mission-uma}}:918) |
{: title="Mandate capability consumption"}

Secondary note, not part of this edit: substrate.md's provider-claim rule (near :905) asks a capability-adding specification to update the base binding's Statement. Authority-server and uma already cite Mandate for Portable Evidence; neither cites it for Independently Verifiable. Whether that gap needs closing is left as an open question below rather than folded into this fix.

### 2. aauth-mission-expiry Conformance section

Target: `draft-mcguinness-aauth-mission-expiry.md`, new `# Conformance {#conformance}` section, inserted after Relationship to Other Specifications (134-147) and before Security Considerations (149).

Edit plan: distill a short PS-only MUST/SHOULD list from Enforcement (111-121) and Security Considerations (149-165); the document defines no other conformance-bearing role. Keep it to one role and roughly six lines; the doc is 185 lines and needs no more.

Sample text:

```
An **AAuth Person Server** conforms to this profile when it:

1. requires `expires_at`, once present in the approved mission blob,
   to be an RFC 3339 `date-time` naming an instant later than
   `approved_at` ({{member}});
2. terminates a mission at `expires_at` itself, rather than at the
   next request under the reference ({{enforcement}}); and
3. documents its clock synchronization, comparison precision, and
   tolerated clock skew ({{security-considerations}}).

Support for `expires_at` remains OPTIONAL, following the approved
blob member it profiles.
```

Alternative: fold this profile's deltas into a requiring document's own Conformance by reference, the pattern aauth-management.md:903 and :927-931 already use for this same document. That pattern is proven, but it does not fit here as the sole fix: this document has two consumers at different obligation levels, required by mission-aauth.md (which requires the member and enforces it "as AAuth requires," restated inline at mission-aauth.md:596 with no citation to this document at all) and OPTIONAL under aauth-management.md. A fold-in target can carry one of those relationships, not both, and mission-aauth.md's uncited restatement is itself evidence of drift risk. A standalone section gives both consumers one canonical list to cite instead of restating.

### 3. Substrate Statement placement

substrate.md prescribes no placement, only that a binding "MUST contain a section titled 'Mission Substrate Statement'" (:833). This is a convention ruling, not a conformance fix.

Two section types are in play here, and their counts differ. The consumer-side consumption declaration (substrate.md:779, titled plainly "Mission Substrate") is front-loaded, right after Conventions, in 12 of 13 documents (audit, authzen, discovery, harness, mandate, metering, orchestration, runtime-evidence, runtime, security-model, shaping, containment); transaction-authorization.md:797 is the lone back-loader. The binding-side Mission Substrate Statement (substrate.md:833's nine-item kernel mapping plus capability table) is rarer and splits the other way: authority-server.md:348 front-loads, aauth.md:758 and uma.md:846 back-load, after Conformance/Security/Privacy.

Recommend standardizing both on front-load, right after Conventions and Terminology: it matches the 12-1 convention for declarations, authority-server.md's own placement for Statements, and concrete forward-reference evidence in aauth.md, whose body cites `{{mission-substrate}}` at :254 and :519, before the section exists, forcing a reader forward. The counter-argument is real (a Statement runs 76-114 lines, closer to a conformance annex, plausibly why aauth and uma placed it late) but the forward-reference cost outweighs it once a document's own body depends on the declared vocabulary.

Fix, three moves:
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth.md`: move Mission Substrate Statement (758-834) to right after Conventions and Terminology (162-198), before AAuth Mission Context Model (199).
- `draft-mcguinness-mission-uma.md`: move it (846-960) to right after the Conventions subsection (379-411), before Mission Roles (412).
- `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-transaction-authorization.md`: move Mission Substrate (797-833) to right after Conventions and Terminology (234-282), before Applicability (283).

### 4. transaction-authorization continuity home

Target: `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-transaction-authorization.md`, end of `# Evidence and Audit {#evidence-audit}` (612-628), before Failure Semantics (636). A paragraph, not a new section: work-products.md earned its own section because provenance-versus-evidence is that document's thesis; here the fact is incidental to a section that already exists.

Edit plan: continuation.md's three-continuities taxonomy (212-224) assigns identity continuity to a Continuation Transport, authorization continuity to the Mission, and owns execution-time evidence itself, recorded against the Mission. Transaction-authorization.md already says it "defines no evidence object of its own" (614); its token and challenge are authorization artifacts, not evidence, so the paragraph should say the profile contributes correlation identifiers to the continuity the runtime owns and grants no continuity of its own kind.

Sample text:

```
Transaction authorization sits with the execution-time evidence
continuity, not a continuity of its own: identity continuity belongs
to a Continuation Transport and authorization continuity to the
Mission, while execution-time evidence is the runtime's, recorded
against the Mission ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-continuation}}).
This document defines no evidence object of its own; the correlation
identifiers its token carries, the Mission reference, `txn`, `jti`,
`parameter_digest`, and idempotency identity, let the runtime
profile's Decision and Execution Evidence attribute to this hop.
Transaction authorization grants no identity continuity and no
authorization continuity of its own.
```

### 5. approval-revision and approval-governance cross-references

Targets: `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval-revision.md`, Integration with the Mission Suite (425-459), and `draft-mcguinness-mission-approval-governance.md`, Consent Evidence Relationship (449-474).

Edit plan: approval-revision.md's Integration section already carries a "Consent evidence:" entry (427-438) and a "Shaping:" entry; add a parallel "Approval governance:" entry naming the AGR by reference. approval-governance.md's Consent Evidence Relationship section already reconciles AGR facts against consent evidence member by member (457-472); add one sentence there naming the revision handshake, since a `revision_required` outcome's `narrowed` consent-evidence decision currently has no AGR counterpart at all.

Sample, approval-revision.md:

```
Approval governance:
: Each `revision_required` outcome is interim: no Mission is created,
  and under the no-Mission-no-record rule of Mission Approval
  Governance ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-mission-approval-governance}}),
  no Approval Governance Record commits for it. The final AGR governs
  the approved, narrowed Mission.
```

Sample, approval-governance.md (Consent Evidence Relationship):

```
Where a deferred approval revises under Mission Approval Revision
({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval-revision}}), each
`revision_required` outcome produces a `narrowed` consent-evidence
decision with no corresponding AGR entry: no Mission yet exists for
the no-Mission-no-record rule to attach to. The final AGR's
`intent_hash` names only the approved intent; the revision chain is
presently visible only through consent evidence's
`predecessor_intent_hashes`, the partial view carrying a fact the
authoritative record does not.
```

That last asymmetry, the AGR calling itself authoritative (449-451) while consent evidence alone carries the predecessor chain, is the sharpest open point here, folded into the closing option pair.

### 6. "Mission Discovery" heading collision

Recommend renaming the heading over adding reciprocal notes. A repo-wide grep for the literal title `"Mission Discovery"` returns exactly two hits: the heading itself (authority-server.md:1030) and mission-discovery.md's own front-matter `abbrev` (unrelated). No other document's prose or link depends on the string, and every internal `{{discovery}}` cross-reference in authority-server.md binds to the anchor id, not the title, so this is a heading-text-only change: rename the title, keep `{#discovery}` unchanged, zero other files touched.

The section is confirmed RFC 8414-style metadata (a well-known-URI JSON document whose members "mirror the Mission suite's Authorization Server metadata members," :1030-1048). Two other family documents already title their analogous section "Authorization Server Metadata" at their own `{#discovery}` anchor: `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md:3953` and `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md:1541`. Rename authority-server.md:1030 to **"Mission Authority Server Metadata"**, both resolving the collision and matching that existing convention, rather than "Mission Issuer Metadata," which matches nothing already in the family.

## Open questions

- Item 1: confirm `produced` (transaction-authorization.md's vocabulary) over `supplied` (substrate.md's Statement-only vocabulary) for the mandate.md consumption table, and whether authority-server.md and uma.md's Statements need an added citation to Mandate for Independently Verifiable, alongside the Portable Evidence citation they already carry.
- Item 3: confirm front-load as the standardized placement for both the consumption declaration and the Statement, since substrate.md itself rules nothing.
- Item 5: does a `revision_required` outcome warrant its own AGR evaluation?
  - Option A, no interim AGR: consistent with the existing no-Mission-no-record rule (approval-governance.md:374-379); the chain stays visible only through consent evidence's `narrowed` entries and `predecessor_intent_hashes`. No change to atomic commitment.
  - Option B, an interim AGR per revision hop: treats `revision_required` as a governance decision in its own right, giving every narrowing step an authenticated, committed record; requires amending atomic commitment ({{atomic-commitment}}) to define a record class that exists without a Mission, and likely giving the AGR its own predecessor-chaining member to match consent evidence's.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh-main review: **partially accept; split and revise before implementation. No core change is needed.**

1. **Mandate declaration:** add the consumption declaration, but do not use `produced` as though it were merely another consumption state. Substrate requires a capability provider to publish an updated Statement or Statement extension identifying the binding, activation, scope, temporal behavior, and failure semantics. Either keep this table consumption-only and point to binding Statements for Independently Verifiable and Portable Evidence, or make the supply portion a proper Statement extension. Add Mission Substrate as a normative reference and update the manifest. The unresolved binding is AAuth under #554; MAS and UMA already have independent-verification mechanisms and activate Portable Evidence with Mandate.

2. **AAuth expiry Conformance:** accepted, but preserve normative strength. Member syntax/time ordering and clock documentation are MUSTs; prompt deadline termination is currently SHOULD and must remain SHOULD. The rationale is role-local clarity, not simply that every other extension has a Conformance section.

3. **Statement placement:** this is an editorial preference, not a conformance defect. Substrate requires the section title but prescribes no location, and UMA's Statement is before—not after—Conformance/Security/Privacy. Avoid 76–114-line move-only diffs. If front-loading becomes a documented style rule, coordinate it with #554; otherwise leave existing Statements where they are.

4. **Transaction Authorization continuity:** rewrite the proposed paragraph. The profile defines no Continuation Transport or continuity guarantee. Its token is a bounded, single-use authorization artifact; Runtime records the execution-time evidence. `txn`, token `jti`, and `parameter_digest` correlate that evidence, while the Operation Profile's idempotency identity correlates the effect and is **not carried by the token**. Add Continuation as an informative reference and update the manifest.

5. **Approval Revision/Governance:** choose Option A. `revision_required` creates no Mission and therefore no AGR under the existing atomic-commitment rule. Consent Evidence owns the narrowing history; the final AGR owns the final approval-governance facts. This is deliberate artifact separation, not an authority conflict. Add short reciprocal informative notes and their front-matter/manifest dependencies. Do not create an interim AGR record class in this hygiene issue.

6. **Discovery heading:** accepted. Rename it to “Mission Authority Server Metadata” and retain `{#discovery}`.

Scope correction: the new Substrate, Continuation, and reciprocal Approval references require front-matter and `family-manifest.json` updates. Transaction Authorization's existing Substrate reference is already missing from its manifest dependency list; fold that correction into this batch or coordinate it explicitly with #565.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: Implementation notes from the PR: (1) the Independently Verifiable premise needed a correction, both the MAS and UMA Statements supply that capability through their own mechanisms, not via Mandate, so the mandate table explains self-contained verification for that row and cites the Statements only for Portable Evidence. (2) Two pre-existing manifest gaps left alone: approval-governance.md lacks its substrate dep despite a normative front-matter reference; transaction-authorization.md lacks an approval-governance dep. (3) mandate.md's "three bindings host Mandate" enumeration is in tension with UMA's Statement activating Portable Evidence via Mandate; predates this PR, flagged for a ruling.

issues.title: Meta: README, manifest, and SPEC_VERSIONS hygiene
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-16 fresh architecture review. Repo/meta hygiene, batched.

1. **`family-manifest.json:2` free-text `$comment` says "37 draft-*.md files"; there are 40.** `scripts/check-family-manifest.mjs:134-135` validates only the structured `count` field, so the free text drifts silently.
2. **README architecture diagram is stale.** `README.md:113-163` omits the five newest drafts (transaction-authorization, cross-org-delegation, approval-governance, runtime-evidence, capability-binding). The manifest-validated catalog below it is fully current; drift is confined to hand-maintained prose.
3. **Naming-rule prose is stale and incomplete.** `README.md:454-467`'s example list predates five mission-* drafts, and the third naming pattern (`aauth-mission-*` = AAuth-native extension vs `mission-aauth-*` = Mission's binding to AAuth, consistent with the aauth-budget sibling repo) is stated nowhere.
4. **SPEC_VERSIONS.md has no row for the family's own approval profile.** `services/authorization-server/src/kernel/deferred.ts` realizes `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval`, but only the external DTR and Txn-Challenge substrates are pinned.
5. Non-action note: `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-completion.html/.txt` at repo root are git-ignored local build leftovers from before the fold into Status (commit `ae8654e`); local clutter only.

Sketch and tradeoffs follow in a comment.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Sketch and tradeoffs

**1. `family-manifest.json:2` stale count**

One-line fix: change `"37 draft-*.md files"` to `"40 draft-*.md files"` in the `$comment`.

Related drift found in research: `README.md:28`'s "At a glance" bullet also hardcodes "37 drafts, deliberately decomposed," the same failure, and `scripts/check-family-manifest.mjs` never touches that line either (it only parses README's "The documents" catalog and "Adoption order" sections, per lines 161-201).

Guard options: (A) drop the count from free text entirely, rewording `$comment` (and the README bullet) to describe the manifest without a number, pointing at the validated `count` field as the source of truth; (B) extend `check-family-manifest.mjs:134-135` to regex-extract the number embedded in `$comment` and assert it equals `drafts.length`.

Recommend A. The count already lives, validated, in `manifest.count` (`check-family-manifest.mjs:134-135` already fails the build on `count` drift). A regex against free-text prose is brittle to wording changes ("37 draft-\*.md files" vs "37 drafts") and B would only close the manifest's own copy, leaving the identical README bullet unguarded unless the same regex-and-assert logic is duplicated a second time. Removing the number is the smaller diff and removes the drift vector instead of chasing each copy of it.

**2. Stale README architecture diagram**

Concrete additions, no new rows, respecting bindings-as-peers:

- `enforce each action` row: add two peer lines beside "Runtime contract -> AuthZEN binding": Transaction Authorization (fresh, cross-org, no-callback decision profiling the OAuth transaction-authorization challenge) and Runtime Evidence (Decision/Execution Evidence, Refusal Record, and the portable Mission Receipt). Both are `runtime-enforcement` group, same as the existing line.
- `project` row: add Cross-Organizational Delegation as a peer of Cross-Domain Projection. Both are `cross-domain-projection` group; the draft's own abstract names Projection as "the adapter" that admits the attenuation chain locally.
- `approve and record` row: add Approval Governance Record directly under the existing "THE MISSION: ..." line, as a binding-agnostic overlay (issuer-retained provenance behind the approval event, never a wire artifact), not a fifth box in the four-binding peer block.
- `run and wind down` row: add Capability Binding as a peer of Harness and Orchestration, per its manifest `group: agent-runtime`.

The capability-binding placement is the one soft call: its abstract is entirely about the AuthZEN decision request and `capability_drift` denial, reading closer to `enforce each action` than to session/wind-down concerns, but its manifest group says `agent-runtime`. Placed per the manifest for consistency; flagged below.

Guard evaluation: a maintenance note pointing at the manifest, vs extending `check-family-manifest.mjs` to grep the diagram block for each draft's slug/title token. The script already runs two structurally identical checks (README catalog-link presence, adoption-order nickname presence, lines 161-201) using the same `readFile`/section-slice helpers. Recommend extending it a third time for the diagram block: it reuses proven machinery in this file and turns future drift into a build failure, where a note only turns it into documentation someone can still forget to read.

**3. Naming-rule prose**

Verified against disk: 20 `mission-*` (non-`oauth-`, non-`aauth-`-prefixed) drafts exist. The `README.md:454-467` enumeration names roles for 14 of them. Six are unnamed: the Agent Access Model binding (`mission-aam`), the UMA 2.0 binding (`mission-uma`), AAuth mission management (`mission-aauth-management`), approval governance provenance (`mission-approval-governance`), capability-source binding (`mission-capability-binding`), and runtime evidence records (`mission-runtime-evidence`). That is six, not the five the issue estimates; corrected count.

Sketch addition to the enumeration, inserted before "and the mandate": "...consumption metering, open-world discovery, the Agent Access Model binding, the UMA 2.0 binding, AAuth mission management, approval governance provenance, capability-source binding, runtime evidence records, and the mandate."

Third naming pattern, verified against `draft-mcguinness-aauth-mission-expiry.md`'s abstract ("AAuth's approved mission blob MAY carry `expires_at` ... This document profiles that member"), confirming it profiles a member of AAuth's own approved mission blob:

"A third pattern distinguishes direction at the AAuth binding. `aauth-mission-*` names an AAuth-native extension, a profile of a member already inside AAuth's own approved mission blob (as `draft-mcguinness-aauth-mission-expiry` profiles `expires_at`), consistent with the sibling `draft-mcguinness-aauth-budget` repository's own AAuth-native extensions. `mission-aauth-*` names the Mission family's binding to AAuth and its companions (`draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth`, `draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth-management`), specified the same way as the family's other non-OAuth components."

**4. SPEC_VERSIONS.md missing approval-profile row**

Pin (last commit touching the draft): `11f4d4d` (2026-08-12). Grepping `deferred.ts` and `txn-challenge.ts` for `@spec` tags finds "AROP DTR binding," "expansion," and `mission#...` anchors, but zero `approval#` tags, despite the draft's own section anchors (`#deferred-approval`, `#deferred-sequencing`, `#state-machine`, `#pending-staleness`, `#decision-set`, `#queue-pressure`).

Sketch row:

| Spec | Pinned version | Component | Surfaces | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval` | `11f4d4d` (2026-08-12) | `services/authorization-server/src/kernel/{deferred,txn-challenge}.ts` | `approval#deferred-approval`, `approval#deferred-sequencing`, `approval#state-machine`, `approval#pending-staleness`, `approval#decision-set` | `services/authorization-server/test/{arop,dtr-endpoint,txn-endpoint}.test.ts` |

Alternative reading: fold this into the existing DTR row, since `deferred.ts` already carries it. Worth an explicit row anyway: the DTR row pins only the external `-00` wire mechanics (`deferral_code`, poll/redeem, RFC 8628 backoff codes) under a spec with its own independent revision lifecycle. The Mission-authored sequencing, state machine, staleness rule, and governance-record hook are a separate document with its own commit history and section anchors. Folding them in leaves a future edit to `oauth-mission-approval.md`'s state machine with no row to bump and no anchor to grep, breaking the "diff spec, grep anchors, list affected tests" loop the matrix's own Conventions section defines. An explicit row matches how AuthZEN AROP already gets its own row alongside DTR and Txn Challenge on the same component. None of item 2's five newest drafts, including transaction-authorization (which also touches `txn-challenge.ts`), appear anywhere in `SPEC_VERSIONS.md` yet; out of scope here since they are not yet implemented.

**5. Completion .html/.txt leftovers**

Confirmed git-ignored (`git check-ignore -v` matches both against `.gitignore:1` `*.html` and `.gitignore:5` `*.txt`), left over from `ae8654e` (2026-07-11), which deleted `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-completion.md` folding it into Status. No repo action needed. `lib/main.mk` defines a `clean::` target (line 260); `make clean` removes local build output including these, optional.

## Open questions

- Item 2: should Capability Binding's diagram placement follow its manifest group (`agent-runtime`, "run and wind down") or its content (enforcement-facing, arguably "enforce each action")? Sketched per the manifest for consistency; the tension is worth a second look.
- Item 3: six drafts are missing from the naming-rule enumeration, not five as estimated in the issue body.
- Item 1: README.md:28 carries the identical hardcoded "37 drafts" drift; not in the issue's stated scope but the same guard fix would naturally cover it.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `main@883b497`: **proceed with the README/manifest hygiene, but drop item 4 as currently proposed.**

1. The count drift is confirmed in both `family-manifest.json:2` and `README.md:28`; structured `count: 40` is correct and already validated. Delete both prose counts rather than teaching CI to parse prose.

2. Refresh the architecture diagram, but keep in mind that it is conceptual rather than an exhaustive manifest projection; it already omits older companions. Add the meaningful nodes and label the view as conceptual. Only add a CI check if the manifest first gains explicit diagram-inclusion/display metadata—requiring every draft to appear would make the diagram less useful.

   Semantic placement:

   - Approval Governance → `approve and record`
   - Transaction Authorization → `enforce each action`
   - Runtime Evidence → output of `enforce each action`, linked to `prove`
   - Cross-Organizational Delegation → `delegate/project`
   - Capability Binding → `enforce each action`, not `run and wind down`

   Capability Binding is a decision-time AuthZEN binding. Its conflicting `agent-runtime` manifest group is a separate taxonomy issue, best coordinated with #563.

3. The naming paragraph is missing six non-OAuth drafts, not five. Rather than extending another exhaustive list, replace it with durable category rules and examples, including the useful direction rule: `aauth-mission-*` is AAuth-native extension material; `mission-aauth-*` is the Mission family's AAuth binding/companion.

4. **Do not add `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-approval` to the Implemented matrix yet.** That draft requires pending state before any Mission exists and atomic Mission creation at asynchronous approval. `DeferralStore` instead starts from an existing active Mission and issues a narrowed token carrying that Mission unchanged; that is the AROP/DTR behavior the existing rows already describe. `txn-challenge.ts` is transaction approval, not deferred initial Mission creation. A planning/not-implemented row is truthful if useful, but an Implemented row would overclaim conformance. It would also lack the `@spec approval#...` tags the traceability matrix requires.

5. The ignored completion `.html`/`.txt` files remain local cleanup only.

Recommended result: a small documentation/meta PR for counts, conceptual diagram, and durable naming rules; no Deferred Mission Approval implementation row.

issues.title: Architecture/Runtime: composed kill-switch reality table and the post-taint read posture
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-17 design critique. Two compositions of individually-disclosed facts, stated together nowhere.

**1. The post-taint read window.** Containment's paradigm protected event is a tainted read (`containment.md:472`). Baseline containment is a new-derivation kill only (`containment.md:584-593`); the action-time kill requires a state-observable, Runtime-Enforced check (`containment.md:595-605`). Runtime's RECOMMENDED freshness posture for a consequential read is "token lifetime or a short state lease", the loosest tier (`runtime.md:1753`). Composed: containing a Mission in response to a tainted read does not stop further reads under already-issued tokens until they age out, which is the exposure window containment was invoked to close. Each half is disclosed on its own; the composition is not.

**2. The kill-switch cost, per route.** The core path requires RAR (#220). The MAS ramp's Baseline is audit-only, "no kill switch of any kind exists" (`architecture.md:2271-2279`), until the full PEP/PDP buildout #238 prices as an enterprise target. The Issuance Grant middle path still requires the estate AS to build an RFC 7523 redemption endpoint plus Mission-state integration for refresh (`issuance-grant.md:499-512`). No document composes rung x binding x what actually stops, and when. The OAuth-core freshness half-step exists only in architecture prose (`architecture.md:2288-2295`), absent from README's ladder table.

Producer-side availability under incident is tracked at #250/#310 and is not re-filed here.

Ask: a composed kill-switch-reality table (rung x binding x what stops, when) in the architecture document, and a tighter recommended read posture following a tainted-read trigger.

Sketch and tradeoffs follow in a comment.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Sketch and tradeoffs

Citations checked against source lines; all match exactly (containment.md:472, :584-593, :595-605; runtime.md:1753; architecture.md:2271-2279, :2288-2295; issuance-grant.md:499-512; README:278-283). No correction needed.

### 1. The composed table

Placement: a new `##` subsection in architecture.md, after the cross-cutting-obligations paragraph and the evidence-is-not-prevention note (ending line 2418), before the `## Assurance Claims` heading (line 2420). That keeps the existing ladder table (2399-2404) intact and closes the Mission Assurance Levels section with the rung x binding view before the claims axis opens.

One disambiguation the table must carry as a preamble line: "Baseline" and "Runtime-Enforced" name two different things that share spelling. containment.md uses them for a containment property a consumer gets (:584, :595). architecture.md uses them for an assurance level a deployment adopts (:2248, :2336). The two are not 1:1: a deployment at the Runtime-Enforced level can still get only the Baseline containment property for an action class its Enforcement Scope Statement leaves lifecycle-gated-only, because the property requires a state-observable substrate per class, not per deployment (runtime.md:1640-1651, containment.md:602-605). The table's "Property" column names the containment property; "Rung" names the level; a row can carry a Runtime-Enforced rung and a Baseline property together without contradiction.

Columns: Rung | Binding | Property | Stops at commit | Runs to its own bound.

Four representative rows:

| Rung | Binding | Property | Stops at commit | Runs to its own bound |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline Issuance | OAuth core, structured-authority | Baseline (containment.md:584-593) | New derivation, delegation, cross-domain projection, and offline attenuation roots carrying the contained capability | Tokens already issued, to `exp`; consequential reads under the token-lifetime default (runtime.md:1753), same bound |
| Baseline Issuance | Standalone MAS, no credential-carried authority | Neither (architecture.md:2271-2279) | Nothing at the resource; the transition is recorded and visible in Mission Status (containment.md:654-661) | Every action, indefinitely, until a freshness half-step (architecture.md:2288-2295) or the issuance join restores a gate |
| Runtime-Enforced | Any binding, high-consequence classes | Runtime-Enforced for the classes whose ESS declares an active source; any class left lifecycle-gated-only at that same deployment gets Baseline only, regardless of level (runtime.md:1644-1651, containment.md:602-605) | The gated action, within staleness bound plus permit window plus execution bound (runtime.md:1684-1687, containment.md:595-605) | Ungated paths, bounded by token lifetime |
| Baseline Issuance | MAS as estate control plane, issuance-grant join at each consuming AS | Baseline, contingent on the AS's own state integration (issuance-grant.md:499-512) | With integration: refresh gated each cycle (MUST), access tokens re-checked at redemption (SHOULD). Without: refresh MUST NOT be issued at all | Without integration: an access token already minted runs to its own short lifetime, the grant's minting-time gate only |

What the table must not do: assert a property beyond what its cited clause grants, or generalize a per-class result (the Runtime-Enforced row) into a per-deployment one. It is informative, indexes the four normative documents, and carries no RFC 2119 language of its own. A conflict between a cell and its citation is a table bug, not a new rule.

### 2. The post-taint read posture

(a) rejected. Tightening the RECOMMENDED default for every consequential read taxes every route for every Mission, contained or not, contradicting the freshness dial's own framing that a deployment picks a position per action class (runtime.md:1729-1731), and erases Baseline Issuance's zero-per-action-cost value for deployments that never contain anything.

(c) is not a standalone option; the architecture table above already does (c)'s job. The real question is whether to also do (b) on top of it.

(b) recommended, scoped precisely. Home: runtime.md's state-freshness section, as a new paragraph immediately after the RECOMMENDED-defaults table (after line 1758), not containment.md. Containment already declines to restate freshness rules and defers to runtime's (containment.md:698-702); the tightening belongs where the freshness dial already lives.

Sample sentence, for runtime.md:

> For a Mission carrying a nonzero containment overlay ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-containment}}), the RECOMMENDED consequential-read posture tightens for the overlay's duration to an active source: immediate check or a state lease no longer than the deployment's containment response target. The tightening applies only while the overlay is nonzero; an uncontained Mission's default posture is unchanged.

No new channel needed: containment.md's Visibility section already MUST-carries `containment_version` on the Mission Status Response and the introspection projection (containment.md:654-661), the exact surfaces a runtime state source already reads. This is a policy change, not a new signal.

Scope limit, stated plainly: (b) tightens the posture only where the affected class already has a state-observable source available to move to. A Baseline consumer that checks only `exp` is unaffected and stays bounded by token lifetime, which containment.md:607-610 states is not a deployment failure. (b) narrows the window for deployments that can act on the signal; it does not close the Baseline residual composition #1 names, and this issue should say so rather than imply closure.

Conformance consequence: an Enforcement Scope Statement adopting (b) must publish both the ordinary and the under-containment staleness bound for the affected class, per runtime.md:1680-1684's existing rule that a bound published without its latency consequence is non-conformant.

Availability interaction: (b) inherits the fail-closed rule at runtime.md:1653 (refuse when `active` cannot be established within the bound), so tightening on incident increases dependence on state-source availability exactly during the incident that triggered containment. That composes with the producer-availability tracking at #250/#310, not re-litigated here.

### 3. README half-step

Footnote, not a row. A fifth row would contradict architecture.md:2288-2295's own framing, "a half-step into the next level, not a level of its own." Row 280's "prompt cutoff needs the Runtime-Enforced level" stays true, prompt meaning per-action, if the footnote avoids claiming promptness:

> A deployment can add just a freshness surface (Mission Status or introspection with a published staleness bound) atop Baseline Issuance, without the rest of Runtime-Enforced: a half-step that bounds the revocation cutoff to that staleness window, not prompt, and without per-action enforcement. See the architecture document's Mission Assurance Levels.

Placed directly below the ladder table, after line 283.

### 4. Interactions and blast radius

#220 (RAR-free first tier) changes the core row's mechanism, not the row's kill-switch shape; the table cites derivation gating generically enough to survive either outcome. #238 is what the Runtime-Enforced row's buildout cost is tracking; not re-priced here. #250/#310 covered above. #561/#570 (containment through the UMA outer ring) is a binding-specific composition the UMA document owns; the table stays at the four documents this issue names and adds no UMA row.

Files touched: draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md (new subsection and table), draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime.md (new paragraph in state-freshness), draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-containment.md (one forward-pointer clause in Propagation, not a restatement), README.md (one footnote). issuance-grant.md is cited only. No touch to draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md.

## Open questions

- Should the containment-conditioned tightening key on any nonzero overlay, or only when the overlay narrows a class the affected read touches? The broader trigger is simpler; the narrower one matches the freshness dial's per-class philosophy.
- Is the containment response target a value the deployment must publish in its Enforcement Scope Statement, or can it stay implicit the way ordinary staleness bounds sometimes do before #310 lands?
- The containment response target is currently plain prose in containment.md's Materialized-Capability Residual section, not an anchored term. Now that runtime.md's proposed rule depends on it normatively, does it need promotion to a defined term with its own anchor, so one document's normative text is not pointing at another's prose by phrase match alone?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against current `main` (`73e4557`): **agree with the gap and the composed-table direction, with corrections before drafting.** The Rung-versus-Property distinction is necessary: Architecture's levels are deployment bundles, while Containment's Baseline and Runtime-Enforced properties are obtained per consumer/action class. A Runtime-Enforced deployment can therefore still provide only Baseline containment on an ungated class.

Four changes are needed:

1. **Require a containment-aware freshness source, not merely an “active source.”** Runtime's active-source set includes Status Lists (`runtime.md:1693-1700`), but a contained Mission remains `active`, so its Status List bit does not move (`containment.md:678-684`). A tightened read posture must use a source that can observe the active-to-active authority change: full Status or introspection carrying `containment_version`, Signals carrying the version/overlay change, or fresh state-gated derivation that re-materializes the narrowed authority (`containment.md:649-696`). The under-containment staleness bound belongs in the Enforcement Scope Statement per affected class (`runtime.md:1680-1688`). If “containment response target” becomes a normative input, define and anchor it first; today it is prose at `containment.md:569-575`.

2. **Scope the table to deployments that actually run Containment.** A rung and binding alone do not confer either containment property. The table should say it is composing a Containment-capable deployment with the binding/rung, and every cell remains informative with the cited normative profile controlling.

3. **Correct the residual cells.** Baseline residuals include not only already-issued access tokens but pre-transition cross-domain projection grants and offline attenuation roots, which continue to their own lifetime/depth (`containment.md:535-567`). In the Issuance Grant row, an outstanding grant can still redeem once at a consuming AS that lacks the optional redemption-time state check, until the grant's maximum 300-second lifetime; state-at-redemption is only SHOULD, while refresh is MUST state-gated (`issuance-grant.md:492-512,666-673`). For standalone MAS, “indefinitely” is too absolute: the path runs to whatever native credential, session, or resource-local bound exists, if any. The Runtime-Enforced property is also not inherently limited to high-consequence classes; it applies wherever a class uses a containment-aware source within its published bound.

4. **Prefer an affected-class trigger.** Tighten consequential reads whose authorizing entry/action class intersects the overlay. “Any nonzero overlay” is a defensible conservative default, but it imposes incident-time availability load on unrelated reads and should be labeled as that tradeoff. Also, the overlay never clears on the same Mission—restoration creates a successor—so “for the overlay's duration” means the remainder of that Mission.

The README footnote is worthwhile if it keeps the existing claim precise: a freshness surface is a half-step, not a level, and bounds cutoff without claiming prompt per-action prevention.

**Disposition: approve with those changes.** The architecture table, scoped runtime recommendation, Containment forward pointer, and README footnote make the kill-switch reality legible and narrow the post-taint window where a containment-aware path exists; they do not close the conforming Baseline residual, and the text should continue to say so plainly.

issues.title: Approval: recency and consequence-class bounds on policy-authority approvers
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-17 design critique.

**1. Policy-authority approval has no recency or consequence-class bound.** Core defines the Approver as "a human or an authorized policy authority" (`oauth-mission.md:710-714`). Approval governance lets a `policy` assertion satisfy the accountable-approver rule outright, with the human standing pushed back to whenever the policy itself was approved (`approval-governance.md:268-275`, `:363-367`). No document bounds how stale that upstream human sign-off may be, or restricts which consequence classes may use a policy-authority approver rather than a live human. Security-model's load-bearing answer, "authority is fixed by an approval the agent cannot move" (`security-model.md:389-395`), is equally true of a policy decision made months earlier by someone who never saw this Mission. The architecture permits the human-as-ceremony outcome by name, not by drift.

**2. The approval-time/decision-time split does not state which half carries which guarantee.** The subset rule compares members, not meaning (`oauth-mission.md:1662-1668`); data-dependent conditions, amounts-in-context, and sequencing migrate to runtime policy, metering, and transaction approvals that are never re-rendered to the original Approver (#252 is the family's own admission on sequencing). What the committed Authority Set still guarantees at approval time (a monotone envelope plus a revocation gate) is real but narrower than the consent-evidence machinery's framing suggests.

Ask: a recency bound and consequence-class restriction on policy-authority approval, and a stated answer to which half of the approval-time/decision-time split is load-bearing for which guarantee.

Sketch and tradeoffs follow in a comment.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Sketch and tradeoffs

Citations verified against current main: `oauth-mission.md:710-714`, `:1662-1668`, `:4361-4390`, `approval-governance.md:268-275`, `:363-367`, and `security-model.md:389-395` are all exact. One correction to the premise, noted once: approval-governance.md contains no occurrence of "source"; the #316 authority-source taxonomy (`user_delegated`/`service_owned`/`organizational`) is core's `authority_source` member (`oauth-mission.md:2599-2619`, `{{authority-sources}}` at 752). That taxonomy, approval-governance's assertion `kind` (`human`/`service`/`policy`), and architecture's derivation-boundary ceiling composition (`architecture.md:1516`) are three different axes; none bears on which is fixed here.

### The recency bound

The gap is concrete. An AGR `policy` assertion's `authority` carries `policy_id`, `version`, and `approved_by` (`approval-governance.md:268-275`), no timestamp. `decided_at` is required on the assertion (`:266`) but records when the policy asserted, not when the human approved the policy: the worked example shows both at the same second (`:313`, `:319`). Staleness is not computable from the record as it stands, so a maximum age cannot be enforced until there is a fact to compare it against.

Recommended fix, two layers:

- **The measurable fact (companion-only).** Add `authority.approved_at`, an RFC 3339 timestamp, beside `approved_by` on a `policy` assertion's `authority` object: the human decision instant that authorized the policy version, not the assertion instant. Add a sixth bullet to `{{assertion-requirements}}` (345-370): *"For a `policy` assertion, the issuer MUST NOT count it toward the evaluation if `authority.approved_at` exceeds the deployment's declared maximum policy-approval age for the referenced class."* This inherits the existing consequence at 368-370 (excluded from evaluation), which through `{{atomic-commitment}}` (372-379) means the record does not commit, and core's existing `access_denied` (`2123-2127`) already covers the resulting Approver-facing error. No new error surface, no new wire endpoint.
- **Where the ceiling is declared.** Approval-governance can state its own declaration obligation ("a deployment MUST declare the maximum policy-approval age it enforces per consequence class") without touching core; this is a second publication discipline beside core's existing floor statement. Folding it into the single statement core already requires (`2107-2121`, PR #566's normative home) is the unification option: one statement, one place a relying party reads, at the cost of a third edit to that passage (#424's ruling, PR #566, now this). Flagged as a core touch; not required for (a) to work.

Enforcement lands at AGR evaluation time, inside the existing atomic-commitment step, before the Mission is created `active`. It is issuance-only: it cannot reach back into a Mission already active when the policy was fresh. Consistent with the family's TTL-first posture (bound at issuance, not re-evaluated against later state).

**Scope limit.** This bounds the AGR `policy` assertion path only, and approval-governance is an Optional Extension (`:140`): a deployment that skips it is unbounded by this fix. The identical gap recurs on core's own standing-consent bases: `approval_basis` types `template` and `policy_drawdown` let "a policy approve an instance at machine speed within a bound a human already consented to" (`oauth-mission.md:2086-2094`), tracing only through `consent_principal` and `root_commitment`, an integrity anchor, not a timestamp. `authority_source.policy` for the `organizational` source (`2610-2614`) has the same shape. Neither carries a human-approval instant. That gap's home is core (`approval_basis`) and the companions that define standing-consent types (template, child-delegation, progressive), not approval-governance. Worth a companion issue; out of scope for this sketch.

### The consequence-class restriction

Anchor on core's existing four high-risk classes: irreversible, external-commitment, privileged-administration, or a consumption bound (`oauth-mission.md:2109-2112`). Approval-governance can reference these without a core edit; consent-evidence already does exactly this, restating the same four classes as its "high-risk notice classes" (`consent-evidence.md:535-540`) and citing core's floor by reference rather than duplicating its normative text (`:556`). Approval-governance follows the same pattern.

Rule shape, as a new bullet near `{{assertion-requirements}}` or a short new subsection: *"Where the Mission's derived Authority Set carries a high-risk class (irreversible, external-commitment, privileged-administration, or a consumption bound, as core classifies them), the assertion matching the accountable `approver` MUST be `kind: human`. A deployment MAY declare an exception admitting a `policy` assertion for a named class; the declaration carries its own maximum `approved_at` age under the recency bound above."*

The valve matters: policy-authority approval is a deliberate capability (core 2086-2094 blesses it by name), and a flat prohibition across all four classes for every deployment reads as removing that capability for exactly the cases it was built for. The rule bounds it (human by default for high-risk classes, a declared and staleness-bounded exception if a deployment wants otherwise) rather than removing it. The exception's declaration obligation lives in approval-governance's own text, same as the recency ceiling above; unifying it into core's single statement is available but is the same core-touch tradeoff, not a separate one.

### The split-honesty passage

Home: `architecture.md`'s Capability Envelope (580-609), Informational, using the document's existing "Home: ..." attribution idiom (see Approval Fidelity, 1372-1388) rather than core:4361-4390. This is attribution of an existing split, not a new guarantee, so the informative register fits; core already states the structural fact in two places (the "first of two deliberate enforcement layers" at 332-338, and `{{runtime-boundary}}` at 4361-4390) without ever naming which half of approval-time versus decision-time carries which guarantee in one place.

Draft passage, appended after 609:

> What the committed Authority Set guarantees at approval time is a monotone envelope (narrowed only, per {{subset}}) plus a revocation gate over further derivation ({{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission}}); the Approver consents to this, and only this, at the approval event. Data-dependent conditions, amounts-in-context, and action sequencing are decision-time properties, evaluated later by runtime policy, metering, or action-bound (transaction) approval, and are not re-rendered to the original Approver ({{runtime-boundary}}). The two halves compose but do not substitute: an envelope real at approval time can still admit, at decision time, an effect the Approver never saw rendered.

A core touch at 4361-4390 would make this normative rather than an informative echo, which is stronger but higher blast radius; not recommended given the companion-side option says the same thing without one.

### Interactions and blast radius

- **#316** (authority sources): orthogonal; the recency bound rides approval-governance's assertion `authority`, not either core member the ruling named. The scope-limit note above is where they touch.
- **#252**: the split-honesty passage names the sequencing gap in one sentence rather than closing it; #252 stays open.
- **#424** (parked): adjacent, not blocking. The statement mechanism this sketch extends is the passage #424's ruling made the normative home for; #424 is about serialization, which neither option here requires.
- **#240 / AGR ruling**: adds a member and a bullet inside the record the ruling shaped; no change to atomic-commitment or authenticated-assertion invariants.
- **Blast radius**: recency fact plus companion-only declaration is one companion file, additive, no core touch, no IANA impact. Consequence-class restriction same shape. Unifying either declaration into core's 2107-2121 statement is a small, additive core touch, flagged, optional. The split-honesty passage is architecture-only.

## Open questions

- Does the recency ceiling apply per consequence class, per policy, or globally per deployment? The rule above assumes per class, matching how the floor statement already scopes by class.
- Should `authority.approved_at` be REQUIRED on every `policy` assertion, or only when the deployment has declared a maximum age (conditionally required)? The latter avoids a wire change for deployments that never adopt the bound.
- Does an expired policy-approval age block only new issuance, or also affect an already-`active` Mission approved while the policy was fresh? The mechanism here lands inside atomic commitment, so the answer is issuance-only; worth stating explicitly.
- Is the standing-consent gap (`approval_basis`, core) worth its own issue now, or does it wait for whichever companion next touches `template`/`policy_drawdown`?

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against current `main` (`73e4557`): **the gap is real and the companion-side direction is sound, but the proposed rule needs a reproducible policy and tighter timestamp semantics.**

`decided_at` is the assertion instant. A `policy` assertion currently carries policy identifier/version and `approved_by`, but no fact identifying when a human approved that exact version (`approval-governance.md:249-275,315-322`). Adding `authority.approved_at` is appropriate, provided it is defined as the human approval instant of the exact policy version and is verified from retained, authenticated governance state—not accepted as a policy assertion's uncorroborated clock value.

Three points should be normative:

1. **Apply the strictest applicable ceiling to the whole committed Authority Set.** An AGR assertion is bound to the approval event and `authority_hash`, not to one entry or “referenced class” (`approval-governance.md:349-357`). At evaluation, classify the derived Authority Set, select the strictest maximum age across every class it carries, and name any policy-authority exception by class. Measure age at `evaluation.evaluated_at`/the atomic commit; require version-specific provenance and sensible ordering (`approved_at <= decided_at <= evaluated_at`, subject to a declared bounded clock-skew policy), and reject future timestamps.

2. **Commit the ceiling and exception policy used.** Put the maximum-age mapping and exception valve in the retained `approval_policy` snapshot/digest, or commit a separate versioned declaration from it. A mutable out-of-band deployment statement would make the evaluation impossible to reproduce, contrary to the AGR's promise that retained policy lets an auditor re-run the decision (`approval-governance.md:227-247,598-615`). State explicitly that this is issuance-time eligibility unless the design also intends to cap Mission expiry; do not leave readers guessing whether age expiry retroactively changes an active immutable Mission.

3. **State the scope honestly.** Human-by-default for core's high-risk classes is a conservative AGR-profile default, not a family-wide guarantee, because Approval Governance is optional (`approval-governance.md:140-147`). “Human” is also not assurance by itself: the existing authentication-strength, rendering, and accountable-principal requirements still carry the security property. A class-declared, staleness-bounded policy exception is the right valve.

The standing-consent residue deserves its own follow-on. Core's `approval_basis` forms can activate machine-speed `template`/`policy_drawdown` authority while carrying a consent principal and commitment but no human-policy approval instant (`oauth-mission.md:2086-2094,2544-2588`). `authority_source.policy` is related provenance, but it is not an approval basis and should not be treated as closing that gap.

The architecture “split honesty” passage also needs precision. Approval commits the structured Authority Set plus the rendered intent context, effective expiry, and controls; concrete request values, current consumption, and sequence are decision-time facts. Say core **does not require** those concrete facts to be re-rendered to the original Approver, not that they are “never” re-rendered—action-bound approval may do exactly that. Likewise, the lifecycle control is a gate on new derivation; already-materialized credentials remain usable to their own bound. Avoid “consents to this, and only this,” which omits other rendered and committed context.

**Disposition: approve with these changes**, and open the core standing-consent timestamp issue separately rather than claiming this optional AGR fix closes the family-wide case.

issues.title: Lifecycle: widening with live children (expansion cascade vs drawdown block)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-17 design critique.

**Widening and fan-out are structurally hostile to each other.** Any expansion, fresh-approval or in-ceiling, terminally cascades every non-terminal Child Mission; the successor does not inherit them and each child must be re-created and re-validated (`child-delegation.md:1256-1271`). Separately, the Mission Issuer MUST NOT policy-adjudicate an in-ceiling drawdown while the predecessor has non-terminal Child Missions (`progressive.md:328-331`), falling back to full human approval.

Composed: an orchestrator that has fanned out sub-agents and then needs broader scope has no path that both widens and keeps the live subtree. It either tears down and rebuilds every child (churn, lineage loss) or is blocked from machine-speed widening entirely (approval fatigue). A planner spawning parallel workers that escalates mid-task is arguably the modal agent workload shape, and it has no good path.

Adjacent to #207 (Mission Model split) and #213 (revision-based evolution); the specific interaction is named nowhere in the family.

Ask: name the interaction explicitly, and either design a child-preserving expansion path or state the teardown cost as a priced limitation.

Sketch and tradeoffs follow in a comment.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Sketch and tradeoffs

Citations verified exact against current text: child-delegation.md:1256-1271 (the `superseded` non-transfer rule through the successor re-run of {{strict-subset}}) and progressive.md:328-331 (the MUST NOT policy-adjudicate sentence). No line correction needed.

### Why each rule exists

The cascade rule (child-delegation.md #cascade, 1256-1266) is not caution for its own sake. A Child Mission's authority is validated once, at creation, against a specific parent entry ({{strict-subset}}), and `parent.authority_hash` commits to the exact predecessor set it was checked against ({{parent-member}}). A successor's Authority Set is freshly derived, never inherited by reference (expansion.md ~827-828, ~954-960). If a superseded parent silently kept its children, a child's authority would be resting on a check that was never run against the set it now lives under. Cascade forces that check to happen again, at a fresh approval boundary, rather than assuming it still holds.

The drawdown block (progressive.md 328-331) is narrower than "widening is unsafe." A policy-adjudicated in-ceiling drawdown can never exceed the pre-consented ceiling (progressive.md 333-346), so the authority itself isn't the risk. The risk is that skipping the interactive prompt also skips the expansion profile's child-cascade consent notice (expansion.md 731-742): no human sees that live children are about to cascade. The block exists to guarantee a human witnesses that collateral damage before it happens, by forcing the one path that renders the notice.

Both rules are protecting the same thing from two directions: a Child Mission's basis must always trace to a committed approval event it was actually checked against, and any commitment that removes children from existence must pass in front of an accountable human first.

### Options

**(a) Re-parent in place.** Forecloses immediately: `parent` is immutable after creation (child-delegation.md ~1005), and the mission-level `predecessor`/`successor` links are immutable too (expansion.md 843-846). There is no committed record to repoint. Any "re-parenting" has to mint a new Child Mission record, which collapses (a) into (b). Repointing a live child's basis onto a different ceiling without a fresh approval event is also the shape of the in-Mission basis reset #547 rules out for actor chains: a descendant's basis must trace to *something committed*, never float between two approvals.

**(b) Batched subtree re-derivation.** This is already named, unbatched, as the escape hatch: expansion.md:738 says a child still needed is "re-created under the successor through ordinary child creation, in generation order." Today that is N separate Token Exchanges, one per child, each needing its own parent-possession proof. The fix is batching an existing path, not inventing one.

**(c) Scoped drawdown exception when disjoint.** Looks cheap, isn't. A drawdown successor still supersedes the predecessor (progressive.md 290-297 routes through the same expansion machinery). If children survive untouched, their immutable `parent.id`/`parent.authority_hash` now name a `superseded`, non-active Mission, and cascade's own enforcement ties a child's continued derivation to its parent's *current* state at commit, not just at creation (child-delegation.md "Cascade Failure", ~1602-1613: "no dependent Child Mission derives again" once the terminal trigger commits). Leaving children live past that point isn't a narrow carve-out; it's a new exception to cascade's core enforcement, and it has no disclosure surface to justify it, since policy adjudication has no interactive Approver by construction. (c) is bigger than (b), not smaller, and buys nothing (b) doesn't already cover once the path falls back to full approval.

**(d) Price it.** Cheap, and worth doing regardless of what else ships. Alone, it leaves the modal "fan out then widen" workload with no path, which is the issue's actual complaint.

### Recommendation: (b), generalized, plus (d) for the drawdown path specifically

Batch (b) into a single mechanism, Child Mission Carryover, that rides the expansion approval event itself rather than N separate exchanges. Keep (c) out: the drawdown-with-live-children case stays blocked and gets (d) instead, but the fallback to full approval composes with carryover, so the total cost of "widen and keep children" drops even on that path.

Price what carryover does not remove, since that is the actual teardown-cost answer the issue asked for: each carried child is a new Child Mission record, so the parent still receives a new {{RFC7523}} assertion per child and still has to convey it to the child actor ({{grant-type}}), exactly as ordinary child creation already requires. There is a window in which one worker holds valid credentials under two `mission_id`s: its tokens issued under the old (now `cascaded`) child stay valid to their own `exp`, same as any cascaded child's outstanding tokens ("Cascade Failure", ~1610-1613). Carryover removes the re-approval storm and the lineage break; it does not remove the per-worker credential handoff.

Mechanism, at expansion completion, for an interactively-approved (non-policy-adjudicated) expansion:

- Eligibility per non-terminal child, re-checked against the successor, never assumed, and sufficient on its own with no separate global condition on the successor: (i) the child's own Authority Set entries still pass {{strict-subset}} against the successor's set; (ii) the specific parent entry that justified the child ({{fanout-accounting}}'s recorded justification mapping, {{child-evidence}}) is identifiable in the successor's set, not just any surviving entry, so `max_children` and `max_child_depth` accounting stay meaningful; (iii) the successor's justifying entry allows the carried generation's `parent.depth` ({{parent-member}}), since a strict-subset pass on entries doesn't imply the depth budget carries. A child failing any check is not carried; it cascades exactly as today, and the deployment falls back to ordinary manual re-creation for it alone.
- Mechanics: this cannot be modeled as ordinary child creation, because that gates on the requesting parent proving possession of a `subject_token` confirmation key ({{grant-type}}, {{request-processing}}), and no successor-derived token exists yet at the instant the successor activates. Carryover is issuer-internal, driven by expansion completion itself, substituting the expansion's own request-time possession proof of the predecessor ({{request-binding}}) as the gate.
- Each carried child is a wholly new Child Mission record: its own `authority_hash`, its own `parent` naming the successor, created and activated in the same atomic operation as the successor's activation and the predecessor's supersession, ahead of or together with the old child's cascade transition, so no live child is ever left without an active replacement. The old child's record is never mutated; it cascades to `cascaded` per {{cascade}} unchanged.
- Lineage: reuse the existing bare-identifier `related_to` member ({{predecessor-member}}) on the new child's record and mission claim, naming the terminated child's `mission_id`. No new lineage member is needed.
- A new `approval_basis.type`, `expansion_carryover`, owned by child-delegation.md under core's open `type` set (the same pattern progressive.md uses for `ceiling_drawdown`): `consent_principal` is the expansion's Approver, the one who saw the extended notice below; `root_commitment` is the new child's own `authority_hash`, satisfying the anti-laundering rule that `root_commitment` MUST reference a committed value ({{record-requirements}}).
- `controls.max_derivations` is set fresh on the carried child's own Mission Intent, same as any child creation ({{derivation-budget}}): this is not a new laundering vector introduced by batching, it's the existing re-creation characteristic made cheap enough to repeat. A deployment bounding aggregate subtree spend already needs consumption metering for that, not this counter ({{derivation-budget}}); worth restating at the carryover site since repeated expand-and-carry cycles make it easier to forget.

Sample normative sentences:

> Where the successor's Authority Set independently satisfies {{strict-subset}} for a non-terminal child's own entries and its justifying parent entry, the Mission Issuer MAY create a replacement Child Mission under the successor in the same atomic operation as the successor's activation, rather than cascading that child to a terminal state.

> The Mission Issuer MUST NOT carry a Child Mission forward by mutating its `parent` value or its `authority_hash`; carryover always creates a new Child Mission record and terminates the original ({{cascade}}).

Edit plan by file:

- **child-delegation.md**: add a Child Mission Carryover section near {{cascade}}, defining eligibility, the atomicity requirement, and `expansion_carryover` as a new approval_basis type alongside `direct` and `policy_drawdown`. Experimental initially, same posture as the existing `bounded_staleness`/`status_required` cascade modes ({{experimental-cascade}}): it is new wire behavior, a new anchor, and a new cross-profile atomicity surface.
- **expansion.md**: extend the child-cascade consent notice (731-742) so it discloses, per non-terminal child, whether it will be carried or cascaded, before the Approver consents; this is the same disclosure discipline containment.md already uses for restoration (704-728), applied one generation down. Add the make-before-break ordering requirement at successor activation ({{superseded-state}}).
- **progressive.md**: no mechanism change.
