issues.title: Child-delegation: draft retains the interactive creation path the D62 ruling removed
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-22 reference-implementation family audit. Spec-side finding, no code change proposed.

`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation` (HEAD `66df9f3e`) says of interactive child creation: "This interactive path is retained." The reference implementation removed that path deliberately (#448, D62 / PR #451): child creation is an RFC 8693 token exchange at `/token`; the PAR/interactive carrier was retired, and `adapters/provider.ts` carries comments recording the removal.

Either the draft should stop asserting the interactive path is retained (making the token-exchange wire the single normative path, with interactive completion as the deployment MAY it already describes under `#completion`), or the ruling intends the interactive path to remain a first-class alternative, in which case the implementation dropped a surface it should carry. The D62 ruling reads as the former, but the draft text at HEAD contradicts it, so it needs an explicit resolution rather than a unilateral edit on either side.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**
The issue conflates two surfaces. D62 (`src/PLAN.md`) retired the request-side PAR *entry* carrier: the parent used to submit `parent`/`parent_token`/`child_actor` directly to PAR to create a child; gone, replaced by the single RFC 8693 token-exchange entry at `/token` (`provider.ts:720-728`; #448, a reusable refresh-token `parent_token` MUST NOT carry possession). D62's log is explicit this replaced the entry, not the completion outcome: three completion modes are named, "synchronous / Deferred Token Response ... / the deployment's interactive approval RETAINED," and the same entry records an advisor pass correcting "a 'DTR replaces the interactive leg' overreach (kept three modes)." Interactive-completion retention was a deliberate, already-litigated D62 outcome, not drift.

The draft's `{{completion}}` section (lines 564-601) matches: Interactive is one of three MAY modes completing an already-initiated token-exchange request, via the issuance profile's existing front-channel PAR ceremony (the same UX top-level Mission creation uses), not a bespoke child-creation PAR entry point. The draft never contradicted D62.

The real, mislabeled finding: only synchronous completion is wired. `mode: "synchronous"` is hardcoded in `continuation-grant.ts:1497` and `:1588`; `kernel/child-delegation.ts:15-19` lists the PAR front-channel carve-outs as **deferred**, not removed by design. Both Deferred and Interactive completion are unimplemented today, not just Interactive. A coverage gap against the spec's three modes, not a ruling conflict; worth its own tracking issue if wire coverage is wanted.

**Sketch**
(A) Drop "This interactive path is retained." (line 601 ends at "...grant reference is returned."). The Interactive bullet stands alone, parallel to Synchronous/Deferred, none of which carry a retention aside. Style-only: accurate, but the temporal/historical framing the timeless-spec-prose convention avoids outside pins and changelogs.
(A′) Leave it: true, and now marks a decision re-litigated twice (D62's advisor pass, this issue).
(B) Restore the PAR entry carrier: re-add `parent`/`child_actor` PAR params and a `parent_token` back-channel credential, reopen the dedicated-grant IANA path D62 closed, wire the deferred front-channel carve-outs. Reopens the reusable-refresh-credential hazard #448 fixed.

**Recommendation**
(A), as a proposed ruling awaiting sign-off: capability-preserving, since the Interactive bullet is itself the normative statement and the retention aside is not load-bearing. An Approver-present child creation still occurs under the Interactive completion mode either way.

**Tradeoffs**
(A) is a wording change on a `decide` issue whose substance is otherwise "no action": low cost, spends a review cycle on prose. (A′) costs nothing but leaves the retrospective phrasing standing. (B) is strictly worse: reopens a closed security fix for no capability gain.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: agree that D62 and the draft do not conflict. D62 retired the bespoke PAR **entry carrier**, while deliberately retaining three completion outcomes after token-exchange initiation. The current Synchronous / Deferred / Interactive section matches that ruling.

Drop “This interactive path is retained” as an editorial cleanup. The Interactive bullet itself is the enduring specification statement; the historical aside adds no semantics and conflicts with the repository's timeless-spec style. Do not restore the retired `parent_token`/PAR carrier—it would reopen the reusable-credential problem for no capability gain.

One calibration on the proposed follow-up: the reference implementation currently wires only synchronous child completion, but the Child-Delegation conformance section does not require an implementation to support every completion mode. Deferred and Interactive are optional deployment capabilities, so their absence is not a conformance defect by itself. File a separate enhancement only if the reference implementation is intended to exercise those modes. If filed, scope it to mode negotiation/initiation, preservation of the same idempotency reservation across completion, child-grant delivery, and mode-specific rows/tests; do not describe it as repairing D62 drift.

Evidence: [D62 record](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/src/PLAN.md#L147), [three completion modes](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md#L564-L603), [current synchronous implementation](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/src/services/authorization-server/src/adapters/continuation-grant.ts#L1440-L1504), and [actual conformance bar](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md#L1590-L1615).

Disposition: choose option A as a style fix; no protocol restoration. Treat other completion modes as an optional implementation enhancement.

issues.title: Orchestration: compensates_decision_id vs runtime's compensates_evaluation_id (family-internal rename inconsistency)

From the 2026-08-22 reference-implementation family audit. Spec-side finding, no code change proposed yet.

`draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime` renamed the compensation linkage member `compensates_decision_id` to `compensates_evaluation_id` (the SARC-native evidence rename that also moved `decision_id` to `evaluation_id`). `draft-mcguinness-mission-orchestration` still defines and uses `compensates_decision_id`, so the family is internally inconsistent one level above the code.

issues.title: Impl: PDP amount check fails open on absent amount input; constraint-evaluation fixtures missing
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-22 reference-implementation family audit (catch-up pass over runtime `b5e35e2..f9aaec99`).

The runtime draft's `#parameter-binding` section gained Operation Profile Common-Constraint mapping MUSTs plus required constraint-evaluation fixtures (PRs #638-#640 era). Two findings against `services/pdp`:

1. Fail-open on absent amount: `services/pdp/src/evaluate.ts` (the `if (cap && amt)` guard around lines 402-415) skips the amount-vs-cap check entirely when the `amount` input is absent. Today the PEP always populates it from the invoice record for `needsInvoice` actions (`services/mcp-payments/src/pep.ts`), so the arm is unreachable in this deployment, but the PDP contract itself is not fail-closed: a caller that omits the amount input gets a permit an amount-capped entry should refuse. The check should refuse (or classify indeterminate) when a cap exists and no comparable amount was supplied.
2. Missing required fixtures: `services/pdp/test/evaluate-amount.test.ts` covers over-cap, float-precision, malformed amount, malformed cap, but not the exact-bound permit, currency mismatch (incomparable EUR vs USD), or absent-amount arms the new fixture requirement names.

The runtime rows stay pinned at `b5e35e2` until this and #648 land.

issues.title: Impl: capability-binding has only a nonconformant PEP placeholder (wrong digest bytes and canonicalization; no record, no capability_drift)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-22 reference-implementation family audit (coverage pass).

`draft-mcguinness-mission-capability-binding` (extracted from the AuthZEN binding, now named in the architecture draft's Runtime-Enforced document map) has no SPEC_VERSIONS row, and the only code touching its surface is a nonconformant placeholder:

- The PEP builds a `context.capability_source` object on every payments tool call (`services/mcp-payments/src/pep.ts`), but its `source_digest` is computed as `sha-256` over plain `JSON.stringify(serverCard)`: the whole catalog, not the per-capability extracted definition, and not JCS. At HEAD the draft explicitly binds `source_digest` to the substrate's default commitment construction (canonical-object digest under JCS), so both the bytes and the canonicalization are wrong; the value is semantically the draft's `catalog_digest` under the wrong member name.
- The validating-server derivation-time recording (capability source members as part of the approved Mission's derived authority, covered by `authority_hash`) has no code: `AuthorityEntry` carries no capability-source members.
- The PDP decision-time verification and the `capability_drift` denial reason have zero hits in the tree; no test references any of it.

Direction: either implement the three conformance roles (PEP present, validating server record, PDP verify and refuse `capability_drift`) or park the draft explicitly. Until then it is listed under "Adopted for planning, not yet implemented" with the placeholder called out, so the PEP object is not mistaken for a realization.

issues.title: Approval-time: template/progressive prohibited sets diverge from the core's high-risk classification
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

The core now hosts the canonical high-risk classification (approval-authentication statement): irreversible action, external commitment, privileged administration, or a consumption bound. consent-evidence (material notices) and approval-governance (policy-approval recency) both cite that set, and approval-governance forces `kind: human` for it.

template (prohibited classes) and progressive (in-ceiling expansion) fix a different set for their machine-speed carve-outs: the same three plus the runtime external-communication predicate and cross-domain authority, dropping the consumption bound. Template's "this is the prohibited set the progressive profile holds back" equivalence claim is true pairwise and false against core.

Net effect: a consumption-bounded instance is policy-adjudicable at machine speed (template dispatch, in-ceiling drawdown) while the same class triggers mandatory human involvement under core/approval-governance's classification.

Ruling: either the two policy-adjudication profiles adopt the core's four-class floor (their external-communication/cross-domain extras can stay), or each states in place why consumption-bounded authority is safe to dispatch or draw down without a human.

Same cut: neither template nor progressive references mission-approval-governance at all, though AGR's own Boundaries section names their standing-consent bases (`template`, `ceiling_drawdown`) as the tracked human-approval-instant gap; `authority.approved_at` recency (#580, landed) reaches the bases but the AGR linkage is still absent.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

The issue's framing is half right. Core's approval-authentication statement (`{{approval-event}}`) sets an authentication-strength floor on whichever approval roots the Mission, not a fresh per-instance human decision: a standing-consent basis "creates no fresh approval event per instance" and still satisfies the floor via `approval_basis.consent_principal` and `approved_at`. template's and progressive's own standing-consent bases (`template`, `ceiling_drawdown`) already carry that trace. consent-evidence's four-class list is a disclosure rule at that same original consent surface, and metering's `{{consent}}` already requires the bound be rendered there. So core's and consent-evidence's inclusion of the consumption bound does not, by itself, force machine-speed dispatch back to a human.

The real conflict is narrower: approval-governance's `{{policy-approval-recency}}` forces `kind: human` for a consumption-bounded Mission's accountable-approver assertion, unless a committed, class-named exception admits `kind: policy`. A template dispatch or progressive drawdown recorded into an AGR is structurally a `kind: policy` assertion (matching the profile's own worked example: policy decides, tracing to the human who approved the policy). Recording an AGR for such dispatches without that exception violates the default and, by `{{atomic-commitment}}`, blocks activation. Neither profile says this or cites approval-governance, so the conflict stays invisible until a deployment combines both.

**Sketch**

Two companions get an addition each; no core edit, no document merge:

- template `{{prohibited-classes}}` and progressive `{{in-ceiling-expansion}}`: after the three-class list, add a paragraph naming core's fourth class (consumption bound), noting it is already satisfied via the standing-consent trace and metering's consent-integrity rendering, and that a deployment recording an AGR for these dispatches needs approval-governance's class-named exception for `kind: policy`, else the Mission fails to activate.
- approval-governance `{{boundaries}}`: name `template` and `ceiling_drawdown` explicitly as the standing-consent bases whose `approved_at` it already tracks, closing the citation gap the issue flags.
- Soften template's "this is the prohibited set the progressive profile holds back" to scope it against progressive only, not against core's larger set.

**Recommendation (proposed ruling, pending owner sign-off)**

Adopt (b) as refined above, not the blanket floor of (a). Do not add the consumption bound to either profile's MUST-NOT/fresh-approval-required list; cross-reference core's classification and reuse approval-governance's existing exception instead of inventing new machinery.

**Tradeoffs**

(a) would gut both profiles: budget-capped machine-speed dispatch is their premise, and a consumption bound is the containment mechanism, not a risk amplifier like the other three classes. (b) preserves that capability by default and closes the gap only where it actually bites (AGR-adopting deployments), reusing an already-defined primitive over a new opt-in flag. Cost: two denser cross-reference paragraphs, and a footgun where forgetting the exception fails the Mission closed rather than silently. (c), each profile restating its own safety case in place, reaches the same conclusion without closing the AGR linkage, leaving the real conflict unaddressed.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: I support the proposed ruling not to add consumption bounds to Template's or Progressive's prohibited sets. Core permits standing-consent activation at machine speed, and its four-class rule is an approval-authentication floor. A consumption bound is the containment mechanism these profiles draw down under, not another irreversible-action class.

One addition is needed before execution: the AGR composition cannot be closed by cross-reference alone. Template keeps the consenting human as the Mission `approver` while the Dispatcher/policy activates the instance, but AGR requires exactly one approving assertion whose `principal` matches that `approver`. Please specify the standing-consent AGR mapping for both `template` and `ceiling_drawdown`: which identity occupies `assertions[].principal`; how `kind: policy`, `policy_id`, `version`, `approved_at`, and the activation actor relate; and how that assertion satisfies the accountable-approver match without pretending a fresh human assertion occurred. Then require the existing class-named exception when an AGR records a consumption-bounded activation.

AGR's Boundaries paragraph should be corrected, not merely expanded: it currently says standing-consent bases carry no equivalent human-approval instant, while core now requires `approval_basis.approved_at` and both profiles populate it. Name `template` and `ceiling_drawdown`, describe the two recency paths as analogous but distinct, and scope Template's "same prohibited set" sentence expressly to Progressive.

Evidence: [core standing-consent and class floor](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2105-L2140), [Template activation](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-template.md#L481-L509), [Progressive basis](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-progressive.md#L288-L324), and [AGR assertion/default rules](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-approval-governance.md#L374-L511).

Disposition: approve with that explicit AGR mapping and the Boundaries correction.

issues.title: Cross-boundary freshness: projection's lease vs cross-org's live check, one boundary, two mandatory postures
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

Two profiles govern a destination AS in another trust domain honoring Mission-bound authority it did not issue, with different mandatory freshness regimes:

- cross-domain (cross-domain revocation): "short downstream lifetimes remain the only cross-domain control"; Mission Status is informative, named only as opt-in tightening ("Tighter cross-domain revocation is opt-in").
- cross-org-delegation (verification step 9): MUST "establish that the Mission is `active` from a locally available state source within the deployment's declared freshness bound"; Mission Status is normative.

Each document now names its own posture; neither acknowledges the other's, and a deployment running both at one boundary enforces two staleness postures depending on which flow a request took. If the split is deliberate (the TTL-first lease as the floor, the live check as the recursive-delegation overlay), one paragraph in each naming the two postures and when each applies settles it.

Adjacent tier question, same ruling: attenuation makes mission-runtime a normative precondition ("available only to deployments running the runtime enforcement profile"); cross-org-delegation profiles attenuation and inherits its kill-switch conditions but lists mission-runtime only informatively, with the substitution (the step-9 state check) now disclosed in its Security Considerations. Bless the disclosed substitution as final, or make runtime normative there.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

Cross-Domain Projection's Introduction frames Project as "single-hop, issuer-mediated, audience-scoped." Its Cross-Domain Revocation Latency section (`{{cross-domain-revocation}}`) bounds exposure with two declared caps: the 300-second projection grant lifetime (`{{cross-domain-grant}}`), which stops new downstream tokens after revocation, and the Resource AS's MUST to issue short-lived local tokens. Status/Signals stay opt-in because those caps already bound this profile's exposure.

Cross-Org Delegation's Introduction names the other case: "Delegate... recursive... verifies every narrowing without a callback." Its Trust Model (`{{trust-model}}`) runs on the substrate's Bounded Reliance floor, cached state with a declared freshness ceiling, since a holder-mediated chain has no per-hop issuer mediation to re-bound exposure. Step 9 of Destination Verification makes the check mandatory for that reason; Security Considerations cites Mission Status as the normative dependency. This extends the documents' existing cross-reference practice (delegation-depth scoping, Cross-Domain Projection lines 1184-1202) to freshness posture.

Disambiguator for "which posture at one boundary": the presented artifact, not the deployment. A cross-domain grant redeems under the lease; a Chain Presentation (registered `mission-delegation-chain+json`) redeems under step 9. No collision: Cross-Org's Local Projection caps its mint's expiry by leaf and local policy, never by adopting the 300s cap, so a Resource AS accepting both types runs both caps side by side.

Tier question: mission-runtime appears in Cross-Org Delegation only once, informatively, for fan-out *observability*, distinct from step 9's freshness check. `family-manifest.json`'s reference-security-architecture stack treats freshness sourcing as pluggable even at the Runtime-Enforced level (`freshness_one_of`: Status, Signals, or core token-introspection); the kill-switch is continuous per-presentation, not the point-in-time read step 9 needs. Per CONTRIBUTING's test ("requires implementing or consulting"), step 9 requires only Mission Status: informative plus disclosed substitution is the correct tier.

**Sketch**

Cross-Domain Projection, appended to `{{cross-domain-revocation}}`: "This posture bounds a single issuer-mediated hop, redeemed under its own grant and local-token caps. The cross-organizational delegation profile governs a recursive, holder-mediated chain outliving those caps, with no issuer mediation after root minting; for a presented Chain, that profile makes the live check this profile leaves opt-in mandatory (Mission Cross-Organizational Delegation for OAuth 2.0, Destination Verification, step 9)."

Cross-Org Delegation, appended to Security Considerations: "This mandatory check answers a different exposure than Cross-Domain Projection's lease: a recursive chain unmediated by the issuer past the root. For a presented cross-domain grant, that profile leaves the same check opt-in, since its own caps already bound a single issuer-mediated hop (Mission Cross-Domain Projection for OAuth 2.0, Cross-Domain Revocation Latency); a deployment accepting both types applies whichever check the presented artifact requires."

**Recommendation**

Name both postures as deliberate: add the two paragraphs above, and bless the step-9 substitution as final (mission-runtime stays informative).

**Tradeoffs**

Forcing Status normativity into Cross-Domain Projection breaks TTL-first: a mandatory live-state surface on the family's cheapest hop, already bounded by its declared caps, and it blurs Project (single-hop) from Delegate (recursive). Promoting mission-runtime to normative in Cross-Org Delegation costs little functionally (step 9 needs no enforcement machinery beyond a state read) but adds an unneeded `Requires:` edge and breaks the family's freshness-source pluggability pattern.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: the mutual cross-reference direction and artifact-type disambiguator are right, but I would not ratify “Runtime stays informative” or describe Cross-Org step 9 as a substitution.

Cross-Domain's lease posture is clear: ID-JAG and the local token are capped, with Status/Signals as optional tightening. Cross-Org's distinct Chain Presentation makes a fresh state check mandatory at redemption. The incoming artifact therefore tells the Resource AS which verification regime applies at that boundary.

Runtime is nevertheless already an inherited normative dependency. Cross-Org requires Offline Attenuation; Attenuation is available only to Runtime deployments and requires every chain presentation to be evaluated under Runtime. Step 9 is Cross-Org's realization of that inherited Runtime kill switch, not a replacement for Runtime. A redundant direct manifest edge is optional if typed edges remain direct-only, but the semantic dependency is not informative.

Two wording corrections:

- Do not say the Chain “outlives” the 300-second caps. It is not governed by those caps and may happen to be shorter.
- Scope artifact-type disambiguation to the Resource AS redemption boundary. After either path mints an ordinary local access token, later provenance is not generally recoverable from token type alone.

Evidence: [Cross-Domain caps](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-cross-domain.md#L615-L670), [Cross-Org checks](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-cross-org-delegation.md#L467-L515), and [Attenuation's Runtime prerequisite](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-attenuation.md#L160-L191).

Disposition: approve the two deliberate freshness postures and mutual pointers, but retain Runtime as a normative inherited dependency.

issues.title: Audit: three experimental normative down-references vs CONTRIBUTING's maturity bound
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133). The only such edge family-wide (front-matter graph check).

mission-audit (std) lists three Experimental drafts under normative:: mission-discovery, oauth-mission-containment, oauth-mission-work-products — their Evidence Types rows need each profile's canonical-bytes definitions. CONTRIBUTING's Reference Classification rule is unconditional: "A Standards-Track draft never lists an Experimental draft as normative. A requirement that would create such a dependency moves into the Experimental draft... the Standards-Track draft keeps the reference informative."

The critique-residue pass (PR #642) added a rationale in the evidence-types section calling these "conditional normative down-references, binding only a deployment that produces that row's evidence." That borrows the conditional-reference rule but does not satisfy the separate, unconditional maturity bound — the draft and the convention now contradict each other explicitly rather than silently.

Two clean exits, one ruling:
1. Apply CONTRIBUTING's own remedy: each Experimental profile hosts its evidence-type row (canonical bytes, preimage content type, producer); audit keeps the catalog with informative pointers.
2. Amend CONTRIBUTING's maturity bound to admit scoped conditional down-references, making audit's in-place rationale the documented policy.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

Confirmed against the tree. Audit's normative front matter lists `mission-discovery`, `oauth-mission-containment`, `oauth-mission-work-products`, all `category: exp`. The Evidence Types table's rationale paragraph ({{evidence-types}}) calls the Discovery Evidence, Containment evidence, Protected event receipt, and Work Product Binding rows "conditional normative down-references," borrowing CONTRIBUTING's conditional-reference language without meeting the separate maturity bound in the same section ("A Standards-Track draft never lists an Experimental draft as normative"). Grepping every `category: std` draft's normative front matter, this is the only such edge by front-matter classification (body-text BCP-14 refs unchecked, so the claim is bounded, not closed).

The four rows are not evenly weighted. `oauth-mission-containment` already normatively fixes its own canonical bytes and registers both media types in its own IANA section ({{evidence-canonical}}, {{protected-event-receipt}}). `oauth-mission-work-products` ({{binding-verification}}) already fixes canonical bytes, `payload-preimage-content-type`, and producer in its own body. For those three rows, audit's table is a restatement, not the sole locus: the remedy is demotion and wording, not new authoring.

Discovery Evidence is the exception. Audit's IANA section lists media types "defined elsewhere" by companions, and Discovery Evidence is absent from that list; `mission-discovery` itself calls its `typ` a "local-use identifier pending registration," not a registered one. Containment's Protected Event Receipt text even claims to mirror "the Child and Discovery Evidence registration conventions," a convention Discovery hasn't implemented. No document stands behind that media type today. That gap is real regardless of which exit wins.

**Sketch**

Exit 1: keep each row's substance where it already normatively lives (containment, work-products); add the missing IANA text to `mission-discovery`. Move the three entries from audit's `normative:` block to `informative:`. Reword the table's "a producer MUST commit to the canonical bytes named here" to the property form the surrounding prose already uses ("registered where it is, by the profile the row cites"), citing informatively. Touch containment's own forward-pointer that currently sends the registration duty back to "an audit or transparency profile," the direction Exit 1 reverses. Registration-policy's Work Product Binding MUSTs survive unchanged: they bind to a property (mediator identity/role), not to the schema.

Exit 2: add a clause to CONTRIBUTING's bound admitting a down-reference scoped to a row a std draft cites only where a deployment adopts the exp profile, codifying audit's rationale as policy.

**Recommendation**

Exit 1. The presumed cost (three Lab drafts) is mostly already paid: two of three rows need demotion and wording, not authored content. Close the Discovery Evidence gap regardless of which exit wins.

**Tradeoffs**

Exit 1 keeps the bright line absolute and gives each evidence type one home for its bytes, at the cost of touching four files instead of one paragraph. Exit 2 is cheap but converts an unconditional bound into a judgment call future std drafts will cite; it also defers rather than resolves the RFC 3967 downref question a Standards-Track normative reference to an Experimental document raises, independent of house convention.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: Exit 1 is the right ruling, with one precision. Moving the three front-matter references to `informative` is necessary but not sufficient. Audit currently calls the table a normative catalog and says a producer MUST commit to the canonical bytes named there. Companion-defined rows therefore need to become an informative catalog of properties normatively owned by the cited profile. Audit can retain normative ownership only for its own evidence types and for its relying-party registration rules stated as properties.

The implementation cost is small for Containment and Work Products: both already self-host their canonical bytes, preimage type, operational form, and producer. Demote Audit's restatement and correct Containment's pointer accordingly.

Discovery is the substantive gap. It defines the Discovery Evidence object, JCS payload, issuer key, and local-use JWS `typ`, but its IANA section makes no request and it never independently fixes the `application/mission-discovery-evidence+json` value Audit currently supplies as `payload-preimage-content-type`. Add that media-type definition/registration text and explicitly state the authoritative producer in Discovery. Then move all three references to informative and remove the conditional normative-down-reference rationale.

Evidence: [house rule](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/CONTRIBUTING.md#L42-L63), [Audit table](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-audit.md#L473-L515), [Discovery definition](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-discovery.md#L627-L684), and [Discovery IANA boundary](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-discovery.md#L798-L801).

Disposition: approve Exit 1 with the ownership split and Discovery media-type repair.

issues.title: Family: three uncross-referenced accounts of what earns 'Mission-bound'
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

Three accounts of what earns the term "Mission-bound", none citing another:

1. architecture, Token Classes: "a binding earns it through the capability claims of its Mission Substrate Statement, not by protocol lineage."
2. core, Conformance: the term turns on core's own gates (anchors at the approval event, subset rule, state-gated derivation) — "a token carrying a `mission` claim is not, by itself, Mission-bound authorization."
3. architecture, Mission Binding Properties (the J-ladder replacement from the #237/#248 ruling): a six-property equivalence vector defining credential-mission-bound, citing neither of the above; Token Classes does not cite it back.

A reader gets a different answer per entry point. Ruling: pick the authoritative account and cross-reference the other two to it. The three look reconcilable: the property vector as the definition, Substrate Statement claims as how a binding evidences it, core's gates as the OAuth binding's discharge of it.

issues.title: Harness/discovery: SHOULD-level taint duties are MUST-strength load-bearing input
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

discovery treats the harness taint report as MUST-strength, missing-is-tainted input: "The taint state MUST be obtained from the harness... The adjudicator MUST treat a missing, stale, or unverifiable taint state as tainted." harness's own session-taint duties are SHOULD-level ("the harness SHOULD either require a fresh action-bound approval... or downgrade that authority"; provenance tracking also SHOULD), and its Conformance MUST list carries no taint duty. The opt-in PDP-enforced path (AuthZEN context.taint) has MUSTs but is gated on the Enforcement Scope Statement.

A fully conforming harness implementing taint loosely silently degrades discovery's ceiling path toward always-route-to-human; the fail-safe absorbs the mismatch without surfacing that the deployment is paying it.

Ruling: raise the harness taint floor conditionally (a deployment that adopts discovery meets a MUST-level taint duty), or have discovery state the degradation explicitly as a conformance note.

issues.title: expires_at is core-native now: retire issuance-grant's stale framing and repoint UMA/GNAP
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

Core now defines expires_at natively (Mission Record REQUIRED member; mission-claim OPTIONAL mirror "named identically to the record member it mirrors"). The family has not caught up:

- issuance-grant's expires-at-member section still says it adds the member "ahead of the issuance profile's revision" — stale; the revision landed.
- UMA's mission-claim section still cites issuance-grant for the member ("as the issuance-grant profile defines it").
- GNAP's mission-claim carries the member with only an internal gating pointer, no citation of core's now-canonical definition.

Mechanical cleanup: issuance-grant's section becomes a profile of core's member (or is trimmed to its redemption-specific behavior); UMA and GNAP repoint to core.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

Core defines `expires_at` twice: the Mission Record member (REQUIRED, lines 880-899) and the mission-claim mirror (OPTIONAL, "named identically to the record member it mirrors," lines 3030-3037: bounding/audit commitment, no liveness, only `active` permits reliance).

issuance-grant's `{#expires-at-member}` section (lines 329-348) predates that. Its opening line, "This profile adds one member... ahead of the issuance profile's revision," is stale (the revision landed), and its body duplicates core 3030-3037 verbatim in substance. What it genuinely adds: the grant's `mission` member (283-286) is REQUIRED and "extended with" `expires_at`, making the member mandatory here versus core's OPTIONAL. That elevation is what Redemption's Lifetime rule (515-521, no issued token may expire later than the grant's `mission.expires_at`) depends on, plus the offline-validation/lifetime-cap-check framing tied to `{{redemption}}`.

UMA's mission-claim (776-779) still cites issuance-grant for the member. GNAP's (867-870) carries it with only the internal `{{gating}}` pointer, no external citation, unlike its sibling `id`/`issuer`/`authority_hash` line one above it. Neither needs a reference-tier change: both already list core normative.

conformance-manifest.json: every issuance-grant row anchors on `#effective-set-projection` or similar; none on `#expires-at-member`. No re-anchoring needed.

Found beyond the issue text: UMA's Status block (line 394, generated from family-manifest.json, exact-matched by `scripts/check-family-manifest.mjs`) reads "Also requires, conditionally: Mission Issuance Grant... (when the `expires_at` member is adopted)," driven by `drafts[22].requires_when`. Repointing the citation makes that conditional dependency false, and issuance-grant then has no remaining use in UMA's body, so its `normative:` front-matter entry and `drafts[22].normative_references` slot become dead too.

**Sketch**

- issuance-grant: rewrite `{#expires-at-member}` in place (keep the anchor; lines 286 and 500 xref it). New body: point to core's member for the definition, state the one real delta (REQUIRED here, OPTIONAL in core, tied to the Lifetime rule), drop the duplicated bounding/audit/no-liveness prose.
- UMA: repoint 776-779 to core ("as the issuance profile defines it," `{{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission}}"), matching the phrasing already used for `id`/`issuer`/`authority_hash`. Drop issuance-grant from front matter, drop `drafts[22].requires_when` and its `normative_references` slot; the generated Status line disappears on next generation.
- GNAP: add the same core citation at 867-870, mirroring the line above it. No ledger change (no conditional-dependency entry exists here).

**Recommendation**

Do all three; only issuance-grant's section needs a content trim, UMA and GNAP are pure citation repoints.

**Tradeoffs**

Essentially none. All churn beyond prose is UMA's family-manifest.json entry (drop `requires_when` + one `normative_references` slot) and its generated Status line; conformance-manifest.json needs no touch.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: accept the mechanical repoint, with one CI correction.

Core now owns the REQUIRED Mission Record member and OPTIONAL claim mirror. Issuance Grant's real delta is its REQUIRED elevation: the grant's `mission` object includes `expires_at`, and tokens minted from the grant carry that object unchanged. Keep `{#expires-at-member}` for existing references, but reduce it to that profile-specific elevation and the Lifetime rule; remove the “ahead of core” framing and duplicated semantics.

UMA should cite core directly, then remove Issuance Grant from normative front matter, `normative_references`, `requires_when`, and `references`; regenerate its Status block. GNAP needs only the direct core citation because core is already normative there.

One correction: `conformance-manifest.json` needs a mechanical touch. Issuance Grant is in `source.specs`; editing any byte invalidates its whole-file `content_sha256`, even though no row is anchored on `{#expires-at-member}`. Re-review the existing rows and bump that source entry's revision/digest. No new requirement row is needed because the REQUIRED carriage already exists at `{#grant}`.

Evidence: [core record/claim members](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2714-L2725), [grant elevation and carriage](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-issuance-grant.md#L283-L286), [UMA stale citation](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-uma.md#L773-L780), and [checksum enforcement](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/scripts/check-conformance-manifest.mjs#L130-L140).

issues.title: Runtime: status citation tier vs its MUST-level use of Effective Authority Set and discharge
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

runtime sources Effective Authority Set and discharge from oauth-mission-status (Terminology: "Effective Authority Set and discharge from {{...status}}") and issues MUST-level clauses over them ("the runtime decision MUST require the action to remain within the Mission's current Effective Authority Set"), while its front matter lists status only under informative:. authzen lists status normatively for the same consumption. CONTRIBUTING's rule ("normative when any BCP 14 requirement... requires implementing or consulting it") calls for normative here, and status is std, so the maturity bound does not block the fix.

Mechanical: move status to runtime's normative list — or, if the informative tier is deliberate floor policy, state that policy where it can be cited.

Optional rider (separate ruling if taken): runtime's consumption of discharge state is SHOULD-level ("a PDP that recognizes terminal_when SHOULD refuse an action within a discharged entry"), so a base-conformant PDP can ignore discharge entirely; decide whether Runtime-Enforced deployments get a MUST.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

Effective Authority Set and discharge are status-owned exclusively: core has zero hits for either term. Substrate's Lifecycle-Gated Authorization and State-Observable capabilities (631-683) define only a binary active/non-active predicate and explicitly defer enforcement to "a consuming runtime profile such as {{...mission-runtime}}." The substrate-repoint branch in the issue's OR does not hold; there is no supersession to repoint to.

runtime's Terminology (448-455) sources both terms from status; its front matter lists status only informative (163); its Input-Authority section issues present-tense MUST clauses over them (1392-1393, "the runtime decision MUST require the action to remain within the Mission's current Effective Authority Set"). CONTRIBUTING's rule (44-47) makes a reference normative when any BCP-14 requirement requires implementing or consulting it; status is category std (line 4), so the maturity bound doesn't block. authzen, same category, same consumption, already lists status normative (75).

No deliberate floor-independence language exists. runtime's "Invariants, Not a Wire Protocol" (365-386) and its "Mission state source" abstraction (527-530) are wire/API independence, not concept independence: the 1392-1393 MUST cannot be evaluated without consulting status's definition of the term it names. Architecture calling Status "the reference choice" for a freshness source (2475-2496) is substitutability of the source, not of the term's definition.

`scripts/check-family-manifest.mjs` drift-checks a draft's front-matter tiers bidirectionally against `normative_references`; runtime's entry (`drafts[17].normative_references`) currently holds only substrate and core. A front-matter-only edit fails that check.

**Sketch**

Move status to normative: one front-matter line plus adding `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-status` to `drafts[17].normative_references`. Both files move together or CI's drift check fails.

Rider, sharper than the issue frames it: the discharge paragraph (1453-1458) states, in the section's normal present-tense register, that the Effective Authority Set input "excludes a discharged entry once the PDP can establish discharge state," then downgrades the actual refusal to SHOULD ("a PDP that recognizes `terminal_when` SHOULD refuse"), itself recognition-conditional. One paragraph down (1462-1466), containment, the sibling narrowing mechanism named alongside discharge at 1451, gets a flat MUST for the same input. Two narrowing mechanisms feeding one MUST-level input, two strengths. The Enforcement Invariants list (312-352) promises nothing about discharge either way.

**Recommendation**

Take the reference-tier fix now; mechanical, no substantive change. Defer the rider: the real question isn't whether Runtime-Enforced gets a new conditional MUST, it's whether the SHOULD is an editorial artifact undercutting the composed MUST and inconsistent with containment's treatment. The fix may be deleting the softener rather than adding a requirement, a different ruling with different conformance-manifest consequences.

**Tradeoffs**

Reference-tier fix: none beyond the two-file move. Rider deferral: leaves a live textual tension unresolved for another cycle; low risk since it reads as a documentation inconsistency, not an unbounded normative gap, and containment's clause already anchors the stricter reading.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: accept the reference-tier fix and defer the discharge-softener ruling, but correct the blast radius from two files to three.

Status is not background reading. Runtime imports Effective Authority Set and discharge from Status, places a governing MUST over the current Effective Authority Set, and cites Status as the authority-input definition. Under CONTRIBUTING, that reference is normative. Status is Standards Track, so the maturity boundary does not interfere.

Add Status to Runtime's normative front matter and `normative_references`. Do not add it to `adoption_requires` or `requires_when`: Runtime depends on Status's definition, but a deployment can supply an equivalent current-authority source without implementing the Status operation. `references` already contains it.

This is a three-file change because Runtime is in `conformance-manifest.json`'s `source.specs`. Changing its front matter changes the whole-file checksum, requiring the Runtime source revision/digest to be re-reviewed and bumped. No new row/test is needed because behavior is unchanged.

Deferring the rider is correct. Runtime says the input excludes discharged entries, then softens actual refusal to a recognition-conditional SHOULD, while containment gets a flat MUST. That is a substantive modal ruling and may change a conformance assertion; it should not hitchhike on citation cleanup.

Evidence: [Runtime import and MUST](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime.md#L444-L455), [authority input](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-runtime.md#L1391-L1460), [typed edges](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/family-manifest.json#L966-L1015), and [checksum rule](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/scripts/check-conformance-manifest.mjs#L99-L140).

Disposition: normative front matter + typed edge + conformance source-pin bump; defer the SHOULD question.

issues.title: Approval-time/delegation: commitment and disclosure strength asymmetries between sibling profiles
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

Structurally identical duties carry different strengths across sibling profiles:

1. Review-cadence commitment: template hashes review_cadence inside template_hash (REQUIRED member of the hashed object); progressive keeps its ceiling review cadence outside ceiling_hash's exactly-two-member preimage (deployment-published only), so a deployment can change how often a human re-blesses a drawdown chain with nothing detectable from the Mission's own anchors.
2. Policy-body commitment: template flags its uncommitted dispatch_policy body and SHOULDs a separate integrity anchor; progressive's drawdown_policy commits only "a string or URI identifying the policy" with the identical defect unflagged (its "reviewed and versioned like other approval policy" line is discipline, not a commitment an auditor can check).
3. Composed-bound disclosure: child-delegation MUST-discloses the composed subtree bound (derivation budget); cross-domain SHOULD-discloses the N x M composed depth across projected domains (Per-Domain Delegation Depth). cross-org's silence is by design: depth never resets there.

Executable by aligning to the stronger sibling in each pair (progressive adopts template's two patterns; cross-domain's SHOULD becomes MUST), or a one-line rationale in place where the weaker form is deliberate.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

All three asymmetries verified in-tree.

1. Cadence: template's `review_cadence` is a REQUIRED member of the Mission Template object (`{{the-mission-template}}`), and `template_hash` hashes "the Mission Template object above" wholesale (`{{template-hash}}`), so cadence sits inside the committed anchor. Progressive's ceiling review cadence is deployment-published only (`{{ceiling-review}}`); `ceiling_hash`'s hashed object has exactly two members, `authority_ceiling` and `drawdown_policy` (`{{progressive-authorization}}`). A deployment can change cadence with nothing detectable from the Mission's own anchors.
2. Policy body: template's `dispatch_policy` entry flags the uncommitted body and SHOULDs a separate integrity anchor or Consent Evidence disclosure (`{{the-mission-template}}`). Progressive's `drawdown_policy` is "a string or URI identifying the policy," same defect, unflagged; the nearby "reviewed and versioned like other approval policy" (`{{progressive-limits}}`) is discipline, not a checkable commitment.
3. Disclosure: child-delegation's `{{derivation-budget}}` is conditional and interface-addressed: "where an approval interface displays `max_derivations`, that interface MUST disclose the composed bound." Cross-domain's Per-Domain Delegation Depth section is unconditional and deployment-addressed: "a deployment SHOULD disclose the composed bound ... at the consent surface." A flat SHOULD-to-MUST raise makes cross-domain's rule stronger than child-delegation's, not matching it, so the fix should mirror the conditional shape, not just flip the modal. M (the domain count) is knowable at that approval event regardless: the resource-to-AS mapping is Pre-Established Trust, fixed before the first grant, computable from the Authority Set's `resource` values at consent.

**Sketch**

Progressive adopts template's two patterns: commit cadence as a third member of the `ceiling_drawdown` approval_basis's `activation` object (alongside `policy_id`/`policy_version`), and mirror template's SHOULD-commit sentence verbatim into `drawdown_policy`'s definition. Cross-domain's depth section is reworded to child-delegation's shape: "where an approval interface displays the per-domain `max_depth`, that interface MUST also disclose the composed bound (`max_depth` times the number of domains the Mission may be projected to)."

**Recommendation**

Align to the stronger sibling in each pair, with cadence committed at the per-drawdown approval_basis rather than inside `ceiling_hash`.

**Tradeoffs**

Expanding `ceiling_hash` to three members is a breaking change to already-issued anchors; progressive is exp/lab-best-effort so the break is acceptable if the family prefers hash-parity with template, but the approval_basis route is cheaper (no anchor migration) and fits progressive's per-drawdown model better than template's whole-object re-consent model. The interface-conditioned MUST on cross-domain matches an existing family pattern rather than inventing a stronger one, but still adds an implementation obligation, closing a real audit gap the SHOULD leaves open (cross-org's silence on depth reset is a separate, deliberate choice, not analogous).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: the policy-body and disclosure directions are sound, but the proposed cadence mechanism does not create the commitment claimed.

The diagnosis is valid: Template's REQUIRED `review_cadence` is inside the whole-object `template_hash`, while Progressive's `ceiling_hash` commits exactly `authority_ceiling` and `drawdown_policy`. But adding `review_cadence` to `approval_basis.activation` does not cryptographically commit it. Core explicitly says `approval_basis` is folded into neither `intent_hash` nor `authority_hash`. The value would be immutable issuer-trusted provenance, not anchor-detectable parity with Template.

Choose explicitly:

1. For true parity, include cadence in `ceiling_hash` or define a standing-consent wrapper anchor over `{ceiling_hash, review_cadence}` and use it as `root_commitment`, with a legacy rule for issued ceilings.
2. To preserve existing anchors, call cadence “recorded and reproducible,” not “committed.” Use core's required `approved_at` plus a class-specific recency ceiling retained in versioned policy, identified by existing `policy_version`. This remains issuer-record trust.

Mirroring Template's policy-body warning is sound; preserve both alternatives—integrity-anchor the body or disclose it through Consent Evidence. Reshaping cross-domain disclosure to child-delegation's conditional interface form is also correct, but fix its arithmetic: `N × M` is valid only when the same N applies to every domain. Report the actual per-domain composition or conservative sum; count distinct Resource AS domains, not resources.

These new/strengthened cadence, policy-body, and disclosure requirements need conformance rows/tests. Progressive and Cross-Domain must be added to `source.specs` when those rows land.

Evidence: [Template commitment](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-template.md#L270-L370), [Progressive hash](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-progressive.md#L227-L258), [unanchored approval basis](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2664-L2671), and [cross-domain formula](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-cross-domain.md#L1184-L1211).

Disposition: adopt the policy/disclosure work, but choose true anchor parity or honestly weaker record trust before implementing cadence.

issues.title: Template: dispatch idempotency claims an expansion apparatus with no dispatch op value
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

template's dispatch-idempotency text: "The dispatch event identifier is this grant's realization of the creation idempotency the expansion profile defines for the family's Mission-creating token exchanges." The apparatus cannot currently realize it:

- expansion's adoption clause is scoped to "delegation-family-creating exchanges" and its adopter list names child-delegation and continuation only;
- the creation fingerprint's op member enumerates exactly two domain separators (expansion, child-creation) — no dispatch value exists;
- template imports none of the fingerprint/reservation/recovery/revalidation machinery (zero references to those anchors).

Fix directions: add a dispatch op value and template to expansion's adoption list, with template adopting by reference (matching child-delegation's pattern) — or reword template's claim to describe its own self-contained idempotency.

Adjacent one-liner while in these files: continuation's "successive refreshes of a single async delegation family are one delegation and do not each count again" and child-delegation's "max_derivations is not an aggregate, concurrency, spend, or subtree bound" narrow the same counter from two angles with no cross-reference in either direction.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

Verified in-tree. Expansion's `{{creation-idempotency}}` adoption clause is scoped to "delegation-family-creating exchanges" adopting the same definitions by reference "each under its own domain-separating `op` value," naming child-delegation and continuation's async-delegation exchange as adopters. Continuation itself declares `op: async-delegation` on its own authority, in continuation.md, under that clause: the family's pattern is that the adopter declares its own op value, not that expansion's `op` enumeration is a closed registry. Expansion's own `{{creation-fingerprint}}` definition happens to list only `expansion` and `child-creation`, but the real gate is the scope sentence: a Mission-creating dispatch exchange is not a "delegation-family-creating exchange," so template cannot adopt under the clause as written. Template's dispatch-idempotency prose ("The dispatch event identifier is this grant's realization of the creation idempotency the expansion profile defines," `{{dispatch}}`) claims adoption anyway, but the Dispatch grant carries none of the apparatus: confirmed zero references to `creation_request_id`, `{{creation-fingerprint}}`, `{{creation-reservation}}`, or `{{creation-recovery}}` anywhere in template.md. `dispatch_event_id`'s own semantics ("a repeated request bearing an identifier the Mission Issuer has already committed returns the Mission it already committed") are the same shape as `creation_request_id`'s; its only extra role is riding into `approval_basis.activation` for audit, a recording detail, not added idempotency semantics.

**Sketch**

Widen expansion's scope sentence from "delegation-family-creating exchanges" to cover Mission-creating dispatch exchanges generally, and name template in the adopter list, an additive edit (nothing already committed changes). Template keeps the parameter name `dispatch_event_id` (already load-bearing in `approval_basis.activation`, the `template` lineage member, the grant-type parameter list, and the conformance bullet), declares it its own domain-separating `op: dispatch` value under expansion's clause exactly as continuation declares `async-delegation`, and adopts the fingerprint/reservation/recovery/revalidation apparatus by reference in place of the current claim-by-assertion sentence.

**Recommendation**

Adopt by reference over self-contained reword. Add mutual cross-references: continuation's `{{authorization-continuity}}`/`{{transport-async}}` refresh-counting sentence and child-delegation's `{{derivation-budget}}` non-aggregate warning narrow the same `max_derivations` counter from two angles with no link either way.

**Tradeoffs**

Self-contained reword is cheaper (no expansion-side change, no cross-file dependency) but forks the family's one idempotency apparatus, losing fingerprint/reservation/recovery/revalidation rigor that machine-speed dispatch (higher retry rates, no human in the loop) arguably needs more than the human-paced exchanges. Adoption by reference costs additive edits to expansion's scope sentence and adopter list, but keeps one idempotency definition family-wide and makes template's claim true instead of aspirational.

comments.author: mcguinness

issues.title: Core/architecture: ground the possession-independent revocation invariant in a profile pointer
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133). Core is issue-first; this is the filed finding.

Core's Revocation section requires "an authenticated means for the Subject, the Approver, or an administrator to revoke a Mission by mission_id, independent of possession of any token" and deliberately defines no wire shape ("no standardized endpoint is required for interoperability"). The architecture's "Revocation is possession-independent" invariant cites only its own validity-model section — the one invariant in the list without a profile anchor. The portable wire exists (status's Mission Lifecycle endpoint, revoke), informative from core by self-containment design.

Doc-only, capability-preserving ask: architecture points the invariant at the Status profile as the portable realization; core's Revocation section names the self-containment trade in one sentence (a core-only deployment satisfies the MUST with a deployment-defined surface; the interoperable wire is the Status companion).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

The issue's uniqueness framing overstates: "Attribution is carried, never inferred" and "Anchors commit; they do not prove semantics" also cite only internal architecture anchors ({{actor-chain}}/{{deployment}}, {{derivation-boundary}}), so revocation isn't the sole invariant without a profile xref. The real gap is internal inconsistency: architecture's own requirements-traceability table already credits the property to a profile, R9 ("Revocation is independent of credential possession... (oauth-mission; oauth-mission-status; oauth-mission-signals)", req-lifecycle section), while the invariant list's "Revocation is possession-independent" entry cites only `{{validity-model}}`. Separately, core already carries an informative pointer to Status in the Revocation section ("A standardized Mission management API, with `suspend`/`resume`/`complete` operations, is specified separately by Mission Status {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-status}}"), but the enumeration omits `revoke`, the exact operation the MUST names and the one Status's Mission Lifecycle endpoint lists first (`operation`: one of `revoke`, `suspend`, ...). The existing pointer doesn't actually name the portable realization of the MUST it sits next to.

**Sketch**

Architecture: give the invariant a second citation matching R9's, `({{validity-model}}; {{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-status}})`, replacing the current `({{validity-model}})` alone.

Core: extend the existing enumeration to `revoke`/`suspend`/`resume`/`complete`, and append one clause to that sentence naming the trade: the MUST is satisfiable by a deployment-defined management surface; where a deployment adopts Mission Status, its Mission Lifecycle endpoint's `revoke` operation is the interoperable wire.

**Recommendation**

Adopt both. Land as a reviewed PR per core's issue-first rule; this issue is that filing.

**Tradeoffs**

Near-zero. No new normative reference: `{{I-D.draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-status}}` is already cited in that core paragraph and already informative, satisfying core-stands-alone. The edit only broadens an existing sentence's operation list and adds one clause, and gives architecture's invariant the same citation its own R9 entry already carries. The only live question, whether the core pointer stays informative, isn't actually live: it already is, unchanged by this edit.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: approve both edits. The corrected analysis is right that revocation is not uniquely missing a profile citation, but the invariant list is inconsistent with Architecture's own R9 traceability row, and core's existing Status pointer omits the exact `revoke` operation named by the adjacent MUST.

Architecture should add Status as the second citation on “Revocation is possession-independent,” matching R9. Core should extend the existing operation list to `revoke` / `suspend` / `resume` / `complete` and state the self-containment trade: a core-only deployment can satisfy the MUST through a deployment-defined authenticated surface; when Status is adopted, its Mission Lifecycle endpoint supplies the interoperable wire.

One precision: do not imply that merely implementing the Status endpoint automatically satisfies core's actor-availability requirement. The deployment still has to authorize the Subject, Approver, or administrator as core requires through Status's explicit lifecycle authorization policy or an equivalent grant. “Provides the interoperable operation” is safer than “therefore satisfies the MUST.”

Evidence: [Architecture invariant and R9](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md#L1119-L1124), [core revocation/pointer](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3420-L3436), and [Status lifecycle authorization](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-status.md#L1280-L1318).

Disposition: approve; informative pointer only, core remains independently implementable.

issues.title: Containment: mid-flight visibility seams (orchestration triggers, management contain, metering settlement)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

A contain transition changes no lifecycle state ("No state change" — containment), which leaves three seams where mid-flight containment is invisible to the machinery that would act on it:

1. orchestration's Trigger Sources list Status polling, lifecycle signals, PDP denial, harness stop, operator action, and deployment governance events — no containment trigger, and state-change behavior never fires on contain. An in-flight or dispatched step whose capability was just contained is caught only by the next ordinary PDP check.
2. containment's containment-plane section SHOULDs "the same dry-run-first posture as bulk lifecycle operations" citing management — but management's bulk verbs are exactly revoke/suspend/resume/complete; the invoked bulk contain operation does not exist.
3. metering and containment never reference each other; whether an open reservation or duration lease against a now-contained capability is force-settled is silent in both.

One coordinated cut, not three drive-bys: containment (or Signals authority_changed consumption) joins orchestration's trigger sources; management either gains contain or containment's pointer is rescoped to per-Mission posture; metering gets a one-rule settlement answer at contain time.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-23, architecture-review follow-through; verified against main @ 2d63119a):**

**Analysis**

All three seams verified, with a correction on (c).

(a) Trigger Sources ({{trigger-sources}}) already lists "Mission lifecycle signals"; a new bullet is cosmetic. The real gap is State-Change Behavior ({{state-change-behavior}}): its entry condition fires only when a Mission is "no longer `active`," but contain leaves `state` unchanged and surfaces only as `authority_changed: true` (Signals {{lifecycle-event}}), so nothing fires today. Its item 1, "stop dispatching... for that Mission," is also the wrong grain: containment narrows entries, not the Mission.

(b) Containment's containment-plane text ({{containment-plane}}) SHOULDs "the same dry-run-first posture as bulk lifecycle operations," naming the plane and drawing an analogy, not invoking a management verb: no dangling reference to repair. Management's bulk verbs (revoke/suspend/resume/complete, {{bulk-lifecycle}}) are status-profile lifecycle operations; contain is not one.

(c) Correction: force-settling an open reservation to "released" on contain is wrong. Settlement already runs on evidence state ({{settlement-states}}): completed execution commits real consumption, and a non-idempotent reservation releases only on affirmative non-execution, never on timeout. Forcing release on contain lets containment do what timeout may not, under-debiting budget for real work. Lease renewal is already covered: renewal needs a fresh permit (`max_duration`), refused by the narrowed Effective Authority Set; unstoppable exhaustion already routes to orchestration's `dispatched_not_committed`/`unknown`.

**Sketch**

1. Orchestration: extend {{state-change-behavior}}'s trigger condition to cover `authority_changed: true` at unchanged `state`, scoped per step: a dispatched-not-committed step on a contained entry stops and re-gates against the current Effective Authority Set; steps on uncontained entries proceed. Re-gating, not the non-active sequence, and not compensation (containment narrows, it does not end the Mission). Reuses existing Orchestration Evidence values (`state_source: signal`, `mission_state: active`, `orchestration_decision: suppress`/`pause`); no new enum member.
2. Management: no verb added. Rescope containment's pointer to name the posture directly (dry-run-then-execute review gate), not a verb that doesn't exist. Record a named trigger for a future bulk `contain` op: an operator console needing fleet containment.
3. Metering: one cross-reference, not a new settlement state: contain does not force-settle an open reservation or lease; settlement still runs under {{settlement-states}}. Containment bars forward draw only: a new reservation or renewal against a contained entry is refused by the ordinary permit check against the narrowed set.

**Recommendation**

Ship (a) and (c). Disposition (b) as park-by-trigger: no core edit beyond de-linking the analogy from a specific verb.

**Tradeoffs**

Adding `contain` to management now would give bulk containment a review gate immediately (the bulk token's five bindings generalize mechanically), but contain isn't a status-profile lifecycle op: forcing it in makes management depend on containment and opens a second authority path into the overlay beside protected events, for a case with no named operator yet. Per-step re-gating costs a branch per step rather than per Mission; a whole-Mission stop is simpler but wrong: it treats a narrowing overlay as if it ended the Mission.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `origin/main` at `2d63119a`: the generic `authority_changed` direction is correct, with two execution gaps to close.

Trigger Sources already includes lifecycle signals, while State-Change Behavior fires only for non-`active` state or staleness. A contain commit remains `active`, so it bypasses that branch. Signals supplies the right discriminator: `authority_changed` covers effective-authority narrowing at unchanged state and requires rematerialization before further consequential reliance.

Define this as a third authority-narrowing branch, not as the existing non-active sequence. After rematerializing the Effective Authority Set, re-evaluate each pending step's concrete resource/action. A `not_dispatched` step now denied is suppressed or paused; a `dispatched_not_committed` step now denied follows its existing `in_flight_behavior`; a committed step is not compensated merely because authority later narrowed. “Stop and re-gate” has the wrong order for already-dispatched work.

The draft must also define how a step is associated with authority. The signal carries no entry digest and the unwind-plan schema records only step/Mission and behavioral classifications. Require a fresh PDP evaluation of the concrete step, or bind it to its permit's Decision Evidence (`authorizing_entry`/`entry_digest`). Otherwise “steps on uncontained entries proceed” is not interoperably decidable.

Management should remain unchanged, including its existing analogy; it does not claim to define `contain`. Metering likewise needs only the informative clarification: containment is not settlement evidence, so it neither releases nor force-commits a reservation; renewal already re-evaluates.

Bookkeeping: a normative orchestration rule consuming Signals makes Signals normative there, requiring front matter and typed-edge changes. The externally observable per-step behavior also needs a conformance row/test; Orchestration is not currently in `source.specs`.

Evidence: [orchestration state branch](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-orchestration.md#L512-L606), [`authority_changed`](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-signals.md#L417-L431), [rematerialization](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-signals.md#L598-L621), and [Metering settlement](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/2d63119a16c29baa80106d8e6cd4b6cae00dfd29/draft-mcguinness-mission-metering.md#L864-L916).

Disposition: accept the trigger/no-management/no-force-settle direction with per-step authority resolution and reference/conformance changes.

issues.title: Family: informative crosswalk for the four failure taxonomies
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08 family architecture review; verified against main @ 2d63119a (D133).

Four verification/failure taxonomies coexist with loose prose nods and no mapping: mandate's five classes (Invalid / Partial / Unverifiable / Stale / Expired), audit's integrity-vs-audit split (shared by consent-evidence), transaction-authorization's deny / terminal refusal / fail closed, and the security model's fail-closed-on-authority / fail-safe-on-inert-evidence principle.

Not a merge: an informative crosswalk table (most naturally in the security model) mapping each taxonomy's classes onto the fail-closed/fail-safe axis, for verifiers who cross artifact types. Low priority; recorded so it stays a decision rather than drift.

issues.title: Core: scope projection can silently discard constrained authority (lossless-or-omit rule)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P0 finding 2); verified against main @ 59b958e5: the scope-projection rules require scope no broader than authorization_details, while the scope-only RS text says such an RS "enforces only the coarse scope projection" and "does not evaluate" per-entry constraints. Both cannot hold for a constrained entry: a journal.write scope at a legacy RS authorizes more than the USD-500-constrained journal.write entry unless that RS independently enforces the identical ceiling. Deriving the scope from RAR does not transmit the missing semantics.

Analysis: agreed; this is the enforcement-plane sibling of the recorded "narrowing is typed" caveat, and it is a real hole in the claimed boundary, not a disclosure gap.

Proposed ruling: an AS MAY project a scope for an entry only when the projection is lossless for that entry (no constraints, or constraints the AS knows the serving enforcement path independently enforces); otherwise it MUST omit the scope or route the entry exclusively through a RAR-aware RS/PEP. The Enforcement Scope Statement is the natural place to declare which resources qualify.

Tradeoffs: fewer unchanged legacy RS deployments qualify for scope-only operation, but the claimed security boundary becomes true. Capability-preserving: constrained entries remain expressible; only the lossy projection is withdrawn.

Core is issue-first; this is the filed finding.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Review — accept the finding, strengthen the solution before implementation

The contradiction is real, but the proposed lossless-or-omit rule is currently too narrow.

### P0 — “No constraints” is not sufficient for losslessness

A scope can widen more than constraints. It can also aggregate multiple actions, cover more resource instances or paths, convey rights implied by the RS's local scope interpretation, or combine several RAR entries into a broader union.

The safe condition should be semantic:

> For every target Resource Server, the effective rights that the RS grants from the projected scopes, together with every independently mandatory control on that path, MUST be a subset of the rights granted by the token's applicable `authorization_details`.

This cannot be reduced to whether an entry carries `constraints`. RFC 9396 deliberately permits `scope` and `authorization_details` to express independent requirements and leaves their combination API-specific. This profile is defining a stronger projection relationship and therefore has to define it completely. See [RFC 9396 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9396.html#section-3.1).

The current core requirement already says scope cannot relax a constraint, while the scope-only RS paragraph contradicts it: [projection requirement](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3025-L3037), [scope-only behavior](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3333-L3340).

### P1 — “Omit or route” assigns behavior to the wrong party

The AS does not route the subsequent protected-resource request. Use an issuance algorithm instead:

1. Determine the target RS or audience.
2. Resolve a trusted, versioned scope-projection mapping for that RS.
3. Establish that the complete effective authorization granted by the projected scopes is no broader than the applicable carried entries.
4. If the target enforcement path consumes `authorization_details`, the AS may omit scope.
5. If the target is scope-only and no safe projection exists, the AS MUST refuse issuance; emitting an unusable token is not a useful security outcome.
