6. For a multi-audience token, the proof must hold independently for every audience; single-audience tokens remain preferred.

Unknown scope semantics, unknown RS behavior, or an ambiguous or stale mapping fail closed.

### P1 — The Enforcement Scope Statement cannot own the baseline rule

The Enforcement Scope Statement exists only when the runtime profile is deployed. Core deliberately supports an issuance-only deployment.

The projection contract belongs in core as issuer knowledge about the target RS/API, established through protected-resource metadata or authenticated out-of-band configuration. Existing metadata already supports declaring enforced constraint keys: [Protected Resource Metadata](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L4251-L4269).

An Enforcement Scope Statement may reference that same mapping for runtime-covered paths, but it must not become a normative core dependency.

### Acceptance criteria

Update every misleading scope-only claim, including the Intent enforcement table, RS section, and minimum-deployment text. Add conformance rows and tests for:

- a constraint discarded by scope;
- scope aggregating a broader action;
- scope covering a broader resource or path;
- multiple scopes whose union widens authority;
- a safe projection with independently enforced constraints;
- an unknown or stale mapping; and
- refresh, Token Exchange, and other derived-token issuance paths.

**Disposition:** accept after replacing the constraint-focused sketch with the complete semantic projection rule above.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition on the review (2026-08-24): all three corrections adopted; amended ruling below supersedes the original sketch.**

1. **Losslessness is semantic, not structural.** The constraint-presence test is withdrawn. The governing condition is the review's subset rule: for every target Resource Server, the effective rights the RS grants from the projected scopes, together with every independently mandatory control on that path, MUST be a subset of the rights granted by the token's applicable authorization_details. Scope aggregation (actions, resource instances, paths, multi-entry unions, RS-local interpretation) is exactly what the structural test missed.

2. **Issuance algorithm replaces omit-or-route.** The AS cannot route protected-resource requests; it can only decide what to issue. Adopted as written: resolve a trusted, versioned scope-projection mapping per target RS; prove the subset condition; omit scope where the enforcement path consumes authorization_details; REFUSE issuance where the target is scope-only and no safe projection exists (an unusable token is not a security outcome); prove per audience on multi-audience tokens; unknown semantics, unknown RS behavior, or stale mappings fail closed.

3. **Core owns the projection contract, not the Enforcement Scope Statement.** The ESS exists only under the runtime profile; core supports issuance-only deployments, so the mapping is issuer knowledge established via protected-resource metadata (which already declares enforced constraint keys) or authenticated out-of-band configuration. An ESS may reference the same mapping for runtime-covered paths, never own it.

**Acceptance criteria adopted verbatim**: sweep every misleading scope-only claim (Intent enforcement table, RS section, minimum-deployment text) and add conformance rows/tests for the seven listed cases, including refresh, Token Exchange, and derived-token issuance paths.

Interlock noted for execution: the concrete projection semantics for mission_resource_access land in the #637 RAR profile; core carries the type-agnostic subset rule and the issuance algorithm.

Retiered decide -> now per the review's acceptance; enters the next core PR wave on go-ahead (core is issue-first; this issue is the record).

issues.title: Core: one approval commitment binding the whole approval transaction
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P0 finding 3); verified against main @ 59b958e5.

Finding: intent_hash, proposal_hash, and authority_hash are independent anchors with no joint binding of mission_id, subject/approver, effective expiry, approval basis, authority source, policy version, and admission evidence; the core discloses the independent-anchor limitation itself, and submission evidence is record-only and uncommitted. Consent Evidence partly repairs this but is optional.

Analysis: the gap is real and already self-disclosed. But the proposed manifest largely EXISTS in the family twice: the Mandate's claim set (mission id/issuer/authority_hash/intent_hash/expires_at, subject, approver, policy_version, approval_event_id) and the Approval Governance Record's envelope both aggregate these facts; both are optional overlays minted beside the record rather than a commitment inside it.

Proposed ruling: define approval_commitment as a core Mission Record member: a digest over a canonical manifest of the component digests plus the immutable approval facts (the review's sketch is close to Mandate's claim set). Existing anchors remain selective-disclosure components; Mandate and AGR become disclosures of the same root rather than parallel aggregations. Privacy: commit hashes of sensitive members, or a Merkle-style manifest.

Tradeoffs: one more committed member and a canonicalization surface in core, against a single root that makes the approval transaction provable without adopting two optional companions. Interacts with #284's ruled Default Commitment Construction (reuse it, do not invent a second construction) and with expansion/child anchors that cite the existing hashes (survey before landing).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Review — revise substantially before ruling

The fragmented-anchor observation is real, but the proposed core `approval_commitment` currently overclaims what an unkeyed digest proves and underspecifies how companion artifacts would verify against it.

### P0 — A digest stored beside its preimage is not independent proof

A malicious or compromised issuer can replace the Mission Record and recompute `approval_commitment`. The existing immutable record already binds its fields under trust in the AS; a new digest adds no independent trust property unless the root is authenticated or pinned outside that record.

The core already states this principle: external pinning is what makes the difference against post-approval substitution. See [commitment pinning limitation](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L4446-L4455).

Therefore this claim is not supportable as written:

> A single root makes the approval transaction provable without adopting two optional companions.

Without a signature, transparency registration, Approver confirmation, or another independently retained authenticated copy, it proves no more than the record already does.

### P0 — Mandate, AGR, and Consent Evidence cannot simply become disclosures of a flat root

They have different semantics and lifecycles:

- Mandate is an issuer-signed portable Mission snapshot and may be minted later.
- Approval Governance Record proves assertion and policy evaluation and is committed atomically with creation.
- Consent Evidence records what was disclosed and decided, including declined and narrowed outcomes for which no Mission exists.

A flat hash can be verified only by disclosing the complete canonical manifest. A Merkle root instead requires normative leaf encoding, ordering, salt, proof format, and verifier processing. Neither follows automatically from the Default Commitment Construction.

The current Mandate also does not carry the proposed complete manifest: some audit fields are optional, and it omits several approval-basis, authority-source, and submission-evidence facts. See [Mandate claims](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-mandate.md#L317-L380).

### P1 — Hashing sensitive members is not a privacy solution

Hashes of low-entropy subjects, approval types, policy identifiers, and timestamps may be dictionary-testable. “Commit hashes of sensitive members” does not provide selective disclosure.

If selective disclosure is required, the design needs salted commitments or an established selective-disclosure construction. It must also decide whether the root appears in access tokens, introspection, evidence artifacts, or only the issuer record; those placements have different correlation and disclosure consequences.

### P1 — Select a verifier and threat model first

The issue should choose one concrete goal:

1. **Record consistency:** detect accidental internal divergence. A local record digest can do this but cannot claim independent proof.
2. **Portable approval evidence:** use a signed artifact such as Mandate, AGR, or Consent Evidence.
3. **Cross-artifact correlation:** define a canonical approval-context manifest that authenticated artifacts reference.
4. **Selective verification:** define a separate Merkle- or SD-JWT-based proof profile.

Only the third potentially justifies a shared root. If selected, it is more naturally an optional approval-context commitment profile than a mandatory core member.

### If a common manifest proceeds

It must be closed and versioned and include only immutable creation facts:

- Mission issuer and ID;
- existing intent, proposal, and authority anchors;
- subject, approver, and client;
- effective expiry and creation instant;
- approval basis and authority source;
- policy identity and a digest where one exists;
- approval event identifier; and
- a normalized submission-evidence commitment.

Mutable lifecycle state, containment, discharge state, counters, and derivation balances must be excluded.

Reuse the Default Commitment Construction from #284, but state that it supplies canonicalization and algorithm handling—not authenticity, approval-time existence, or selective-disclosure proofs. The issue must also inventory Template, Progressive, Expansion, Child Delegation, MAS, Cross-Domain, Mandate, Consent Evidence, AGR, introspection, and any token carriage before calling the change implementable.

**Disposition:** keep the problem, replace the proposed ruling with a verifier- and threat-model-first design investigation. Do not batch this with #698; #698 is an immediate enforcement correction, while this is a larger evidence and cryptographic-composition decision.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition on the review (2026-08-24): corrections accepted, including the retraction below; the proposed ruling is withdrawn in favor of the verifier-first investigation.**

**Retraction.** The original claim that "a single root makes the approval transaction provable without adopting two optional companions" overclaimed. An unkeyed digest stored beside its preimage adds no trust property the record lacks: a compromised issuer recomputes it; the core's own commitment-pinning limitation already states that external pinning is what defeats post-approval substitution. Withdrawn.

**Corrections adopted:**
- Mandate, AGR, and Consent Evidence are not disclosures of a flat root: they differ in signer, lifecycle, and coverage (Mandate minted later and missing manifest facts; AGR atomic with creation; Consent Evidence covering declined/narrowed outcomes where no Mission exists). Any shared-root design must respect those semantics, and a Merkle alternative requires normative leaf encoding, ordering, salts, proof format, and verifier processing that the Default Commitment Construction does not supply.
- Hashing sensitive members is not selective disclosure: low-entropy members are dictionary-testable; salted commitments or an established SD construction are the floor, and root placement (token, introspection, evidence, issuer record) must be chosen per its correlation consequences.
- #284's construction supplies canonicalization and algorithm handling only: never authenticity, approval-time existence, or selective-disclosure proofs.

**Reframed issue (replaces the original ask): a verifier- and threat-model-first design investigation.** Choose the goal before any mechanism: (1) record consistency: a local digest, no independence claim; (2) portable approval evidence: already served by the signed artifacts; (3) cross-artifact correlation: a canonical, closed, versioned approval-context manifest that the authenticated artifacts REFERENCE: the only goal that justifies a shared root, and then as an optional approval-context commitment profile, not a core member; (4) selective verification: a separate Merkle/SD-JWT proof profile.

Investigation lean: goal 3. Deliverables if pursued: the closed manifest (immutable creation facts only: issuer/id, existing anchors, subject/approver/client, effective expiry, created_at, approval basis, authority source, policy identity+digest, approval event id, normalized submission-evidence commitment: mutable lifecycle state excluded) and the consumer inventory (Template, Progressive, Expansion, Child Delegation, MAS, Cross-Domain, Mandate, Consent Evidence, AGR, introspection, token carriage) before implementability is claimed.

**Not batched with #698**, per the review: that is an immediate enforcement correction; this is an evidence and cryptographic-composition decision. Stays decide.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body: **Ruled (2026-08-24, owner):** goal 3. Proceed with the design investigation for an OPTIONAL approval-context commitment profile: a canonical, closed, versioned manifest of immutable creation facts that Mandate, AGR, and Consent Evidence reference (their signatures supply authenticity; the manifest supplies the shared shape). Deliverables before implementability is claimed: the closed manifest definition and the 11-consumer inventory. Goals 1/2/4 declined for now; goal 4 (selective disclosure) revisits only on demonstrated consumer demand.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Design investigation for goal 3, per the ruling above. All citations are to `main` at `59b958e5` unless otherwise marked. This is an investigation only: no PR, no core edit.

## 1. The closed manifest

### Definition

The **Approval Context Manifest** is the [Mission Record](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2508-L2781) minus its one mutable member (`state`), with every bulky consented object replaced by the commitment that already covers it (or a new one, for `submission_evidence`) rather than embedded verbatim. Concretely:

| Manifest member | Type | Source | Presence rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| `issuer` | string | Mission Record `issuer` (2542-2547) | always |
| `id` | string | Mission Record `id` (2538-2540) | always |
| `intent_hash` | string | existing anchor (2572-2576) | always |
| `proposal_hash` | string | existing anchor (2577-2584) | iff record carries `proposed_authority` |
| `authority_hash` | string | existing anchor (2568-2571) | always |
| `subject` | object `{iss,sub}` | Mission Record `subject` (2612-2615) | always |
| `approver` | object `{iss,sub}` | Mission Record `approver` (2616-2619) | always |
| `client_id` | string | Mission Record `client_id` (2745-2747) | always |
| `created_at` | string, RFC 3339 | Mission Record `created_at` (2761-2762) | always |
| `expires_at` | string, RFC 3339 | Mission Record `expires_at` (2764-2775) | always |
| `approval_basis` | object, verbatim | Mission Record `approval_basis` (2621-2721), fixed at the approval event and immutable thereafter | always |
| `authority_source` | object, verbatim | Mission Record `authority_source` (2723-2743) | always |
| `policy_version` | string | Mission Record `policy_version` (2749-2751) | always |
| `approval_event_id` | string | Mission Record `approval_event_id` (2753-2759), the approval idempotency key | always |
| `submission_evidence_commitment` | string | new anchor, defined below | iff record carries `submission_evidence` |

`authority_source` verbatim already carries `policy {id, version, digest}` for the `organizational` source type (2734-2738), so "policy identity + digest where one exists" needs no separate top-level member. `approval_basis` verbatim carries `type`, `consent_principal`, `activation`, `activation_actor`, `root_commitment`, and `approved_at` where applicable (2627-2712), so no field of it is singled out.

**Explicit exclusions.** The manifest excludes mutable lifecycle state, containment, discharge state, counters, and derivation balances. `state` is the record's only mutable member and is dropped by construction (2510-2511, 2549-2553). Containment and discharge state are never Mission Record members at all; they live on their own companions' surfaces, so they were never candidates for inclusion or exclusion here. Operational issuance bookkeeping, including the derivation count and any derivation-budget counter, is explicitly "AS-side state about the Mission, not a member of the immutable record" (2512-2515), so it too never entered the record this manifest is built from, and excluding it needs no special rule beyond building the manifest from record members only.

The manifest never embeds `proposed_authority`, `authority_set`, or `submission_evidence` as objects; each is represented only by its digest, keeping the manifest small regardless of Authority Set size.

**`submission_evidence_commitment`.** A new envelope anchor ([Integrity Anchors](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2321-L2398)) with `typ` `mission-submission-evidence` (candidate name), `iss` the Mission `issuer`, and `value` the record's `submission_evidence` array exactly as recorded (2585-2610): one entry per verified entry, each carrying `type`, `artifact_hash`, `verified_at`, `facts`, in the submission's evidence order, which the record definition already fixes as the one canonical form. This is not new machinery: 2607-2610 already anticipates it, stating that a profile whose threat model needs the evidence-to-Mission association "commits normalized provenance under its own anchor `typ`... this document defines none." The manifest is that profile. It can be defined against today's `submission_evidence` shape independent of #512/#282 landing; #512's ruling fixes what a future Intent Admission entry's `facts` payload contains, not the array's commitment mechanics, so nothing here blocks on it or is invalidated by it.

### Construction and versioning

The manifest is an envelope anchor under [Commitment Mechanisms](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2429-L2506), reusing #284's Default Commitment Construction (JCS, I-JSON conformance, SHA-256, `sha-256:` prefix, reject-unknown-prefix, no-downgrade) without redefining it. `typ` is a single new collision-resistant name (candidate: `mission-approval-context`); `iss` is the Mission `issuer`; `value` is the object above. The result, `approval_context_commitment`, is one `sha-256:`-prefixed string.

**Versioning rule.** The member list above is closed for this `typ`: every member's presence is a deterministic function of the retained Mission Record alone (a companion's own on-record fact, like `proposed_authority`'s presence, never a fact about which companion profiles a deployment happens to run). This is what lets an Approval Governance Record, committed atomically at creation, and a Mandate, minted later, reproduce the identical root independently: every input is fixed at the atomic Mission-creation commit and never changes afterward. Adding, removing, or redefining a member is a new `typ`, under the same no-silent-reinterpretation discipline the family already applies to every anchor (2358-2369, 2490-2497). This document does not make the manifest an open, per-companion-extensible object the way the Mission Record itself is (2528-2536): an extension whose presence depends on deployment configuration would make the root non-reproducible by a party who does not know the active companion set, defeating goal 3. Lineage members that do not live on the Mission's own record (Expansion's `predecessor`, Child Delegation's `parent`, `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-expansion.md` 809-832, `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md` 944-976) therefore stay outside the manifest permanently, not as a future extension point.

One candidate member surfaced by this research but **outside the ruling's enumerated list**, flagged as Gate 2 below: Progressive's `ceiling_hash` (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-progressive.md` 283-298) is recorded directly on the same Mission record, under the same immutability rule, exactly when the record carries `authority_ceiling`/`drawdown_policy`. It satisfies the determinism rule the same way `proposal_hash` does and is a plausible fourth "existing anchor" for the manifest, but the ruling names only intent/proposal/authority, so this needs confirmation before drafting rather than silent inclusion.

### What the construction does not supply

Reusing #284's construction (canonicalization, I-JSON conformance, algorithm identification and agility) buys exactly that and nothing else. It does not supply:

- **Authenticity.** The manifest is an unkeyed digest over Mission Record fields held under the same trust as the record itself. A compromised or malicious issuer that can rewrite the record can recompute the manifest and its root to match; the root's authentication comes entirely from the signature of whichever artifact discloses it (a Mandate's JWS, an AGR's `envelope`, a Consent Evidence's `evidence_envelope`), never from the digest construction. This restates the retraction above and the core's own commitment-pinning limitation ([Consent Binding](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L4445-L4455)): pinning outside the issuer is what defends against post-approval substitution, and nothing here pins anything.
- **Approval-time existence.** The root proves the referenced facts are internally consistent with each other as recorded; it does not prove they were true, or that an approval genuinely occurred, at the time claimed. That property, where it exists at all, comes from an external witness (a transparency service, an Approver confirmation) never from this construction.
- **Selective disclosure.** The root is a flat digest over the complete manifest object; proving anything about one member requires disclosing the whole object. No salting, blinding, or inclusion-proof mechanism is defined here. This is goal 4, explicitly declined for now; the P1 finding about dictionary-testable low-entropy members hashing to guessable digests applies to a selective-disclosure design, not to goal 3, where the manifest is always disclosed alongside, or reconstructible from, the plaintext record it commits. No new privacy exposure exists here beyond what the plaintext record and its existing consumers already carry.

### Where the root may and must not appear

**May appear:**
- The Mission Issuer's own record, as a *derived, recomputable* value. It needs no new persisted Mission Record member: every input is already on the record, so an issuer computes it on demand at minting time. A deployment MAY cache it for efficiency; this document does not require storage (Gate 1 below).
- Mandate, AGR, and Consent Evidence, each as a new OPTIONAL member (Section 2).
- Token introspection, as a new OPTIONAL response member gated by the same member-scoped disclosure privilege that already applies to `proposal_hash` and `derivations_remaining` ([Caller Authorization and Minimization](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3595-L3621)), never in the default audience-filtered Resource Server projection.

**Must not appear:**
- The baseline Mission-bound access token's `mission` claim ([The Mission Claim](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3063-L3121)). #702's disposition is explicit and directly on point: the baseline claim shrinks to `{id, issuer}` and drops `authority_hash` itself, "coordinated with #699 so the family does not invent competing token-carried roots." Adding this manifest's root to that claim would be exactly the outcome #702 rules out.
- The Cross-Domain grant's `mission` claim (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-cross-domain.md` 530-534, "unchanged from the Mission," a 300-second bearer-shaped JWT-bearer grant): already in scope, since #702's own migration-inventory paragraph names "cross-domain carriage" among the sites it re-mechanizes. This manifest adds nothing there beyond confirming the same root-exclusion reading applies.
- The Mission Authority Server's Join Assertion (`draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server.md` 1682-1684, `mission {id, issuer, authority_hash}`, re-minted on every token rotation): carries the identical shape and is subject to the same reasoning, but it is **not** named in #702's migration inventory and should be added to it (Section 2, row 5).

### Not a fourth aggregation

Two other family mechanisms already aggregate creation-time facts under one anchor. Both are distinct in purpose and must not be conflated with this manifest:

- **The operation fingerprint** (`mission-creation-fingerprint`, `draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-expansion.md` 1175-1268, adopted by Child Delegation 759-798 and Template Dispatch): a pre-creation idempotency anchor over request-time inputs (`op`, `client`, `source`, `cnf`, `actor`, `intent`, `evidence`, `proposal`, `requested_token_type`, `cross_check`), domain-separated by `op` across the several creation exchanges that share it. It exists to distinguish a retried request from a new one; its retention contract is the retry horizon, with extension to the audit horizon only RECOMMENDED (1352-1364), never referenced by Mandate, AGR, or Consent Evidence, and it excludes `authority_hash`, `subject`, `approver`, and `policy_version` entirely. It answers "is this the same request," not "what was approved." The `op` domain-separation pattern was considered as a versioning mechanism for the manifest and rejected: `op` separates structurally different objects sharing one `typ`; the manifest has one shape, so a schema change is a new `typ`, per the rule above.
- **The recurring `{id, issuer, authority_hash}` micro-descriptor**, which the original issue undercounted at "twice." It recurs at minimum in: the token `mission` claim (3067-3080), the MAS Join Assertion (above), the Cross-Domain grant claim (above), the Mission Join Assertion (above), Child Delegation's `parent` member (944-962) and its separate Child Evidence object's `parent`/`child` fields (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-child-delegation.md` 1507-1511, 1540-1551), and Consent Evidence's and AGR's `mission` descriptors (Section 2). This manifest does not replace any of them; each keeps its own descriptor for direct lookup, and each is a candidate site for an additive `..._commitment` reference alongside its existing `authority_hash`, never a replacement of it (Section 2).

## 2. The 11-consumer inventory

| # | Consumer | Aggregates/references today | Change if it referenced the manifest | Breaking? | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Template | Dispatched Mission is an ordinary Mission Record; `approval_basis.type` is `template`, `root_commitment` is `template_hash`, `approved_at` is the template's own consent instant (`draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-template.md` 383-406, 427-465). | None. The manifest is a pure function of the dispatched Mission's own record; `template_hash` reaches it already, through `approval_basis.root_commitment`. | No | S (documentation note only) |
| 2 | Progressive | The consenting Mission itself records `authority_ceiling`, `drawdown_policy`, `ceiling_hash` (283-312); a policy-adjudicated successor's `approval_basis.type` is `ceiling_drawdown`, with `root_commitment = ceiling_hash` (340-364); Audit Linkage (613-644) reconstructs the chain from these plus `predecessor`. | `approval_basis` flows into the manifest unchanged, whatever its `type`, so `ceiling_drawdown` needs no special case. `ceiling_hash` itself is the one candidate addition to the closed list (Gate 2, Section 1); if adopted, the edit lands in the manifest companion's member table, not in Progressive itself. | No | S (no change to this document either way) |
| 3 | Expansion | Successor is a fresh Mission Record from a fresh approval event, "authority comes only from new consent" (1618-1630); lineage is `predecessor`/`related_to`/`successor` (809-895), audited by walking the chain (1717-1724); creation-time dedup uses the operation fingerprint (`op: expansion`, 1175-1268), not this manifest. | None required. Each successor gets its own, ordinary manifest instance. Lineage members are deliberately excluded from the closed list (Section 1) since their presence is not a fact of the Mission's own record. | No | S |
| 4 | Child Delegation | Child Mission's `approval_basis` is `direct` or `policy_drawdown`, with `root_commitment` anti-laundering to a committed value (1035-1091); the `parent` member embeds `{id, issuer, authority_hash, depth, ...}` (939-1004); a separate Child Evidence object repeats `parent`/`child` `{id, issuer, authority_hash}` (1484-1567). | None required for the record itself, same reasoning as Expansion. Optionally, `parent` and Child Evidence's `parent`/`child` could each gain an additive `..._commitment` member alongside the existing `authority_hash`, letting a verifier holding only the child cross-check the parent's manifest without a separate lookup. | No (additive only) | S (none required); S if the optional `..._commitment` additions are made |
| 5 | MAS | "The record is the issuance profile's Mission Record, member for member" (`draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server.md` 707-714): inherits whatever core does automatically. The Mission Join Assertion mints a `mission {id, issuer, authority_hash}` JWT per token rotation (1669-1745). | No MAS-specific Mission Record change. The Join Assertion is a "must not appear" site (Section 1) that is **not** named in #702's migration inventory; add it there. | No | S (coordination note only) |
| 6 | Cross-Domain | The cross-domain grant MUST carry `mission {id, issuer, authority_hash}` "unchanged from the Mission" (473-537), a 300-second bearer-shaped JWT-bearer grant. Origin Principal adds `mission.subject` (781-843), untouched by this. | None. #702's migration inventory already names "cross-domain carriage" as a site to re-mechanize; this manifest changes nothing about that scope, it only confirms the grant's `mission` claim gains no root from this profile. | No | S (already tracked by #702) |
| 7 | Mandate | Claims mirror a strict subset of the manifest: `mission {id, issuer, authority_hash, intent_hash, expires_at}` REQUIRED, `subject`, `approver`, `client_id`, `policy_version`, `state_at_issuance` REQUIRED, `created_at`/`approval_event_id`/`authority_set` OPTIONAL (317-405). It omits `approval_basis`, `authority_source`, `submission_evidence`, and `proposal_hash` entirely, confirming the review's finding. | Add one new OPTIONAL claim, `approval_context_commitment`, computed at minting time as a pure function of the already-persisted, immutable Mission Record: Mandate is minted after Mission creation is settled (317-322), so this is an ordinary read-then-hash with no ordering constraint against the creation commit. A short paragraph in Verification states what it does and does not prove (Section 1). No existing claim is removed or reshaped. | No (purely additive JWT claim; no existing Mandate is rehashed or invalidated) | M |
| 8 | Consent Evidence | The `mission` descriptor is `{id, issuer, intent_hash, authority_hash, proposal_hash, consent_rendering_hash}` on the `approved` branch only; `declined`/`narrowed` branches carry `{issuer, intent_hash, authority_hash, proposal_hash}` with no `id`, because no Mission exists yet (756-843). `consent_rendering_hash` commits the rendered disclosure, which the core deliberately does not commit under any Mission anchor ([Consent Binding](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L4481-L4485)), and which the manifest's enumerated list also does not include. | Add one new OPTIONAL member to the `mission` descriptor, valid only on the `approved` branch (a manifest requires a Mission `id`, which `declined`/`narrowed` never have). It can only augment the descriptor, never replace `consent_rendering_hash`, which stays a permanent, separate commitment outside the manifest. | No (additive, approved-branch only) | M |
| 9 | AGR | Record carries `approval_event_id`, `mission {issuer, intent_hash, authority_hash}`, `approval_policy {id, version, digest}`, `assertions[]`, `evaluation` (245-390). It omits `subject`, `client_id`, `expires_at`, `created_at`, and `authority_source` entirely: AGR is *more* incomplete against this list than Mandate, not merely redundant with it, contrary to the original issue's "largely exists twice" framing. | Add one new OPTIONAL member alongside `mission` and `approval_policy`. This is the harder of the two signed-artifact additions, not the easier: the record and the Mission are one atomic commit, and signing "follows evaluation and precedes persistence, never the reverse" (`draft-mcguinness-mission-approval-governance.md`, "Evaluation and Atomic Commitment," 428-447), so the manifest's inputs must be fully materialized inside that same commit before AGR signs. This is an ordering constraint to place correctly, not a new class of risk: AGR already computes `mission.intent_hash`/`authority_hash` at that same point today, so the root is one more value slotted into an existing computation step. | No (additive; AGR's own `envelope` signature covers whatever members the object carries when signed, so past records are unaffected) | S-M |
| 10 | Introspection | Response carries `mission {id, issuer, authority_hash}` plus issuer-only `state`, `derivations_remaining`, `proposal_hash`, each under the caller-authorization and member-scoped disclosure rules (3532-3621). | Add one new OPTIONAL response member under the same member-scoped disclosure privilege as `proposal_hash`/`derivations_remaining`: an audit/correlation consumer opts in per caller, never the default Resource Server projection. | No | S |
| 11 | Token carriage | `mission` claim today is `{id, issuer, authority_hash, expires_at?, approval_basis.type?}` (3063-3121); #702 rules the baseline down to `{id, issuer}` and explicitly excludes a competing token-carried root, naming this issue. | None. This is a documentation-only "MUST NOT," not an engineering task; the manifest's root has no path onto a Mission-bound access token in any mode. | N/A (nothing added) | S |

## Conclusion

**Implementable**, as a scoped, mostly-additive OPTIONAL companion (or a section riding an existing evidence-adjacent document), plus small additive changes to three signed artifacts and one response surface. No consumer requires a breaking change to a committed hash; the only "must not" is enforced by omission (never adding the root where #702 already forbids a second root), and every "may" is a new OPTIONAL member.

Two gates block drafting; the rest can be resolved inside the drafting PR:

- **Gate 1 (storage model):** recompute the root on demand as a pure function of the retained Mission Record (recommended, avoids a new REQUIRED core member and keeps the profile purely additive) versus persist it as a new cached Mission Record member.
- **Gate 2 (list completeness):** whether Progressive's `ceiling_hash` joins the closed member list as a fourth "existing anchor" alongside intent/proposal/authority, given it satisfies the same determinism and immutability rule but is not named in the ruling's enumeration.

Other open questions, non-blocking:

- The collision-resistant `typ` name (`mission-approval-context` and `mission-submission-evidence` are candidates, not commitments).
- Whether Child Delegation's `parent` member and Child Evidence object should gain the optional `..._commitment` field alongside their existing `authority_hash`, or leave the manifest reachable only by resolving the parent Mission directly.
- Whether AGR should also gain the individual missing fields (`subject`, `client_id`, `expires_at`, `created_at`) explicitly, or rely solely on the manifest reference for them; recommend the latter, consistent with goal 3's intent of a shared reference rather than duplicated aggregation.
- Whether #702's migration inventory should be amended to add the MAS Join Assertion as an additional "must stay `{id, issuer}`-shaped" site; this issue cannot decide #702's scope, only flag the gap. Cross-Domain carriage is already named there and needs no addition.

Ordered execution plan:

1. Resolve Gates 1 and 2 above.
2. Draft the new OPTIONAL companion (or section) defining the manifest: the member table, the envelope construction (importing "Integrity Anchors" and "Commitment Mechanisms" normatively, inventing nothing), the versioning rule, and the three explicit non-guarantees (Section 1). Size M: narrow, single-purpose, no restatement of core machinery.
3. Mandate: add `approval_context_commitment` (OPTIONAL claim) and a short Verification paragraph. (M)
4. AGR: add the equivalent OPTIONAL member. (S-M)
5. Consent Evidence: add the equivalent OPTIONAL member, approved-branch only, with the declined/narrowed exclusion stated explicitly. (M)
6. Introspection: add the OPTIONAL response member under the existing member-scoped disclosure privilege. (S)
7. Documentation-only notes: Template, Progressive, Expansion, Child Delegation, Cross-Domain (no engineering change; state why explicitly, so a future reader does not mistake the silence for an oversight); MAS (flag the Join Assertion as a #702 migration-inventory gap). (S each)
8. Family PLAN.md decision-log entry on landing (outside this investigation's scope).

Goals 1, 2, and 4 remain declined per the ruling; nothing above revisits them.

issues.title: Core: specify the Mission-to-OAuth-grant cardinality
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P1 finding 4).

Finding: the README presents a Mission as sitting above and joining many grants; the core creates it atomically with one authorization grant and resolves it from that grant on later derivations. Both readings are workable; neither is formalized, and "above grants" prose does not answer revocation, enumeration, or migration questions.

Proposed ruling, pick one and state it normatively:
1. A Mission is a profiled root OAuth grant with 1:N descendant grants and credentials; or
2. A Mission is an independent task object with an explicit N:M Mission-grant association.

Analysis lean: option 2 matches shipped reality: cross-domain projection mints grants in another AS, MAS hosts the record with no OAuth AS at all, child delegation and expansion create related grants under one lineage. Option 1 reads cleaner for the single-AS case but strains at every boundary the family already crosses.

Follow-through either way: define how refresh families, Token Exchange derivations, cross-domain grants, successors, and Child Missions attach to the chosen relation, and what revoke/enumerate mean over it. This is the formal core of the strategic publication bucket the triage record already names (grant-profile framing).

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `main` at `b4e35419`.

**Disposition: revise the recommendation, then proceed.** Option 2 is directionally right, but the relation must not be described as unconstrained N:M.

The clean model is:

| Relation | Cardinality |
|---|---|
| Mission to Mission-bound OAuth grant lineage/family | `0..N` |
| Mission-bound grant lineage/family to Mission | exactly `1` |
| Mission to derived credentials | `0..N` |
| Mission-bound credential to Mission | exactly `1` |

A Mission is an independent durable authorization-context/task object. It can exist with no OAuth grant at all (the standalone MAS is the proof), and one Mission can support multiple authorization-code/refresh families, Token Exchange derivations, or grants issued in other domains. But a single grant or credential must never bind more than one Mission. That would require unioning distinct approval roots, state machines, expiries, and authority ceilings at every gate.

This is already the direction of the core binding: the AS resolves **the** Mission from the authorization code, refresh token, or Mission-bound `subject_token`, and explicitly refuses a client-supplied `mission_id` as the source of authority ([core grant binding](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2173-L2189)). The MAS separately proves that Mission existence is not cardinally dependent on an OAuth grant: in MAS mode there are no Mission-bound tokens or token introspection ([MAS lifecycle boundary](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server.md#L738-L750)).

The issue should also distinguish a **grant binding** from a **runtime join**. A MAS/PDP may join an ordinary credential to a Mission at request time. The same credential might participate in separately authorized joins for different Missions, but that does not make the OAuth grant Mission-bound and must not be modeled as a persistent N:M Mission-to-grant association. It is a decision-time association with its own authenticated inputs and evidence.

Recommended normative shape:

1. Define a Mission as independent of an OAuth grant and globally identified by `(issuer, id)`.
2. Define a Mission grant binding as an AS-controlled, functional mapping from one Mission-bound grant lineage to exactly one Mission. The protocol need not pretend OAuth grants are universally enumerable objects.
3. Permit zero or more bindings per Mission. Each authorization-code lineage, refresh family, Token Exchange derivation, and cross-domain local grant identifies one Mission only.
4. State that successor and Child Missions have new Mission identities and their own bindings. They are related by lineage, not additional grants of the parent Mission. Expansion changes one Mission's committed authority under its rules; it does not create a second Mission association for a grant.
5. Treat a continuation handle and refresh-token family as execution/credential machinery rooted in one Mission, not as the Mission itself.
6. On Mission non-active state, gate every future derivation through every binding. Do not imply that terminating a Mission necessarily revokes an underlying non-Mission OAuth grant, or that already issued access tokens disappear before their `exp` without a runtime state check.
7. Where fleet management needs cascade or enumeration, require an issuer-side index from Mission to its bound grant families/credentials. Keep that deployment index distinct from the interoperable Mission model.
8. Resolve the unredeemed-code case deterministically. The current `SHOULD revoke ... or allow it to expire` leaves two observable lifecycle outcomes for the same event; pick a deployment policy, record it, and make idempotent replay preserve it.

Acceptance tests should cover: one Mission with two refresh families; one family rejected if rebound to a second Mission; Token Exchange preserving one Mission; a cross-domain grant producing a destination-local family for the same Mission; a MAS decision-time join that does not become a grant binding; and termination gating every family while leaving residual access-token behavior governed by the declared reliance model.

So the ruling should be: **independent Mission object; 0:N Mission-to-binding, N:1 binding-to-Mission; no multi-Mission grant.**

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-24): adopted in full; supersedes this issue's original N:M lean.**

The constrained model is right and the original recommendation was too loose: unrestricted N:M would union distinct approval roots, state machines, expiries, and ceilings at every gate. Ruling adopted as stated: independent Mission object identified by (issuer, id); Mission-to-binding 0..N; binding-to-Mission exactly 1; no multi-Mission grant or credential, ever. The grant-binding vs runtime-join distinction is the keystone: a MAS/PDP decision-time join is an authenticated, evidenced association that never becomes a persistent grant binding, which is exactly what made N:M look plausible. All eight normative-shape points and the acceptance tests are adopted, including the deterministic unredeemed-code resolution (the SHOULD-revoke-or-expire fork becomes recorded deployment policy with idempotent replay preserving it).

Note: reviewed at b4e35419; the cited core/MAS text is unchanged in substance at HEAD (the editorial wave was zero-normative-delta). Retiered decide -> now: enters the core PR wave on go-ahead, alongside #698.

issues.title: Core: name the two approval roles (accountability root vs decision authority)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P1 finding 6).

Finding: the core requires a direct basis to be a human approval and standing consent to trace to an accountable human, then calls that human the approver even when policy adjudicates the instance decision. The review proposes two modeled roles: an accountability root (consent_principal/accountable_owner) and a decision_authority (human, policy engine, workflow, or delegated admin), with human-rooted consent as a strong named profile rather than a core invariant.

Analysis: the separation already exists in substance: approval_basis carries consent_principal and activation_actor, authority_source (#316 ruling) distinguishes the three sources, and AGR's assertions distinguish kind human/policy with policy tracing to the human who approved the policy. What does not exist is clean naming: "approver" does double duty as accountability root and as instance decider, which is exactly the confusion the review hit.

Proposed ruling: adopt the two role NAMES over the existing machinery (rename/alias, not new members): approver stays the accountability root (or is renamed consent_principal-consistently), and the instance decider is named decision_authority sourced from approval_basis.activation_actor/AGR. Do NOT drop the accountable-human root from core: authority never floating free of a traceable human decision is a family design signature, not an OAuth artifact; the review's reusability point is met by the naming split without weakening the invariant.

Tradeoffs: a rename touches every doc citing approver (mechanical, sweep-sized); keeping the human root means service-owned Missions still trace to an accountable person, which some estates will find heavier than bare RFC 6749 semantics: that is the intended posture, now stated as a choice.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `main` at `b4e35419`.

**Disposition: revise before implementation. The current two-role proposal still conflates three different roles.**

The family needs these concepts:

| Role | Question answered | Existing representation |
|---|---|---|
| Accountability/consent root | Who is accountable for the standing or direct authority root? | `approval_basis.consent_principal`, duplicated by top-level `approver` |
| Activation actor | Who or what requested/triggered this Mission instance? | `approval_basis.activation_actor` |
| Adjudicator / decision basis | What human, policy, workflow, or set of assertions decided this instance could be created? | direct approval event, standing-consent policy, and optionally AGR assertions/evaluation |

`activation_actor` cannot be renamed or treated as `decision_authority`. The core already defines it as “who or what triggered this instance” ([record definition](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2566-L2576)). In a Template dispatch, the Dispatcher is the activation actor while the template policy performs the admission check and the template's human approver remains the consent root ([Template construction](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-template.md#L478-L505)). A policy drawdown has the same separation. Calling the requester the decision authority would misstate both.

Nor is “decision authority” necessarily one principal. AGR can carry multiple human/policy assertions and an evaluation result. The better abstraction is a discriminated **adjudication basis** (or decision mechanism), with any participating principals and evidence modeled under the basis/profile that owns them. A simple direct approval can name one human; a policy or workflow can name a policy/version and evidence reference; an AGR-backed decision can reference the AGR rather than flatten its assertion set into a fake singular actor.

Recommended changes:

1. Keep `consent_principal` as the canonical accountability-root name. If the breaking window is available, remove top-level `approver`, which is already normatively equal to it ([duplicate fields](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2539-L2564)); otherwise mark `approver` as a deprecated compatibility alias. Do not introduce `accountable_owner` as a third synonym.
2. Keep `activation_actor` with its current trigger/requester meaning.
3. Name the third concept `adjudication` or `decision_basis`, not `decision_authority`, unless the schema explicitly supports a set of authorities. Prefer a discriminated object/reference over a universally required principal member.
4. Add a role-mapping table for at least direct, Template dispatch, policy drawdown, deferred human approval, and AGR-backed approval. Direct approval is the degenerate case where one human can fill all three roles; that coincidence must not define the model.
5. Reconcile the existing principal-model contradiction: the core says Approver may be a human or authorized policy authority ([principal model](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L701-L714)), while the record requires an accountable human or human-accountable principal and human approval for `direct` ([approval basis](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2560-L2588)). The latter is the more precise current invariant; make the principal model say the same thing.
6. Keep the question “must every source trace to a human-accountable root?” separate from naming the roles. My recommendation is to retain the current family invariant here; weakening it would be a substantive governance-profile decision, not a rename.

Tests/examples should demonstrate that a Dispatcher cannot be reported as the policy adjudicator merely because it activated a Template, that a multi-assertion AGR is not collapsed to one principal, and that the direct case still round-trips without redundant authority-bearing fields.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-24): adopted in full; the two-role proposal is superseded by the three-role model.**

The review's correction stands: activation_actor answers "who triggered this instance" and can never be relabeled decision authority (the Template Dispatcher activates; the template policy adjudicates; the template's human remains the consent root). Adopted: consent_principal stays the canonical accountability-root name with top-level approver removed in the breaking window (or deprecated-alias until then; no third synonym); activation_actor keeps its trigger meaning; the third concept is a discriminated adjudication/decision_basis object (a policy names policy/version and evidence, an AGR-backed decision references the AGR, never a flattened fake singular actor); the role-mapping table covers direct, Template dispatch, policy drawdown, deferred approval, and AGR-backed approval, with direct as the degenerate one-human case that must not define the model.

Also adopted: reconcile the principal-model contradiction toward the record's stricter human-accountable invariant, and keep the human-root question separate from naming (invariant retained, unchanged from this issue's original position).

Retiered decide -> now: the naming/table/contradiction work enters the core PR wave on go-ahead; the approver-member removal itself parks to the #705 breaking window.

issues.title: Core: minimize the token mission claim; make authority_hash and provenance opt-in
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P1 finding 7).

Finding: the mission claim carries authority_hash even though a narrowed-token RS cannot use it to prove inclusion (the core says so); it repeats across audiences and can correlate distinct Missions with identical Authority Sets (envelope binds issuer, not mission id); approval_basis.type is provenance, not enforcement input. Proposal: core claim = {mission: {id, issuer}}; authority_hash, effective expiry, and approval provenance become opt-in profile members; define complete-set retrieval plus subset checking or an inclusion proof where local verification is actually needed.

Analysis: agreed in direction; this session's architecture review reached the same consent-binding conclusion (the RECOMMENDED narrowed-token deployment cannot verify the anchor it carries). Two dependency checks before ruling: (1) offline attenuation carries authority_hash as a lineage anchor, and cross-domain/cross-org reference it: those uses must move to an opt-in member or their own carrying surface, not silently break; (2) mission_expires_at/expires_at mirroring (recently re-homed to core) interacts with "effective expiry opt-in": decide whether expiry stays core (it is enforcement input, unlike provenance).

Tradeoffs: smaller claim = less correlation surface and no anchor an RS cannot validate; the cost is that deployments wanting local set verification must adopt the retrieval/inclusion profile explicitly, which is honest about what the bare anchor never delivered.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `main` at `b4e35419`.

**Disposition: accept the minimal-claim direction, but specify the assurance profiles and migration before changing the wire.**

The baseline token claim should be exactly:

```json
{ "mission": { "id": "...", "issuer": "..." } }
```

That pair identifies the Mission. The token issuer's signature authenticates the claim and the carried `authorization_details` remains the token's concrete authority. `approval_basis.type` is explicitly non-authoritative provenance today ([claim definition](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L2937-L2971)), so it should leave the baseline token.

Removing `authority_hash` is also architecturally honest. The core already says an RS holding only a narrowed token cannot recompute it and gets no independent inclusion proof from it ([full-set verification rule](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L3097-L3106)); the consent-binding analysis repeats that it is only an audit/correlation reference for that RS. It is also not a Mission identity: distinct Missions approving the same set at one issuer can share the same hash ([anchor identity distinction](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission.md#L4590-L4599)).

The issue should not, however, define an “opt-in authority_hash member” without defining what security property the profile buys. Carrying the same bare digest by opt-in still proves no membership. Split the uses:

1. **Baseline Mission reference:** `{id, issuer}` only.
2. **Audit/approval commitment:** keep the Authority Set commitment on the Mission record and evidence/audit surfaces. Coordinate with #699 so the family does not invent competing token-carried roots.
3. **Local approved-set verification profile:** require either (a) authenticated retrieval of the complete committed Authority Set, recomputation of the commitment, and a subset check for the token entries, or (b) a typed selective-inclusion proof covering each carried entry. Define discovery, authorization to retrieve, freshness/version behavior, and fail-closed handling. The digest may accompany that proof, but is not the profile by itself.
4. **Offline lineage/audit profile:** if attenuation or a cross-domain artifact needs a stable commitment for offline audit, that profile owns the member and its verification rules. It must not call equality with an unverified digest an authorization check.
5. **Mission-expiry profile:** `mission.expires_at` can be optional outside the baseline. Every token still must be capped by effective Mission expiry at issuance. A consumer that only validates the current token uses token `exp`; a profile that performs downstream minting or offline lifetime verification must require the Mission expiry or obtain fresh Mission state. Absence where that profile is required is an error, not a silent downgrade.

The family sweep is larger than the issue currently suggests. Attenuation presently requires the same `(id, issuer, authority_hash)` at every hop and calls the hash a lineage anchor ([attenuation semantics](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-attenuation.md#L376-L401)); Cross-Domain carries it unchanged while acknowledging that downstream parties generally cannot recompute it ([cross-domain handling](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/b4e35419abc794b06afd3708ab851aee71670624/draft-mcguinness-oauth-mission-cross-domain.md#L745-L769)). Runtime and AuthZEN currently use it to bind a materialized policy view, and introspection reproduces it. Those uses must be classified as identity, corruption/mix-up detection, audit correlation, or full-set verification and replaced with the right mechanism rather than mechanically deleting a field.

Required migration inventory: core token and introspection schemas; grant-binding and token-response examples; Runtime/AuthZEN policy-view lookup; attenuation; Cross-Domain and Cross-Org; continuation; issuance grant; child/expansion; work-product/evidence schemas; discovery/metadata; code, vectors, and conformance rows. Add downgrade tests showing that a consumer claiming a named verification profile rejects a missing proof/member while a baseline consumer accepts `{id, issuer}` and enforces only the signed token authority.

This produces the right end state: **a small identity claim, commitments on the records they actually commit, and named verification profiles that provide real proofs.**

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-24): accepted as amended; the "opt-in authority_hash member" framing is withdrawn.**

The review's central correction is adopted: an opt-in bare digest still proves no membership, so the split is by security property, not by member presence. Ruling: baseline claim exactly {mission: {id, issuer}}; the Authority Set commitment stays on the record and evidence/audit surfaces (coordinated with #699 so no competing token-carried roots); a Local Approved-Set Verification profile requires authenticated complete-set retrieval + recomputation + subset check, or a typed selective-inclusion proof per carried entry, with discovery, retrieval authorization, freshness, and fail-closed behavior defined; the offline lineage/audit member is owned by the attenuation/cross-domain profile that needs it and never treats unverified digest equality as authorization; mission expiry becomes profile-scoped with absence-where-required an error, never a silent downgrade.

The migration inventory is adopted as the execution gate: every current authority_hash use (attenuation hop anchors, cross-domain carriage, Runtime/AuthZEN policy-view binding, introspection, evidence schemas, vectors, rows, code) gets classified as identity, mix-up detection, audit correlation, or full-set verification and re-mechanized accordingly; plus the downgrade tests (profile consumer rejects missing proof; baseline consumer enforces signed token authority only).

Retiered decide -> coordinated: one family migration cut, sequenced after the #700/#701 core-wave rulings land.

issues.title: Runtime: extract the OAuth Runtime Adapter; AuthZEN base plus feature profiles
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P1 finding 8); verified against main @ 59b958e5: runtime's normative family deps are the OAuth issuance profile, substrate, and status, while its substrate-neutrality claim stands; authzen normatively requires runtime-evidence; the base AuthZEN model (subject/resource/action/context, boolean decision) is buried under the full profile.

Proposed shape (one coordinated arc, not piecemeal):
1. Runtime Core: Mission reference, effective authority, active predicate, action, resource, parameters, permit conditions, failure posture: binding-neutral, no OAuth vocabulary.
2. OAuth Runtime Adapter (extracted): authorization_details/mission_resource_access consumption, JWT claims, act, introspection/status, protected-resource metadata.
3. AuthZEN Mission Profile restructured as a small base profile (evaluation + denial classification) plus selectable feature profiles: state snapshots, parameter binding/idempotency, ARAP, obligations, history, evidence, batch. Runtime-evidence becomes a feature-profile dependency, not an unconditional adoption gate: a PEP/PDP pair can interoperate on decisions before adopting the portable evidence schema.

Analysis: this is the natural stage B/C of the #238 arc (stage A, the Runtime Core regroup, merged as PR #681; the S5 normative-delta pass is still owed). The regroup fixed readability; this fixes the dependency boundary. Sequencing: rule here, then execute together with the #238 residuals so runtime.md is restructured once, not twice. Conformance impact is large (runtime 117 rows, authzen 78) and rows must move with their text.

Tradeoffs: two more documents against a substrate-neutrality claim that becomes true; adopters of "just OAuth runtime" read core+adapter instead of one file.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
Fresh review against `main` at `b4e35419`.

**Disposition: proceed as a coordinated restructuring, after revising the cut line and dependency model.**

The extraction is justified. Runtime currently claims a binding-neutral contract while normatively depending on the OAuth issuance profile and using OAuth token, RAR, introspection, and protected-resource metadata throughout. AuthZEN in turn normatively requires Runtime Evidence, so a deployment cannot claim even simple PEP/PDP decision interoperability without adopting the portable evidence package.

The important correction is that the proposed features are not all freely selectable. Some are prerequisites for a trustworthy remote decision, not optional adornments:

- authenticated, integrity-protected PEP/PDP communication is baseline whenever the boundary is remote;
- exact operation/resource/normalized-parameter binding is baseline whenever a decision can detach from the execution it authorizes; a co-resident implementation may satisfy this structurally, but cannot simply omit the property;
- current-state/freshness enforcement is required to claim Runtime-Enforced behavior, although the state mechanism and reliance window are deployment/profile choices;
- single-use/idempotency controls are conditionally required for non-idempotent or high-consequence operations, not a caller-selected cosmetic feature;
- portable runtime evidence can be optional for a decision-only interoperability profile, but must remain required for any named assurance/profile that promises portable decision or execution evidence.

Recommended document/dependency shape:

1. **Mission Runtime Core** — binding-neutral semantic contract: established Mission reference/controller, effective-authority source, active predicate and freshness bound, subject/actor, action/resource/normalized parameters, local-policy intersection, authenticated permit/deny, execution boundary, and fail-closed behavior. No OAuth claim or endpoint vocabulary.
2. **OAuth Runtime Adapter** — token validation, `mission` and `act`/`cnf`/`aud`, RAR/`authorization_details` mapping, introspection/status, protected-resource metadata, and OAuth registry work.
3. **Mission AuthZEN Decision Base** — the smallest mapping to AuthZEN subject/resource/action/context plus boolean decision and Mission denial classification. State inputs remain required when claiming Runtime-Enforced; do not make stale-state acceptance a selectable feature.
4. **AuthZEN Transaction Assurance** — canonical parameter/operation digest, decision-to-execution binding, replay/single-use/idempotency rules. Depend on the base; make applicability explicit by operation class.
5. **AuthZEN Runtime Evidence** — portable decision/refusal/execution evidence. Depend on the base and Runtime Evidence.
6. **Optional compositions** — Obligations, ARAP access requests, History, and Batch, each with explicit prerequisites. Obligations remain PEP-executed MUST/MAY directives; ARAP remains an out-of-band authority-changing workflow; neither belongs in the transaction-assurance lane.

Publish this as a dependency DAG and capability identifiers, not a profile per parameter. Selection must be issuer/deployment policy plus authenticated capability negotiation; a requester must not be able to omit a required feature to downgrade enforcement. Each named profile needs: prerequisites, producer/consumer roles, required request/response members, failure on absence, and the assurance claim it enables.

Sequence it with #238 rather than performing two semantic rewrites of Runtime: finish the binding-neutral Runtime Core relocation/normative audit, extract the OAuth adapter, then restructure AuthZEN. Move conformance rows with the clauses in the same PRs and add profile/capability attribution rather than overloading the existing `runtime-enforced` label. Current scope is substantial: Runtime has 117 ledger rows and AuthZEN 78, so this is an architecture migration, not an editorial split.

The success criterion is not “more documents.” It is that a non-OAuth binding can implement Runtime Core without importing OAuth semantics, an OAuth RS gets one exact adapter, and an AuthZEN adopter can name a small interoperable decision profile without silently losing the transaction and freshness properties its assurance claim depends on.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition (2026-08-24): proceed as amended; the freely-selectable-features framing is corrected.**

Adopted: the five-document shape (Runtime Core; OAuth Runtime Adapter; AuthZEN Decision Base; AuthZEN Transaction Assurance; AuthZEN Runtime Evidence; plus optional Obligations/ARAP/History/Batch compositions), published as a dependency DAG with capability identifiers, not a profile per parameter. The correction is the load-bearing part: channel authentication/integrity is baseline whenever the PEP/PDP boundary is remote; exact operation/resource/parameter binding is baseline wherever decision can detach from execution (co-resident implementations satisfy it structurally, never omit it); state freshness is required to claim Runtime-Enforced; single-use/idempotency is conditionally required by operation class; portable evidence is optional only for the decision-only interoperability profile. Selection is issuer/deployment policy plus authenticated capability negotiation: a requester can never omit a required feature to downgrade enforcement.

Sequencing adopted: one semantic rewrite, not two: finish the #238 Runtime Core normative audit, extract the OAuth adapter, then restructure AuthZEN, moving the 117+78 conformance rows with their clauses and adding profile/capability attribution rather than overloading runtime-enforced.

Label stays coordinated; the success criterion is recorded as the review states it: a non-OAuth binding implements Runtime Core without OAuth semantics, an OAuth RS gets one exact adapter, and a small AuthZEN decision profile exists that cannot silently shed the properties its assurance claim depends on.

issues.title: Family: standardization bundle composition (substrate timing, MAS classification)
issues.author: mcguinness
issues.body:
From the 2026-08-24 architecture-shape review (P1 finding 9). This one challenges deliberate rulings, so it is framed as trade-offs for an owner decision, not a recommendation to execute.

The review proposes: keep Architecture and Substrate informational until two independently implemented non-OAuth bindings demonstrate the kernel; reclassify MAS as a standalone-controller deployment profile of the OAuth model rather than a peer binding; keep AAuth as the real neutrality test; and lead standardization with the OAuth core (plus, separately, the RAR type) rather than an Architecture+Substrate+OAuth bundle.

Standing rulings this touches: the substrate's standalone-normative posture was deliberate (kernel adoptable outside the family, family bridge appendix, Bounded Reliance floor); MAS-as-peer was re-ruled this month via Mission Binding Properties (#237/#248, executed D115); the v0-preview bundle already ships substrate+core+floor with architecture as preface.

Honest assessment either way:
- For the review's position: MAS normatively imports the OAuth record, Authority Set, Status, Runtime, AuthZEN, and evidence: architecturally it IS the OAuth model on a different topology, and this session's own review reached the same three-tier reading (kernel; OAuth-schema cluster incl. MAS; native bindings). AAuth is the only binding proving kernel neutrality; UMA/GNAP carry the OAuth schema. Leading WG conversations with a 1,369-line normative kernel invites scope objections before the core is even read.
- Against: the substrate is what keeps bindings honest (Statements, ACC rule, checkers); demoting it to informational weakens the one contract with CI teeth. Renaming MAS contradicts a fresh ruling and the Binding Properties vector was built precisely so peer-ness is earned by properties, not lineage.

Middle path worth considering: keep substrate normative in-repo, but define the STANDARDIZATION unit as OAuth core (+ RAR type per #637), with substrate/architecture submitted as informational context: bundle composition is a publication decision, not a document-status decision.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
## Review — revise before ruling

The middle path is directionally right, but the issue currently misses the family’s most important layering defect and conflates document status, submission order, and binding taxonomy.

### P0 — The Substrate is not actually independent of OAuth today

The Substrate normatively references the OAuth core in its front matter, makes the family bridge normative, and normatively publishes the OAuth Mapping Assessment. AAuth then normatively depends on the Substrate. The resulting dependency chain is:

`AAuth → Substrate → OAuth Mission`

That undermines the claim that AAuth proves substrate neutrality. See the [Substrate dependency](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-substrate.md#L28-L41), [normative family appendix and OAuth assessment](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-substrate.md#L1177-L1229), and [AAuth’s normative Substrate dependency](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth.md#L29-L45).

Before deciding when to standardize the Substrate:

- Move the normative OAuth Mapping Assessment into the OAuth binding, or make it informative.
- Make the family vocabulary bridge informative.
- Ensure the Substrate’s normative references contain only substrate-neutral machinery.
- Give the Substrate its own neutral commitment test vectors instead of depending on OAuth vectors.

Making the Substrate Informational would not fix this dependency inversion.

### P1 — “Two implementations before Standards Track” is the wrong standards-process rationale

Implementation experience is desirable but normally not required for Proposed Standard. Two independent interoperable implementations with deployment experience are an advancement criterion for Internet Standard, not entry onto the Standards Track. See [RFC 2026 §4.1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2026.html#section-4.1.1) and [RFC 6410 §2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6410.html#section-2).

The project can still adopt an internal readiness gate based on independent implementation experience, but the issue should call it exactly that—not a reason the document must be Informational.

Recommended disposition:

- Architecture remains Informational.
- Substrate remains a Standards Track candidate in the repository because it defines normative conformance requirements.
- Substrate is omitted from the initial OAuth WG package until the dependency inversion above is removed and non-OAuth implementation feedback exists.

If Substrate were published Informational while AAuth remained Standards Track, that would create a downref. Downrefs are possible, but they carry maturity and review considerations. See [RFC 8067](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8067.html).

### P1 — MAS needs a two-axis classification, not a binary “peer versus deployment profile” ruling

MAS clearly does not demonstrate an independent authorization model: it normatively imports the OAuth Mission record and numerous OAuth-family profiles, and explicitly implements the Mission Issuer role from the OAuth issuance profile. See [MAS model inheritance](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server.md#L260-L298).

But MAS is more than deployment guidance. It defines endpoints, an HTTP field, a well-known URI, media types, and registries. See [MAS IANA surfaces](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-authority-server.md#L2404-L2457).

The accurate description is:

> MAS is a normative standalone-controller protocol binding over the OAuth Mission data model. It is a peer deployment topology, but not an independent substrate model.

That does not contradict D115. The Binding Properties vector expressly separates attachment, credential, and action binding from protocol lineage. See [Binding Properties](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md#L2653-L2685). What should change is the architecture’s blanket statement that all bindings are peers, which currently collapses these two axes. See the [current peer claim](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/draft-mcguinness-mission-architecture.md#L388-L394).

### P1 — “OAuth core plus, separately, the RAR type” is not yet an executable package

[#637](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/issues/637) explicitly leaves the `mission_resource_access` split deferred. Today the core still contains and mandates that type.

Issue #704 must choose a sequence:

- Lead with the current monolithic OAuth core; or
- Trigger #637/#207 first, perform the relocation, and then present core and the RAR profile separately.

It should not record a standardization unit that does not yet exist.

### P2 — The preview bundle is not a precedent constraining WG submission

The preview already says it is an implementation guide, not another Internet-Draft, and distinguishes its seven-document reader union from the one-document Issuance Baseline. See the [bundle definition and profiles](https://github.com/mcguinness/mission-bound-authorization/blob/59b958e566443ca8e0fc68e6f263414b6dfa191f/notes/oauth-mission-baseline-bundle-preview.md#L3-L34).

The issue should distinguish three products:

| Product | Recommended composition |
|---|---|
| Initial WG conversation | OAuth core; separate RAR profile only after #637 |
| Normative dependency closure | Whatever each selected specification actually imports |
| Implementation reader bundle | Architecture preface plus Substrate and runtime floor, as appropriate |

The preview can remain unchanged even if the WG conversation starts with the core.

### Recommended ruling text

> Adopt the middle path with corrections. Lead initial standardization conversations with the OAuth Mission core. If #637 is executed first, present `mission_resource_access` as a separate RAR profile; otherwise disclose that it remains part of the core. Architecture remains Informational context. Substrate remains a Standards Track candidate in-repository but is not part of the initial OAuth package; before separate submission, remove its normative dependency on the OAuth binding and obtain independent non-OAuth implementation feedback. Classify MAS as a normative standalone-controller binding over the OAuth Mission model: a peer deployment topology, not evidence of substrate independence. The implementation preview bundle remains a separate publication artifact.

This resolves the architectural question without undoing the Binding Properties work or confusing implementation maturity with RFC category.

comments.author: mcguinness
comments.body:
**Session disposition on the review (2026-08-24; claims verified against main @ 59b958e5):**

**P0 confirmed, and it is a regression.** The substrate's front matter now normatively references the OAuth core, the family appendix declares itself normative, and the OAuth Mapping Assessment is hosted in the substrate; AAuth normatively depends on the substrate. The chain AAuth -> Substrate -> OAuth Mission exists at HEAD. At the 2026-08-22 baseline the substrate's normative references were crypto/canonicalization RFCs only; the hosted-Statement rounds (D129-D131) introduced the edge. The prerequisite fix is filed as its own coordinated issue: #708 (assessment placement, bridge tier, front-matter re-tier, neutral vectors), gated on this ruling's adoption.
